title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
會試錄序
皇上嗣登寶位之六載是為正德
辛未舉會試之典一又再矣
及是試期伊邇適臣忠以病
在告累疏請謝政
上既賜旨諭留即日復
命臣暨學士臣費為考試官其同
===
考試則侍講臣一鵬修撰臣
文叙編修臣廷相臣仁和臣
永臣玘臣銑臣若水臣鑾臣
縉檢討臣孔暉給事中臣卿
臣磐臣瀚主事臣䋲臣元吉
臣守仁監試則御史臣秉倫
臣茂達凡諸執事亦皆慎柬

會試錄序

皇上嗣登寶位之六載，是為正德辛未，舉會試之典一又再矣。及是試期伊邇，適臣忠以病在告，累疏請謝政。上既賜旨諭留，即日復命臣暨學士臣費為考試官。其同考試則侍講臣一鵬、修撰臣文叙、編修臣廷相、臣仁和、臣永、臣玘、臣銑、臣若水、臣鑾、臣縉、檢討臣孔暉、給事中臣卿、臣磐、臣瀚、主事臣䋲、臣元吉、臣守仁。監試則御史臣秉倫、臣茂達。凡諸執事亦皆慎柬
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the sixth year since His Majesty succeeded to the imperial throne, the xinwei year of the Zhengde reign [1511], the Metropolitan Examination had been held once and now was being held a second time. As the examination drew near, I, your servant Zhong, happened to be on sick leave and repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement from government service. His Majesty issued an edict instructing me to remain in office and, that same day, further appointed me and your servant Fei, Academician, as Examiners.

The Associate Examiners were your servants Yipeng, Hanlin Reader-in-Waiting; Wenxu, Hanlin Senior Compiler; Tingxiang, Renhe, Yong, Qi, Xian, Ruoshui, Luan, and Jin, Hanlin Junior Compilers; Konghui, Hanlin Assistant Compiler; Qing, Pan, and Han, Supervising Secretaries; and Sheng, Yuanji, and Shouren, Bureau Secretaries. Those overseeing the examination were your servants Binglun and Maoda, Investigating Censors. All the other functionaries were likewise carefully selected…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
以往舊制同考合五經分房
為十四人近以易詩書卷浩
繁各增官一試院廨宇少加
增創試事條格少加增置綜
理防範視往歲加詳密凡此
皆禮部尚書臣宏侍郎臣紀
臣遜學先事具請而奉行者
也會試士以期集者合新舊
三千五百有竒所取僅三百
五十亦宏等臨事具請而臣
等所遵行者也至於精白公
慎務期得才少罄以人事君
之意此則臣等之責亦臣等
之心以求無負於

臣遜學先事具請而奉行者
===
也會試士以期集者合新舊
三千五百有奇所取僅三百
五十亦宏等臨事具請而臣
等所遵行者也至於精白公
慎務期得才少錖以人事君
之意此則臣等之責亦臣等
之心以求無負於
punctuated: 以往。舊制，同考合五經分房，為十四人。近以易、詩、書卷浩繁，各增官一。試院廨宇少加增創，試事條格少加增置，綜理防範視往歲加詳密。凡此，皆禮部尚書臣宏、侍郎臣紀、臣遜學先事具請而奉行者也。會試士以期集者，合新舊三千五百有竒，所取僅三百五十，亦宏等臨事具請而臣等所遵行者也。至於精白公慎，務期得才，少罄以人事君之意，此則臣等之責，亦臣等之心，以求無負於
translation_en:
…to undertake their duties. Under the old regulations, fourteen Associate Examiners were assigned to separate sections for the Five Classics. Recently, because of the great volume of examination papers on the Book of Changes, Book of Odes, and Book of Documents, one additional official was appointed for each. The examination compound’s official premises were modestly expanded, and some additions were made to the examination regulations. Overall administration and precautions were more detailed and thorough than in previous years. All these measures were proposed in advance by your servants Hong, Minister of Rites, and Ji and Xunxue, Vice Ministers, and implemented upon approval.

The candidates who assembled by the appointed date for the Metropolitan Examination, including both new and earlier provincial graduates, numbered somewhat over 3,500; only 350 were to be selected. This number, too, was requested by Hong and the others when the matter arose, and we, your servants, acted accordingly. As for maintaining purity of purpose, impartiality, and care, striving to obtain talented men, and thereby fulfilling in some measure our intention to serve our sovereign by finding worthy men: this is our responsibility and also our heartfelt desire, that we may not fail to live up to…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
明命而愧厥職者也錄成將以
陛見之日上
獻臣當有言序諸首竊念臣往
歲承乏南省甞於職事之餘
恭訪我
聖祖興王之迹凡江山偉觀都邑
勝跡時出一登覽之而見所
===
謂禮賢館者詢諸父老則曰
此
聖祖甫入建康首徵青田劉基輩
與之論經史詢治道而為之
建設以居者也臣乃仰而歎
曰卓哉
帝王之見方渡江之初顧何時哉

明命而愧厥職者也錄成將以
陛見之日上
獻臣當有言序諸首竊念臣往
歲承乏南省嘗於職事之餘
恭訪我
聖祖興王之迹凡江山偉觀都邑
勝跡時出一登覽之而見所
謂禮賢館者詢諸父老則曰
===
此
聖祖甫入建康首徵青田劉基輩
與之論經史詢治道而爲之
建設以居者也臣乃仰而歎
曰卓哉
帝王之見方渡江之初顧何時哉
punctuated: 明命而愧厥職者也。錄成，將以陛見之日上獻，臣當有言序諸首。竊念臣往歲承乏南省，甞於職事之餘恭訪我聖祖興王之迹。凡江山偉觀、都邑勝跡，時出一登覽之，而見所謂禮賢館者。詢諸父老，則曰：「此聖祖甫入建康，首徵青田劉基輩，與之論經史，詢治道，而為之建設以居者也。」臣乃仰而歎曰：「卓哉，帝王之見！方渡江之初，顧何時哉！
translation_en: …the illustrious command, and bring shame upon my office. Now that the record is complete, it will be presented to Your Majesty on the day of our audience. I should therefore offer some words as a preface at its beginning. I recall that in former years, when I served, for want of someone better, in the southern capital, I respectfully sought out, in the intervals between my official duties, traces of our Sagely Founder's rise to imperial power. From time to time I went out to climb to and survey the magnificent river and mountain vistas and the celebrated sites of the city. In this way I came upon what is called the Hall for Honoring Worthies. When I asked the local elders about it, they said: “When the Sagely Founder first entered Jiankang, he summoned Liu Ji of Qingtian and others before all else, discussed the classics and histories with them, and consulted them on the way of governing. This was the hall he built to house them.” Looking up in admiration, I sighed and said: “How outstanding was the sovereign's vision! Consider what a time it was, when he had only just crossed the Yangzi! …

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
即以崇儒右文談經訪治為
首政而斯文一脉不絕如綫
者賴之以復續所以正士習
敦民風以綿億萬載文明之
治其兆於是乎有在是即求
懿德肆時夏之心而所謂投
戈講藝又有不足言者矣
===
列聖紹述以及
今日百四十餘年于兹仰承
佑啓循用彌篤自國都以及里
巷一皆有學自句讀以及講
授一皆有師自日試月程以
及歲校一皆有規而士以縫
掖遊庠校有不談王道者雖

即以崇儒右文談經訪治爲

敦民風以緜億萬載文明之

懿德肆時夏之心而所謂投
戈講藝又有不足言者矣
===
列聖紹述以及
今日百四十二年餘于茲仰承
佑啓循用彌篤自國都以及里
巷一皆有學自句讀以及講
授一皆有師自日試月程以
及歲校一皆有規而士以縫
掖遊庠校有不談王道者雖
punctuated:
即以崇儒右文、談經訪治為首政，而斯文一脉不絕如綫者，賴之以復續。所以正士習、敦民風，以綿億萬載文明之治，其兆於是乎有在。是即求懿德、肆時夏之心，而所謂投戈講藝，又有不足言者矣。

列聖紹述，以及今日，百四十餘年于兹，仰承佑啓，循用彌篤。自國都以及里巷，一皆有學；自句讀以及講授，一皆有師；自日試月程以及歲校，一皆有規。而士以縫掖遊庠校，有不談王道者，雖
translation_en:
…he immediately made honoring Confucian learning, esteeming literary culture, discussing the classics, and inquiring into governance his foremost tasks. This cultural tradition, whose surviving thread was as tenuous as a filament, depended on him for its renewal. Here lay the beginnings of the means to rectify scholars’ habits, enrich the people’s customs, and perpetuate enlightened rule for countless ages. This was precisely the intention to seek excellent virtue and extend it throughout the central lands; beside it, even the celebrated act of laying aside weapons to discuss the arts of learning scarcely merits mention.

The successive sage emperors carried on his work down to the present day, for more than a hundred and forty years. Reverently receiving his protection and guidance, they have followed his example with ever greater devotion. From the imperial capital to the lanes and alleys, everywhere there are schools; from instruction in distinguishing phrases and sentences to lectures and teaching, every stage has its teachers; from daily tests and monthly assignments to annual examinations, every practice has its regulations. Scholars in their broad-sleeved robes frequent the schools; if any among them fail to discuss the Way of the Kings, even…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
市人亦得過而笑之肆今士
挾藝而来者雖風簷寸晷之
下畧見展布而英鋭之詞昌
大之氣高邁之識使人為之
駭心眩目而健羨不置文之
盛其有徵於
今日者固如是哉頃者
===
皇上大奮乾斷討僭叛鋤姦萌正
糾繆釐訛之令一時紀綱法
度士習民風煥然一出於新
不啻雲漢星日障翳於重陰
久噎之餘一旦披露抉裂而
萬類得於仰瞻者欣欣然舉
有生氣自非有文為之經緯

皇上大奮乾斷討僭叛鋤姦萌正
紏繆釐訛之令一時紀綱法
度士習民風煥然一出於新
不啻雲漢星日障翳於重陰
久曀之餘一旦披露抉裂而
萬類得於仰瞻者欣欣然舉
有生氣自非有文爲之經緯
punctuated: 市人亦得過而笑之。肆今士挾藝而来者，雖風簷寸晷之下畧見展布，而英鋭之詞、昌大之氣、高邁之識，使人為之駭心眩目，而健羨不置。文之盛，其有徵於今日者，固如是哉！頃者，皇上大奮乾斷，討僭叛，鋤姦萌，正糾繆釐訛之令。一時紀綱法度、士習民風，煥然一出於新。不啻雲漢星日障翳於重陰久噎之餘，一旦披露抉裂，而萬類得於仰瞻者，欣欣然舉有生氣。自非有文為之經緯，
translation_en:
…even people in the marketplace may reproach and laugh at him. Thus, the scholars who now come bearing their literary accomplishments, though they display them only briefly beneath the wind-swept eaves in the scant time allotted, possess brilliant, incisive language, a grand and flourishing spirit, and lofty discernment. These astonish the heart and dazzle the eyes, inspiring unceasing admiration. Such indeed is the evidence in our own day of the flourishing of literary culture!

Recently, His Majesty vigorously exercised his sovereign resolve, punished usurpers and rebels, rooted out the beginnings of treachery, and set right the ordinances for correcting errors and rectifying falsehoods [?]. At once, the principles of government and its laws, the habits of scholars and the customs of the people, all shone with renewed freshness. It was as though the Milky Way, the stars, and the sun, long obscured and stifled by dense clouds, were suddenly revealed as the darkness was rent apart; all living things able to gaze upward rejoiced, filled with vitality. Had literary culture not provided the warp and weft of this ordering, …

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
何以及此則我
聖祖崇儒之澤
列聖及
皇上用文之效不於是益有徵哉
文之盛誠至矣雖然臣於是
又不能無懼焉盖質本也文
末也文盛質衰而不知以道
損益以即乎中則其流也為
浮靡之習華藻之飾而所言
所行皆為無本而不足觀矣
以是形諸民風為偷薄為陵
踰形諸士習為諛佞為憸邪
形諸政議為頗僻為瑣屑將
使天下國家于何所賴焉文
alt_text:
何以及此則我
聖祖崇儒之澤
列聖及
皇上用文之效不於是益有徵哉
文之盛誠至矣雖然〔臣〕於是
又不能無懼焉蓋質本也文
末也文盛質衰而不知以道
===
損益以即乎中則其流也爲
浮靡之習華藻之飾而所言
所行皆爲無本而不足觀矣
以是形諸民風爲偷薄爲陵
踰形諸士習爲訑倿爲憸邪
形諸政議爲煩僻爲瑣屑將
使天下國家于何所賴焉文
punctuated: 何以及此？則我聖祖崇儒之澤、列聖及皇上用文之效，不於是益有徵哉？文之盛誠至矣！雖然，臣於是又不能無懼焉。盖質本也，文末也。文盛質衰，而不知以道損益，以即乎中，則其流也為浮靡之習、華藻之飾，而所言所行皆為無本而不足觀矣。以是形諸民風，為偷薄，為陵踰；形諸士習，為諛佞，為憸邪；形諸政議，為頗僻，為瑣屑。將使天下國家于何所賴焉？文
translation_en: …how could matters have reached this point? Is this not further proof of the beneficent legacy of our Sagely Progenitor’s esteem for Confucian learning, and of the efficacy with which the successive sage emperors and Your Majesty have employed literary culture? Literary culture has indeed reached the height of flourishing! Even so, your servant cannot but feel apprehension here. Substance is the root; literary refinement is the branch. If refinement flourishes while substance declines, and one does not know how to reduce or augment them in accordance with the Way so as to attain the mean, the result will be habits of superficial extravagance and ornate embellishment. What people say and do will then lack any foundation and be unworthy of regard. Manifested in popular customs, this becomes moral laxity and transgression of proper bounds; manifested in the habits of scholars, flattery and deceitful wickedness; manifested in deliberations on government, bias and triviality. On what, then, will All Under Heaven and the state be able to rely? Literary culture…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
之盛而至於不足為世賴則
何以文為哉我
國家右文及
今日以文取士之意果如是哉
忠與爾諸士皆以文進者盍
相與求其本而謹之
光祿大夫柱國少傅兼太
===
子太傅吏部尚書
武英殿大學士劉忠謹序

光祿大夫柱國少傅兼太
子太傅吏部尚書
武英殿大學士劉忠謹序
punctuated:
之盛而至於不足為世賴，則何以文為哉？我國家右文，及今日以文取士之意，果如是哉？忠與爾諸士皆以文進者，盍相與求其本而謹之？

光祿大夫柱國少傅兼太子太傅吏部尚書武英殿大學士劉忠謹序。
translation_en:
…if literary refinement flourishes yet reaches the point where the world can no longer rely upon it, what use is it? Our dynasty honors literary cultivation; can this truly be its intention in selecting men through literary accomplishment down to the present day? I, Zhong, and all you gentlemen have advanced through literary accomplishment. Why should we not together seek its foundation and carefully attend to it?

Preface respectfully composed by Liu Zhong, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Mentor and concurrently Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Personnel, and Grand Secretary of the Hall of Military Glory.

Metropolitan Examination of the Sixth Year of Zhengde (1511).

Directors of the Examination:
Fei Hong, Grand Master for Aid in Governance and Minister of Rites, had the courtesy name Zichong and was from Yanshan County, Jiangxi. He became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the dingwei year (1487).
Mao Ji, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Rites, had the courtesy name Weizhi and was from Ye County, Shandong. He became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1487).

Examiners:
Liu Zhong, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Mentor and concurrently Grand Mentor of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Personnel, and Grand Secretary of the Hall of Military Glory, had the courtesy name Sizhi and was from Chenliu County, Henan. He became a metropolitan graduate in the wuxu year (1478).
Jin Gui, in charge of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, Left Vice Minister of Personnel and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Chongdao and was from Dantu County in the directly administered metropolitan region. He became a metropolitan graduate in the gengxu year (1490).

Associate Examiners:
Wu Yipeng, Expositor of the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Nanfu and was from Changzhou County in the directly administered metropolitan region. He became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1493).
Lun Wenxu, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Scholarly Service, had the courtesy name Bochou and was from Nanhai County, Guangdong. He became a metropolitan graduate in the jiwei year (1499).
Li Tingxiang, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service, had the courtesy name Mengbi and was from Pu Subprefecture, Shandong. He became a metropolitan graduate in the renxu year (1502).
Wen Renhe, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service, had the courtesy name Minhuai and was from Huayang County, Sichuan. He became a metropolitan graduate in the renxu year (1502).
Zhao Yong, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service, had the courtesy name Erxi and was from Linhuai County in the directly administered metropolitan region. He became a metropolitan graduate in the renxu year (1502).
Dong Qi, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service, had the courtesy name Wenyu and was from Kuaiji County, Zhejiang. He became a metropolitan graduate in the yichou year (1505).
Cui Xian, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service, had the courtesy name Zizhong and was from Anyang County, Henan. He became a metropolitan graduate in the yichou year (1505).
Zhan Ruoshui, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service, had the courtesy name Yuanming and was from Zengcheng County, Guangdong. He became a metropolitan graduate in the yichou year (1505).
Zhai Luan, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service, had the courtesy name Zhongming and was registered with the Embroidered-uniform Guard. He became a metropolitan graduate in the yichou year (1505).
Xu Jin, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service, had the courtesy name Zirong and was from Wu County in the directly administered metropolitan region. He became a metropolitan graduate in the yichou year (1505).

第壹場

四書
「如切如磋」者，道學也；「如琢如磨」者，自脩也。
德行：顔淵、閔子騫、冉伯牛、仲弓。言語：宰我、子貢。政事：冉有、季路。文學：子游、子夏。
是集義所生者，非義襲而取之也。行有不慊於心，則餒矣。

易
火在天上，大有；君子以遏惡揚善，順天休命。
上九，白賁，无咎。
夫坤，其靜也翕，其動也闢，是以廣生焉。
和順於道德，而理於義。

書
協和萬邦，黎民於變時雍。
奉先思孝，接下思恭，視遠惟明，聽德惟聰。
曰其稽我古人之德，矧曰其有能稽謀自天。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“Like cutting and filing” refers to learning; “like chiseling and polishing” refers to cultivating oneself.

In virtuous conduct: Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Boniu, and Zhonggong. In speech: Zai Wo and Zigong. In government affairs: Ran You and Jilu. In literary learning: Ziyou and Zixia.

It is generated by the accumulation of righteous deeds; it cannot be obtained by a sudden act of righteousness. If one’s conduct leaves the heart dissatisfied, it becomes starved.

Book of Changes

Fire above heaven: Great Possession. The noble man accordingly restrains evil and promotes good, complying with Heaven’s beneficent mandate.

Nine at the top: plain white adornment. No blame.

Kun, the Receptive, is closed when still and opens when moving; thus it brings forth life abundantly.

In harmony and accord with the Way and virtue, and ordered according to righteousness.

Book of Documents

He brought the myriad states into concord, and the common people were thereby transformed and became harmonious.

In serving your ancestors, think of filial piety; in dealing with those below, think of respect. In looking afar, seek clarity; in listening to virtue, seek discernment.

Say that he examines the virtue of our men of antiquity; how much more, then, that he is able to seek counsel from Heaven.

遡洄從之，道阻且長；遡游從之，宛在水中央。
經始靈臺，經之營之，庶民攻之，不日成之。經始勿亟，庶民子來。
日就月將，學有緝熙于光明。
天命降監，下民有嚴。不僭不濫，不敢怠遑。

冬，公如晉〔文公十三年〕。春，王正月，公至自晉〔文公十四年〕。
十有一月，公如楚〔襄公二十八年〕。春，王正月，公在楚〔襄公二十九年〕。

季孫意如、叔弓、仲孫貜帥師伐莒〔昭公十〕
translation_en:
Whenever people have not yet seen a sage, they seem anxious lest they never see one; once they have seen a sage, they still cannot follow him. Be warned! You are the wind; the common people are the grass.

Book of Odes
I follow upstream in search of that person: the way is difficult and long. I follow downstream in search: there that person seems to be, in the middle of the water.
They began laying out the Spirit Terrace, measuring and planning it. The common people worked upon it and completed it in less than a day. When beginning the work, he told them not to hurry; the common people came like children to their parent.
Day by day he achieved more; month by month he advanced. Through learning, he continually increased his brilliance until he attained illumination.
Heaven looks down in its majesty; the common people stand in awe. With neither excess nor indiscriminate action, he dares not be idle or seek leisure.

Spring and Autumn Annals
The duke paid court at the king’s residence〔twenty-eighth year of Duke Xi〕. The duke went to the royal capital〔thirteenth year of Duke Cheng〕.
In winter, the duke went to Jin〔thirteenth year of Duke Wen〕. In spring, in the first month of the king’s calendar, the duke returned from Jin〔fourteenth year of Duke Wen〕.
In the eleventh month, the duke went to Chu〔twenty-eighth year of Duke Xiang〕. In spring, in the first month of the king’s calendar, the duke was in Chu〔twenty-ninth year of Duke Xiang〕.
The Earl of Shan returned from Qi〔fifteenth year of Duke Wen〕. Shusun Chuo returned from Jin〔twenty-fourth year of Duke Zhao〕.
Shu Gong led an army to demarcate the fields of Yun〔first year of Duke Zhao〕. The Central Army was disbanded〔fifth year of Duke Zhao〕.
Jisun Yiru, Shu Gong, and Zhongsun Jue led an army to attack Ju〔Duke Zhao, tenth …〕

translation_en:
…Tang and Wen? Reverently considering our Emperor Taizu Gao: while he remained a hidden dragon in the Huai region, although endowed with imperial virtue, he possessed virtually none of the resources of the two emperors. The times he encountered were exceedingly difficult, and exerting his strength was exceedingly hard. Yet with one sweep of his heavenly spear, the rival warlords surrendered their heads. He swept away more than ninety years of rank and foul rule and suppressed thirteen generations of usurpation. He cleared Heaven and Earth of darkness and restored the cardinal bonds and constant norms of human relationships from their fallen state. His achievement in winning All under Heaven surely tallies with those of the two emperors, though they lived in different ages. Could it be that true emperors and kings possess an inherent quality and need not rely upon territory and people as their resources? Or, beyond their achievements and virtue, is there some other Way that provides their foundation? Please set forth all these matters in your essay. Your views will be conveyed to His Majesty to assist him in preserving the inherited achievement.

Question: After the Three Dynasties, those that enjoyed long possession of the realm were the Han, Tang, and Song. Although their founding achievements and the traditions they bequeathed were not entirely alike, the institutions established by each dynasty sufficed to receive Heaven’s Mandate and secure the people’s allegiance. Why, then, did further changes under Emperors Zhao and Xuan produce competent officials and a populace at peace? text:

坤之功其間名臣論議亦各不同若賈
誼董仲舒余靖宋綬之徒皆嘗有更制
之請而如魏相霍光司馬光呂公著則
固以守法為賢者果孰為得歟抑各有
所見歟若唐則其法每變而治每下似
與二代異豈仁義之治創立者獨詳歟
其後陸贄李泌乃不滿于當時之稅法
兵制者抑又何歟仰惟我
===
皇祖以聖神之德掃胡元之亂奉天明命肇造
寰宇凡帝王善政史傳所稱載者無不
斟酌時宜著為令典大綱正萬目舉盖
集帝王之大成而自古所未有也又何
漢唐宋之足儗邪
列聖相承嗣守洪業重熈累洽今百餘年治久
而弊乗之亦勢所不容無者我
皇上天錫勇智洞燭弊源比奮乾斷以新泰道
明詔中外百司凡政令奉行有少異其

…the realm became beset with troubles. Why, then, did another change during the Yuanyou era achieve the feat of turning Heaven and Earth around? The deliberations of eminent ministers in these periods likewise differed. Which were actually right? Or did each have his own insight? As for the Tang, each change in its laws brought a further decline in governance, seemingly unlike the other two dynasties. Could it be that those who founded its government of benevolence and righteousness alone made thorough provisions? Why, then, were Lu Zhi and Li Bi later dissatisfied with the tax laws and military institutions of their time?

Of all the good policies of emperors and kings praised and recorded in historical writings, there were none that he did not weigh against the needs of the times and embody in authoritative statutes. The main guiding principles were set right, and all their myriad particulars put into effect. 否歟虞廷惟精惟一之訓程門主敬致
知之說韓歐終身之所見豈嘗有及於
是而知所從事歟不然蘇子之說非矣
此道統所在諸士子雅所究心者其毋
諉曰不暇
問古之為政者必本之以仁義而輔之以
寬猛豈不以仁義乃出治之本而寬猛
實濟時之具者乎嘗稽諸往牒而亦有

齊魯者乎後世如漢文帝以寬厚長者

…Mengzi: was this relationship likewise comparable to that of Mengzi to Confucius, with a true grasp of the essential meaning of what was transmitted and received? The instruction at the court of Shun to be discerning and single-minded, and the teaching of the Cheng school to maintain reverence and extend knowledge—did the understanding attained by Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu throughout their lives ever reach this level, so that they knew where to direct their efforts? If not, Master Su’s assertion was mistaken. Where this succession in the transmission of the Way lies is a matter to which you candidates have long devoted careful thought. Do not plead that you have had no time to investigate it.

Question: Those who governed in antiquity invariably took benevolence and righteousness as their foundation and supplemented them with leniency and severity. Was this not because benevolence and righteousness are the foundation of good government, while leniency and severity are the means of meeting the needs of the times? Yet examination of historical records reveals matters that invite doubt. By honoring those worthy of honor and cherishing kin, Zhou Gong’s government of Lu was benevolent; yet in later generations there arose the troubling prospect of laxity and gradual decline. By promoting the worthy and esteeming achievement, Tai Gong’s government of Qi was righteous; yet in later generations there arose the calamities of oppressive urgency and struggles for power. Benevolence and righteousness had both been practiced effectively under the Three Dynasties, yet when Qi and Lu practiced them, neither escaped harmful consequences. Could government through benevolence and righteousness have been suitable only for the Three Dynasties, but unsuitable for Qi and Lu? In later times, Emperor Wen of Han, a generous and magnanimous elder, devoted himself to transforming the people through virtue. His government was also benevolent. Why, then, do we hear of no failings arising from indolence and neglected affairs? Emperor Xuan comprehensively scrutinized names and actual performance, and faithfully…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
賞必罰其政亦義也何以不聞其有督
責已甚之失豈文宣之賢有過於周公
太公者乎洪惟我
祖宗以仁義創鴻基以寬猛保盛治陽施陰斂
秋肅春温期與海內涵養安寧於仁壽
之域振刷掃滌其因循之弊其視漢之
治盖已超越而邁逺矣何殷富之風未
盡形奉職之吏未盡聞乎兹欲民安於
殷富吏奉其職業上有仁義之政下有
===
仁義之風以追邁三代之盛治必何如
而後可
問天下太平治之極也而君子有憂焉怠
荒之戒盖拳拳而不容已觀之虞廷則
可見矣後之名臣何莫不然故有當漢
文之時而進治安策者有當晋武之世
而著徙戎論者有當仁義既效之後而
陳十漸以規之者有當勵精政事之初
而舉十事以要之者有志切先憂而條

問：天下太平，治之極也，而君子有憂焉。怠荒之戒，盖拳拳而不容已，觀之虞廷則可見矣。後之名臣，何莫不然？故有當漢文之時而進治安策者，有當晋武之世而著徙戎論者，有當仁義既效之後而陳十漸以規之者，有當勵精政事之初而舉十事以要之者，有志切先憂而條
translation_en:
…rewards and invariably imposed punishments; his government, too, embodied righteousness. Why, then, do we not hear of his having erred through excessive demands and harsh supervision? Could the worthiness of Emperors Wen and Xuan have surpassed that of the Duke of Zhou and Taigong?

We reverently consider how our dynastic ancestors founded their great enterprise upon benevolence and righteousness and preserved flourishing government through leniency and severity. They bestowed like yang and restrained like yin, stern as autumn and warm as spring. Their aim was to nurture peace throughout the realm, bringing all into a domain of benevolence and longevity, while vigorously sweeping away the abuses of complacent adherence to old ways. Compared with Han government, theirs has surely surpassed it by far. Why, then, have conditions of prosperity not yet fully emerged, and why are officials who fulfill their duties not yet universally reported? If we now wish the people to enjoy settled prosperity and officials to discharge their duties, with benevolent and righteous government above and benevolent and righteous customs below, so as to emulate and surpass the flourishing government of the Three Dynasties, what must be done to achieve this?

Question: Peace throughout the world is the highest achievement of government, yet the gentleman still finds cause for concern. His warnings against indolence and neglect are earnest and unceasing, as can be seen by observing the court of Yu. Which of the celebrated ministers of later ages was not likewise concerned? Thus, there was one who presented a Policy Essay on Good Government and Security during the reign of Emperor Wen of Han; one who wrote a Discourse on Relocating the Rong during the reign of Emperor Wu of Jin; one who, after benevolence and righteousness had already proved effective, set forth ten gradually developing dangers as an admonition; and one who, at the beginning of an energetic effort to govern, raised ten matters as essential requirements. There was also one whose resolve to be the first to worry was so earnest that he itemized…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
十事以答天章之問者有明炳先見而
䟽十事以沮元豐之相者其言雖殊其
為保治計一也然則政固有異道邪將
亦各因其所急而圖之邪使當時盡用
其言果有益于其治否邪我
國家海內寧謐四夷賓服太平無事乆矣時
之所急其亦有可憂者邪夫守令所以
安民生而民生則有由之以病者若之
何使人有恒心而潢池無弄兵之警樂
===
歲有擊壤之歌邪學校所以育人才而
人才亦有由之以壞者若之何使學有
成效德立而無奔競之風才充而有經
濟之實邪今之可憂者盖不止此而此
其急也諸士子皆心古人之心者其具
以實言毋讓

===
歲有擊壤之歌邪學校所以育人才而
人才亦有由之以壞者若之何使學有
成效德立而無奔競之風才充而有經
濟之實邪今之可憂者蓋不止此而此
其急也諸士子皆心古人之心者其具
以質言毋讓
punctuated: 十事以答天章之問者，有明炳先見而䟽十事以沮元豐之相者。其言雖殊，其為保治計一也。然則政固有異道邪？將亦各因其所急而圖之邪？使當時盡用其言，果有益于其治否邪？我國家海內寧謐，四夷賓服，太平無事乆矣。時之所急，其亦有可憂者邪？夫守令所以安民生，而民生則有由之以病者，若之何使人有恒心，而潢池無弄兵之警，樂歲有擊壤之歌邪？學校所以育人才，而人才亦有由之以壞者，若之何使學有成效，德立而無奔競之風，才充而有經濟之實邪？今之可憂者盖不止此，而此其急也。諸士子皆心古人之心者，其具以實言，毋讓。
translation_en:
…ten matters in answer to the questions posed in the Tianzhang Pavilion; and there was one whose lucid foresight led him to submit a memorial on ten matters opposing the chief councilor of the Yuanfeng era. Though their words differed, their purpose in planning to preserve good government was one. Does government, then, truly admit of different approaches? Or did each devise his proposals according to the most urgent needs of his time? Had their words been fully put into practice at the time, would they indeed have benefited the government?

Within our realm all is tranquil, and the peoples of the four quarters submit as guests. Peace has long prevailed without disturbance. Among the urgent concerns of the present, are there nevertheless grounds for anxiety? Prefects and county magistrates are meant to secure the people's livelihood, yet they can also cause it harm. How can we ensure that the people maintain steadfast hearts, that there are no alarms of armed unrest even in the smallest pools, and that in years of plenty they sing songs while playing at striking the ground, celebrating peaceful contentment? Schools are meant to nurture talent, yet they can also cause its corruption. How can we ensure that learning produces results, that virtue is established without the habit of scrambling for advancement, and that abilities are fully developed with genuine capacity to order the realm and aid its people?

The concerns of the present surely extend beyond these, but these are the urgent ones. All you candidates share the aspirations of the ancients. Set forth your views fully and truthfully, without holding back.

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“‘As if cut, as if filed’ refers to learning; ‘as if chiseled, as if polished’ refers to cultivating oneself.”

Ma Xuan

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Acting Bureau Director: In composing an essay, one must fully bring out the meaning and import of the text. On a topic such as this, the essays written in the examination hall number several thousand. In discussing learning and self-cultivation, apart from a few words from the Collected Commentaries, their authors merely introduce extraneous, empty phrases as padding. What purpose does such writing serve? This essay develops its argument from the text, accords closely with the explanations and commentaries, and is brilliant in both expression and meaning. Its author must be an accomplished writer.

Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Supervising Secretary: For a true grasp of principle and wording that is neither constrained nor diffuse, no essay surpasses this one.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhan, Compiler: In discussing learning and self-cultivation, the author assimilates the meaning of the sages’ canonical text without being bound by its wording. The treatment is also thorough and carefully ordered. He is presumably someone who has himself devoted thought to this learning.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Compiler: Most writers on this topic gather stock phrases about knowledge and action and pile them together into an essay; this is exceedingly tiresome. This essay integrates the explanations and commentaries, has a notably firm basis, and is orderly in its expression. It does not seem to seek mere novelty; therefore, I have selected it for inclusion.

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
考試官學士靳批大學義如此作乃是
考試官大學士劉批得旨
傳者釋詩以明君子知行之功皆欲求其至焉
夫功已至而益求其至則理無不明而德無不
成矣明德之止于至善也有以哉大學引衛風
淇澳之詩以釋止于至善之義至此蓋謂詩所
謂如治骨角者既切之以刀鋸復磋之以鑢錫
治之有緒而益求其精者何邪蓋言君子講學
之事如此耳誠以理非學不明學而不求其精
===
則至善之所在不可得而知也君子講習於麗
澤之間而察言以求其心討論於遜志之餘而
因事以考其迹理已窮矣而探索之益深心已
明矣而緝熈之益至朝益暮習務求造乎精義
入神之妙一物之不知弗措也日就月將務求
至乎窮神知化之域一理之不明弗措也君子
學問之事若是此其所以真知夫至善之所在
而不惑也歟詩所謂如治玉石者既琢之以椎
鑿復磨之以沙石為之有緒而益致其密者何

考試官學士靳批：大學義如此作乃是。
考試官大學士劉批：得旨。
傳者釋詩，以明君子知行之功皆欲求其至焉。夫功已至而益求其至，則理無不明而德無不成矣。明德之止于至善也，有以哉！大學引衛風淇澳之詩，以釋止于至善之義。至此，蓋謂詩所謂如治骨角者，既切之以刀鋸，復磋之以鑢錫，治之有緒而益求其精者，何邪？蓋言君子講學之事如此耳。誠以理非學不明，學而不求其精，則至善之所在不可得而知也。君子講習於麗澤之間，而察言以求其心；討論於遜志之餘，而因事以考其迹。理已窮矣，而探索之益深；心已明矣，而緝熈之益至。朝益暮習，務求造乎精義入神之妙，一物之不知弗措也；日就月將，務求至乎窮神知化之域，一理之不明弗措也。君子學問之事若是，此其所以真知夫至善之所在而不惑也歟！詩所謂如治玉石者，既琢之以椎鑿，復磨之以沙石，為之有緒而益致其密者，何
translation_en:
Examiner Jin, Academician, comments: “This is how an essay on the meaning of the Great Learning should be written.”
Examiner Liu, Grand Secretary, comments: “It grasps the purport.”
The author of the commentary explains the poem to make clear that the gentleman seeks the utmost attainment in both knowing and acting. When his efforts have already reached a high point and he seeks still greater attainment, no principle remains unclarified and no virtue remains unperfected. There is indeed a reason why illuminating virtue comes to rest in the highest good! The Great Learning quotes the poem “The Bend of the Qi” from the Airs of Wei to explain the meaning of resting in the highest good. At this point, it means: when the poem speaks of working bone and horn, first cutting them with knives and saws, then filing them with rasps—proceeding methodically in the work and seeking ever greater refinement—what does this signify? It simply means that the gentleman’s pursuit of learning is like this. For principles cannot be understood without learning; and if one learns without seeking refinement, one cannot know where the highest good lies.
The gentleman studies and practices with companions, like adjoining lakes replenishing one another, examining their words to seek the intentions behind them. With a humble disposition, he discusses and investigates, considering affairs to examine the traces of those intentions. Though he has already thoroughly investigated principles, he probes them ever more deeply; though his mind is already illuminated, he continually brings that illumination to greater perfection. Advancing in the morning and practicing in the evening, he strives to attain the subtle mastery of refining his understanding of meaning and entering into the spiritual; so long as a single thing remains unknown, he does not desist. Making daily progress and advancing month by month, he strives to reach the realm of fathoming the spiritual and knowing transformation; so long as a single principle remains unclear, he does not desist. Such is the gentleman’s pursuit of learning. Is this not how he truly knows where the highest good lies and remains free from confusion?
When the poem speaks of working jade and stone, first carving them with mallets and chisels, then polishing them with sand and stones—proceeding methodically in the work and bringing it to ever greater exactness—what …

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
邪盖言君子自脩之功如此耳誠以德非脩不
成自脩而不求其密則至善之所在不可得而
止也君子省察於念慮之微而思有以審其幾
克治於身心之間而思有以致其决禮已復矣
而涵養之愈密欲已去矣而檢束之愈嚴自強
不息萬理必欲其常存撓之不能亂也日進無
疆一私必欲其淨盡誘之不能遷也君子自脩
之功若是此其所以能得夫至善之所止而不
移也歟是則講學者擇善之功始條理之事也
===
自脩者固執之功終條理之事也明德之所以
求止至善者不在於此哉抑古人之論學多矣
然皆未有若此詩之親切而有味者宜乎曾子
特引之以為學大學者法也他日子貢論學能
及乎此而夫子許之豈其博學多識之餘而亦
有見於是邪要其功效所極雖成周文武之聖
所以延萬世親賢樂利之澤者亦原於此君天
下者尚知務哉
德行顏淵閔子騫冉伯牛仲弓言語宰我

邪？盖言君子自脩之功如此耳。誠以德非脩不成，自脩而不求其密，則至善之所在不可得而止也。君子省察於念慮之微，而思有以審其幾；克治於身心之間，而思有以致其决。禮已復矣，而涵養之愈密；欲已去矣，而檢束之愈嚴。自強不息，萬理必欲其常存，撓之不能亂也；日進無疆，一私必欲其淨盡，誘之不能遷也。君子自脩之功若是，此其所以能得夫至善之所止而不移也歟？是則講學者，擇善之功，始條理之事也；自脩者，固執之功，終條理之事也。明德之所以求止至善者，不在於此哉？抑古人之論學多矣，然皆未有若此詩之親切而有味者，宜乎曾子特引之以為學《大學》者法也。他日子貢論學能及乎此，而夫子許之，豈其博學多識之餘而亦有見於是邪？要其功效所極，雖成周文武之聖，所以延萬世親賢樂利之澤者，亦原於此。君天下者尚知務哉！
德行：顏淵、閔子騫、冉伯牛、仲弓。言語：宰我、
translation_en:
…? It simply means that the gentleman’s work of cultivating himself is like this. Indeed, virtue cannot be perfected without cultivation; if one cultivates oneself without seeking thoroughness, one cannot attain and abide in the highest good. The gentleman examines the subtlest stirrings of his thoughts, seeking to discern their incipient tendencies; he disciplines his person and mind, seeking to make his resolve decisive. Even after ritual propriety has been restored, he nurtures himself with ever greater care; even after selfish desires have been removed, he restrains himself with ever greater strictness. Strengthening himself without cease, he insists that all moral principles remain constantly present, so that disturbances cannot throw him into disorder. Advancing daily without limit, he insists that every selfish impulse be utterly eliminated, so that temptations cannot divert him. Such is the gentleman’s work of self-cultivation. Is this not how he attains the resting place of the highest good and remains there unwaveringly?
Thus, the investigation and discussion of learning constitute the work of choosing the good, establishing an ordered coherence at the outset; self-cultivation constitutes the work of holding firmly to it, bringing that ordered coherence to completion. Is this not how one seeks to make luminous virtue abide in the highest good? The ancients said much about learning, yet none of their statements is as immediately pertinent and rich in meaning as this poem. It was fitting that Zengzi singled it out for quotation as a model for those studying the Great Learning. On another occasion, Zigong reached this understanding in discussing learning, and the Master approved of him. Might he, beyond his extensive learning and broad knowledge, also have perceived this truth?
Considering the ultimate reach of its efficacy, even the sage kings Wen and Wu of the flourishing Zhou derived from this the means of extending to all succeeding generations the blessings through which people cherish their kin, esteem the worthy, enjoy happiness, and benefit from good government. May those who rule the realm understand what they must attend to!
In virtuous conduct: Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Boniu, and Zhonggong. In speech: Zai Wo …

…Zigong; in governmental affairs: Ran You and Jilu; in literary learning: Ziyou and Zixia.

Niu Feng.

Associate Examiner Li, Acting Vice Director, comments: In discussing the four disciplines, the wording is carefully weighed, and the supporting examples are clear and apt. This is no carelessly composed work.

Associate Examiner Mu, Examining Editor, comments: The exposition follows the topic without a single superfluous word. Writing that serves as a standard should be precisely like this.

Associate Examiner Dong, Compiler, comments: The difficulty of this topic lies not in elaboration but in concision and aptness. Readers of this essay should grasp this for themselves.

Associate Examiner Lun, Senior Compiler, comments: The language and cadence are ample and composed; the portrayal of the attainments of these worthies is nearly exhaustive. It deserves to be recorded as a model for interpreting the Analects.

Examiner Jin, Academician, comments: The exposition of the various worthies’ strengths is most apt.

Examiner Liu, Grand Secretary, comments: The expression is refined and substantial.

The recorder lists the four disciplines of the Sage’s school and associates with them its ten eminent disciples. These ten eminent disciples in the Sage’s school had each attained something of the Way. Looking at those listed under the four disciplines, was this not a flourishing assemblage of one age? Formerly, our Master recalled the disciples who had accompanied him in Chen and Cai. His disciples accordingly recorded these men and also identified their particular strengths in this manner. Now, what is stored in the heart and manifested in personal conduct, whose moral principles suffice to serve as a model for the world, is virtuous conduct. Among those who excelled in this at the time were Yan Yuan and Min Ziqian…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
焉有冉伯牛仲弓焉觀其仁不違於三月孝不
間於内外謹疾而致南牖之惜敬簡而獲南面
之許則其德行也盖有以超乎其類矣出乎身
而加乎民其詞命足以愜人之聽聞者言語也
當時長於此者有宰我焉有子貢焉觀其賢於
堯舜之賛萬世可傳君容俯仰之辨料事屢中
則其言語也盖有以異乎衆人矣德行也言語
也宛然孔門之懿矩也若乃達於為國治民之
理而徵諸實用者非政事乎而冉有季路其人
===
也從政而有足民之志治蒲而得三善之稱則
其政事之卓異莫能或之先焉邃於詩書六藝
之旨而發其英華者非文學乎而子游子夏其
人也為宰以禮樂為教論詩以忠信為先則其
文學之純懿孰能出其右焉政事也文學也儼
然洙泗之家法也噫羣賢之所長如此則聖人
之追思豈特以其相從陳蔡之故哉嗟夫天生
聖賢所以為世道計以顏閔諸賢生於春秋之
時而又得聖人為之依歸固一時之幸也使當

其政事之卓異莫能或之先焉邃於詩書六藝
之旨而發其英華者非文學乎而子游子夏其
人也為宰以禮樂為教論詩以忠信為先則其
文學之純懿孰能出其右焉政事也文學也儼

聖賢所以為世道計以顔閔諸賢生於春秋之
時而又得聖人為之依歸固一時之幸也使當
punctuated:
焉，有冉伯牛、仲弓焉。觀其仁不違於三月，孝不間於内外，謹疾而致南牖之惜，敬簡而獲南面之許，則其德行也，盖有以超乎其類矣。出乎身而加乎民，其詞命足以愜人之聽聞者，言語也。當時長於此者，有宰我焉，有子貢焉。觀其賢於堯舜之賛，萬世可傳；君容俯仰之辨，料事屢中，則其言語也，盖有以異乎衆人矣。德行也，言語也，宛然孔門之懿矩也。若乃達於為國治民之理，而徵諸實用者，非政事乎？而冉有、季路其人也。從政而有足民之志，治蒲而得三善之稱，則其政事之卓異，莫能或之先焉。邃於詩書六藝之旨，而發其英華者，非文學乎？而子游、子夏其人也。為宰以禮樂為教，論詩以忠信為先，則其文學之純懿，孰能出其右焉？政事也，文學也，儼然洙泗之家法也。

噫！羣賢之所長如此，則聖人之追思，豈特以其相從陳蔡之故哉？嗟夫！天生聖賢，所以為世道計。以顏閔諸賢生於春秋之時，而又得聖人為之依歸，固一時之幸也。使當
translation_en:
…and there were Ran Boniu and Zhonggong. Consider how their benevolence did not lapse for three months, how their filial devotion was beyond reproach within and outside the family, how careful conduct amid illness [?] occasioned the Master's lament at the south window, and how reverence joined with simplicity won his approval as fit to face south and rule. Their virtuous conduct thus surpassed that of their fellows.

What proceeds from oneself and reaches the people, through words suited to pleasing their hearers, is skill in speech. Those who excelled in this at the time included Zai Wo and Zigong. Consider their praise of the Master as worthier than Yao and Shun, which could be transmitted for myriad generations, and their discernment of rulers' bearing, whether looking down or up, which repeatedly enabled them to predict events correctly. Their skill in speech thus distinguished them from ordinary men. Virtuous conduct and skill in speech: these were splendid exemplars of the school of Confucius.

As for comprehending the principles of governing a state and ordering its people, and proving them in practical application—is this not governmental service? Ran You and Jilu were such men. In office, one aspired to provide sufficiently for the people; in governing Pu, the other earned praise for three good achievements. In the distinction of their governmental service, none could surpass them. To penetrate the purport of the Odes, the Documents, and the Six Arts, and bring forth their finest qualities—is this not literary learning? Ziyou and Zixia were such men. Serving as an administrator, one taught through rites and music; discussing the Odes, the other gave precedence to loyalty and trustworthiness. Who could surpass the purity and excellence of their literary learning? Governmental service and literary learning: these were indeed the established traditions of the school by the Zhu and Si rivers.

Ah! Since the assembled worthies excelled in these ways, could the sage's fond recollection of them have been merely because they had accompanied him in Chen and Cai? Alas! Heaven brings forth sages and worthies out of concern for the moral order of the world. That Yan Hui, Min Ziqian, and the other worthies were born in the Spring and Autumn period and also had the sage to rely upon and turn to was truly a blessing for that age. If, at that…

translation_en:
… had the state then been entrusted to them and they been given charge of its government, each would surely have put his particular strengths to use for the world. Transforming the Spring and Autumn age into the age of Tang and Yu would indeed have been no difficult matter. What a pity! They served only to bring glory to the Way of the Sage, while the people never received their beneficent influence. Alas!

“This is generated by the accumulation of righteousness; it cannot be obtained through an isolated act of righteousness. If one’s conduct leaves the heart dissatisfied, it will starve.”

Xu Zhiluan

Comment by Associate Examiner Ma, Left Supervising Secretary: The three clauses of this topic illuminate one another, but writers seldom manage to make them clear. For concise and lucid expression, no essay surpasses this one.

Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Compiler: The purport of accumulating righteousness and nourishing vital energy is indeed difficult to express. This essay shows a precise and penetrating understanding, and its language adequately conveys that understanding. Its author, too, has probably attained some measure of cultivation.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhai, Compiler: The work of nourishing vital energy is fully encompassed in these three clauses. The two characters meaning “accumulating righteousness” are especially crucial; the final clause elucidates this by reversing the statement. Candidates lack a true understanding and often divide the clauses into separate, contrasting propositions. Even those who occasionally grasp the meaning fail to make clear their transitions, the rise and fall of their argument, and their elucidation of distinctions. This essay alone integrates the commentaries into a coherent composition. It contains scarcely a single superfluous phrase, yet its meaning is complete. It should be recorded as a model.

Comment by Associate Examiner Cui, Compiler: This essay develops its argument in accordance with the commentary. Several phrases elucidating distinctions in its middle portion make it all the more lucid and precise. Its author is someone who devotes himself deeply to the learning of principle.

有不慊者乎孟子告公孫丑不動心之故及此

大賢原氣由善養而充，必指失養之弊以明之也。盖集義乃養氣之本，義集則氣充矣。不然，其有不慊者乎？孟子告公孫丑不動心之故，及此，意謂氣配乎理，則氣固所當養；理主乎氣，則理在所當循。方其養之之始也，必當裁制於念慮之方形，以擴充其義之端，由小及大，無一事而不合於宜也；審察於應酬之已著，以充滿其義之量，或順或逆，無一時而不循乎理也。由是自反常直，而氣之至大者油然自生於不憂不懼之餘，足以塞天地而無外矣。豈以一事偶合其宜，便可襲取於外，而遽謂得氣之本然哉？內省不疚，而氣之至剛者勃然自生於不愧不怍之
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Wu, Expositor, comments: In writing on the nourishment of qi, even a slight intrusion of one's own ideas [?] runs counter to Zhu Xi's commentary. This composition alone grasps the meaning closely and clearly. Its author must be someone who has thoroughly investigated the fundamentals; hence its inclusion.

Examiner Jin, Academician, comments: It brings out profound subtleties with concision and rigor—certainly no immature hand.

Examiner Liu, Grand Secretary, comments: The vital force is abundant, and the language flows freely.

The great worthy traced the fullness of qi to its proper nourishment, and necessarily pointed out the harm caused by failing to nourish it, to make this clear. For accumulating righteousness is the foundation of nourishing qi: when righteousness accumulates, qi becomes full. Otherwise, would there not be something unsatisfying within? When Mengzi explained to Gongsun Chou why his mind remained unmoved, he came to this point. His meaning was that, since qi accords with principle, qi must indeed be nourished; and since principle governs qi, principle must be followed. At the outset of this nourishment, one must regulate thoughts and reflections just as they take shape, thereby expanding the beginnings of righteousness. Proceeding from small matters to great ones, one must leave no affair out of accord with what is fitting. One must scrutinize one's dealings with others once they have taken manifest form, thereby bringing righteousness to its full measure. Whether circumstances are favorable or adverse, there must be no moment when one fails to follow principle. In this way, self-examination will always find uprightness, and the supremely vast qi will spontaneously arise from freedom from anxiety and fear, sufficient to fill Heaven and Earth and leave nothing outside it. How could one, merely because a single deed happens to accord with what is fitting, seize it from outside and hastily claim to have attained qi's original nature? When inward examination finds no cause for remorse, the supremely firm qi vigorously arises of itself amid freedom from shame and embarrassment …

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
際足以配道義而有為矣豈以一事偶循乎理
便可掩取於外而遽謂得氣之浩然哉氣必以
集義而生如此何以見之彼人有一行之非義
則疑懼交集即為此心之累心累則氣隨以歉
而四體有所不充至大者於是而欿然矣况能
塞于天地乎有一事之不直則惶惑不暇即為
此心之害心害則氣隨以沮而一身有所不足
至剛者於是而靡然矣况能配于道義乎是則
浩然之氣一義之得而未必生一事之失而遂
===
自餒生之甚難而餒之甚易如此然則集義之
功可一時而忽哉抑孟子養氣之論誠擴前聖
之所未發而集義一言尤有得於吾夫子義以
方外之旨然果能此道則獨立不懼遯世無悶
無入不自得矣孟子在當時却萬鍾藐大人巖
巖氣象天下仰之誠所謂善養是氣者而其功
皆本於此後之學孟子者尚當以是為法
易
上九白賁无咎

punctuated:
際，足以配道義而有為矣，豈以一事偶循乎理，便可掩取於外，而遽謂得氣之浩然哉？氣必以集義而生如此，何以見之？彼人有一行之非義，則疑懼交集，即為此心之累；心累，則氣隨以歉，而四體有所不充，至大者於是而欿然矣，况能塞于天地乎？有一事之不直，則惶惑不暇，即為此心之害；心害，則氣隨以沮，而一身有所不足，至剛者於是而靡然矣，况能配于道義乎？是則浩然之氣，一義之得而未必生，一事之失而遂自餒。生之甚難，而餒之甚易如此，然則集義之功，可一時而忽哉？抑孟子養氣之論，誠擴前聖之所未發，而集義一言，尤有得於吾夫子義以方外之旨。然果能此道，則獨立不懼，遯世無悶，無入不自得矣。孟子在當時，却萬鍾，藐大人，巖巖氣象，天下仰之，誠所謂善養是氣者，而其功皆本於此。後之學孟子者，尚當以是為法。

易
上九，白賁，无咎。
translation_en:
…at such a moment, it is sufficient to stand alongside the Way and righteousness and accomplish deeds. How could one, merely because a single deed happens to accord with principle, seize it from outside and hastily claim to have attained the flood-like fullness of qi? That qi must arise through the accumulation of righteous deeds is thus established; how can this be demonstrated? If a person commits a single unrighteous act, doubt and fear converge, burdening the heart. When the heart is burdened, qi consequently grows deficient, leaving the four limbs less than fully sustained. What is supremely great thereby becomes diminished; how, then, could it fill Heaven and Earth? If a single deed is not upright, alarm and perplexity leave one no respite, harming the heart. When the heart is harmed, qi consequently falters, leaving the whole person deficient. What is supremely firm thereby becomes enfeebled; how, then, could it stand alongside the Way and righteousness?

Thus, flood-like qi does not necessarily arise from a single righteous achievement, yet a single misstep causes it to waste away of itself. Since bringing it forth is so difficult and causing it to waste away so easy, can the work of accumulating righteous deeds be neglected even for a moment? Moreover, Mencius’s discussion of nurturing qi truly develops what the earlier sages had left unexpressed. The phrase “accumulating righteous deeds,” in particular, grasps the purport of our Master’s teaching that “righteousness squares one’s outward conduct.” If one can truly practice this way, one can stand alone without fear, withdraw from the world without distress, and remain at ease in every situation. In his own time, Mencius rejected a stipend of ten thousand zhong of grain and regarded great men with disdain. His lofty bearing commanded the admiration of all under Heaven. He truly was what is meant by someone skilled in nurturing this qi, and his achievement was entirely grounded in this practice. Those of later times who learn from Mencius should take this as their model.

Book of Changes
Top Nine: Plain adornment. No blame.

聖人於賁爻之在上者，著其得賁之本，善其免賁之失。夫賁之失，生於本之不足也。能得其本，則何咎之有哉？聖人以是繫賁上爻之象占，開物成務之意精矣。且賁之為卦，加艮於離而成體，兼文明以止而為義，本以賁飾為尚也。爻至

Yang Shen

Associate Examiner Li, Acting Vice Director, comments: “The intention of honoring the root and restraining the branches is expounded almost exhaustively. This deserves to be selected.”

Associate Examiner Mu, Examining Editor, comments: “The diction and tone are full and weighty, worthy of emulation. At the conclusion, he further speaks of foreseeing the abuses of later developments and guarding against them in advance. These words are especially incisive.”

Associate Examiner Dong, Compiler, comments: “The Duke of Zhou certainly drew the image from the line itself, and the principle of remedying abuses naturally follows as well. This composition aptly relates the matter to its subject and conveys profound meaning. It is writing of consequence.”

Associate Examiner Lun, Senior Compiler, comments: “He develops his exposition from the line itself, and its meaning vividly emerges. He deeply grasps the purport of examining what is substantial and awaiting what is as yet unmanifest. Surely he is deeply versed in the study of the Book of Changes!”

Examiner Jin, Academician, comments: “Is this not how an exposition of a line’s meaning ought to be written?”

Examiner Liu, Grand Secretary, comments: “The passage explaining ‘unadorned grace’ is excellent. Here is someone who understands how to strengthen the root.”

In the uppermost line of the hexagram Bi, Grace, the sage makes clear that it attains the root of adornment and commends its avoidance of adornment’s faults. For the faults of adornment arise from insufficiency at the root. If one can attain that root, what blame can there be? title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
上九周公乃繫其辭以為位有終始而上則居
賁之終盖賁極反本之時也爻有剛柔而上則
於德為剛乃剛上文柔之質也以剛上文柔之
質居賁極反本之時則是斂離之文明尚艮之
篤實當禮儀嘉會之際慮其過乎文也而凡自
一身以措於萬用者雖未嘗无威儀度數之飾
而惟忠信之是敦處人文化成之後恐其流之
敝也而凡自朝廷以達之天下者雖未嘗无典
章文物之用而惟樸素以為質殆猶畧其華美
===
而復於无華其視以朱紱而致困者異矣損其
采色而復於无色其視假黃裳以為文者異矣
是非白賁之象乎占者能然則率其素履不作
偽以失真成而有渝不務華而失實以之為己
盖惡文之著而有尚絅之誠者也心逸而德日
休矣尚何咎之可言以之為治盖救文之敝而
有尚忠之政者也本立而道自生矣尚何咎之
可舉吁周公於賁飾之卦而示人以反本之義
其為世道慮也不亦遠哉抑論天下之理无本

translation_en:
…the top nine, the Duke of Zhou attached his statement to it, considering that positions have a beginning and an end, and that the uppermost occupies the end of Adornment (Bi): this is the time when adornment reaches its limit and returns to its root. Lines are either firm or yielding, and the uppermost is firm in its virtue: its substance is that of the firm above adorning the yielding. With this substance, occupying the time when adornment reaches its limit and returns to its root, it restrains the cultural brilliance of Li and esteems the solidity of Gen. Amid the splendid convergence of ritual observances, it considers the danger of excessive ornament. Thus, in everything extending from one's own person to the myriad applications of conduct, although the adornments of dignified deportment and prescribed measures are never absent, it cultivates above all loyalty and trustworthiness. After human culture has brought about transformation, it fears the abuses into which its course may lead. Thus, in everything extending from the court throughout the realm, although institutions and cultural refinements are never without their uses, it takes simplicity alone as its substance. It is as though one set aside splendor and returned to the unadorned: this differs from becoming beset through the vermilion knee-covering. It is as though one diminished colors and returned to the colorless: this differs from borrowing a yellow lower garment for adornment. Is this not the image of “white adornment”?

If the diviner can act thus, he follows his plain course of conduct, without falsification that would forfeit authenticity; “accomplished, yet undergoing change” [?], he does not pursue splendor at the expense of substance. Applied to cultivating oneself, this means disliking conspicuous ornament and possessing the sincerity expressed by wearing a plain outer garment over it. The mind is at ease and virtue grows finer each day: what blame could there be to speak of? Applied to government, this means remedying the abuses of ornament through policies that esteem loyalty. Once the root is established, the Way grows of itself: what blame could there be to cite?

Ah! In the hexagram concerned with adornment, the Duke of Zhou showed people the principle of returning to the root. Was his concern for the course of the world not far-reaching? Yet, considering the principles of all under Heaven, without a root…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:

質敝則濟以文文敝則承以質終而復始如循

同考試官檢討穆批：「翕闢廣生處，士子亦知本乾而言。至用意精到，致辭明潔，讀之使人潛思而樂玩者，無如此篇。」

同考試官編修董批：「乾坤雖各有動靜，其實坤因乎乾也。士子講翕闢處，掇拾支離，而去理遠甚。獨此篇發揮透徹，且見乾坤不相離處，必究心理學者。」

…cannot stand; without refinement, it cannot function. Neither of these two should predominate. In the Way of the Three Kings, when plain substance became defective, refinement supplied the remedy; when refinement became defective, plain substance succeeded it. Ending and beginning anew, like a revolving cycle, this was simply a matter of establishing instruction suited to the times. In the Duke of Zhou’s day, refinement was still esteemed, yet he already spoke in these terms. Was this because he foresaw the defects of its later development and took precautions against them? Alas! The Duke’s admonition was so earnest and thorough, yet in later ages there were still those who afflicted the people through boundless extravagance and indulgence of their desires. Why indeed was this so?

“As for Kun, in stillness it closes; in movement it opens. Thus it brings forth things far and wide.”
By Yin Xiang.

Associate Examiner Li, Acting Vice Director, comments: “The subtle workings of the Way of Kun are inherently difficult to express, and many examination candidates were baffled by them. This essay develops the subject fully and thoroughly, with clarity and precision. It is included as a model for those writing essays on the meaning of the Book of Changes.”

Associate Examiner Mu, Examining Editor, comments: “In discussing closing, opening, and bringing forth things far and wide, the candidates also understood that they should base their explanations on Qian. But for precision and depth of thought, clarity and purity of expression, and the ability to draw readers into quiet reflection and delighted contemplation, none equals this essay.”

Associate Examiner Dong, Compiler, comments: “Although Qian and Kun each have movement and stillness, Kun in fact depends on Qian. When candidates explain closing and opening, they assemble disconnected scraps and stray very far from the underlying principle. This essay alone expounds the matter thoroughly and also reveals how Qian and Kun are inseparable. Its author must be someone who has devoted himself deeply to the Learning of Principle.”

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
於是乎上躋勾者畢出萌者盡達盖有以悉顯
直遂之氣於咸亨之表矣非闢歟翕者二之合
也闢者二之分也惟二而虛而廣不生於是邪
是故專一之氣渾淪无涯而坤則翕之是其形
有涯而容乎无涯之氣也直遂之氣充塞无外
而坤則闢之是其形有外而貫乎无外之氣也
博厚而萬物載焉人皆曰此坤之廣也而不知
所以博厚者在是至哉之德合于大哉之乾而
同一无疆矣均布而萬物養焉人皆曰此坤之
===
廣也而不知所以均布者在是隤然之簡配乎
確然之易而同一不測矣坤之廣如此則易書
之所以廣者不外是矣非夫子發以示人其孰
能知之抑吾於此得心學焉天地之道不專一
則不能直遂不翕聚則不能發散盖雖各有動
靜而未嘗不以靜為主也世之學者自私用智
而不知究心于本原之地其何以一天下之動
而立人極哉夫子以貞為事之榦亦此意也周
子主靜之學盖出於此

子主靜之學蓋出於此

於是乎上躋，勾者畢出，萌者盡達，盖有以悉顯直遂之氣於咸亨之表矣，非闢歟？翕者，二之合也；闢者，二之分也。惟二而虛，而廣不生於是邪？是故專一之氣渾淪无涯，而坤則翕之，是其形有涯而容乎无涯之氣也；直遂之氣充塞无外，而坤則闢之，是其形有外而貫乎无外之氣也。博厚而萬物載焉，人皆曰此坤之廣也，而不知所以博厚者在是。至哉之德，合于大哉之乾，而同一无疆矣。均布而萬物養焉，人皆曰此坤之廣也，而不知所以均布者在是。隤然之簡，配乎確然之易，而同一不測矣。坤之廣如此，則易書之所以廣者不外是矣。非夫子發以示人，其孰能知之？

抑吾於此得心學焉。天地之道，不專一則不能直遂，不翕聚則不能發散。盖雖各有動靜，而未嘗不以靜為主也。世之學者自私用智，而不知究心于本原之地，其何以一天下之動而立人極哉？夫子以貞為事之榦，亦此意也。周子主靜之學，盖出於此。
translation_en:
…thereupon rises upward. All curled shoots emerge, and all sprouts grow forth. Thus the qi that advances directly is fully displayed in the outward manifestation of universal flourishing. Is this not opening? Closing is the joining of the two; opening is the separation of the two. Precisely because Kun is twofold, it is receptive; does its breadth not arise from this? Thus, the qi that is concentrated and unified is undifferentiated and boundless, and Kun gathers it in: its form has bounds, yet accommodates boundless qi. The qi that advances directly fills everything, leaving nothing outside it, and Kun opens it out: its form has an outside, yet is permeated by qi that has no outside. Through its breadth and thickness, the myriad things are borne upon it. Everyone says, “This is the breadth of Kun,” yet they do not know that the source of its breadth and thickness lies here. Its virtue, acclaimed as “utmost,” accords with Qian, acclaimed as “great,” and both alike are boundless. Through its even distribution, the myriad things are nourished. Everyone says, “This is the breadth of Kun,” yet they do not know that the source of its even distribution lies here. Its yielding simplicity matches Qian’s firm ease, and both alike are unfathomable. Such is the breadth of Kun; the source of the breadth of the Book of Changes lies in nothing beyond this. Had the Master not expounded it to instruct others, who could have understood it?

Moreover, I find here the learning of the mind. In the Way of Heaven and Earth, without concentration and unity there can be no direct advance; without closing and gathering there can be no issuing forth and dispersal. Although Heaven and Earth each have movement and stillness, they invariably take stillness as primary. Scholars of the present age pursue private ends and employ cleverness, yet do not know to apply their minds to the original source. How, then, can they unify all the movements of the world and establish the ultimate standard for humanity? The Master’s statement that constancy is the trunk of affairs also conveys this meaning. Master Zhou’s teaching that takes stillness as primary surely derives from this.

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
乃化天下之本也聖君推其德以及天下而天
下化之放勳之盛固如是哉昔虞史記帝堯放
勳之實及此謂夫我帝堯以克明俊德之聖推
而為家國天下之治而其所以平天下者果如
何哉彼分土分民其國以萬數也堯則合而和
之悉此德以為之甄陶建師建長其邦以萬計
也堯則協而和之一此德以為之沾濡推欽明
文思之餘為涵養薰融之澤視天下猶一家也
以允恭克讓之德為鼓舞作興之具視萬姓猶
===
===
一人也豈但以親九族平章百姓而已哉堯之
德化如此史臣羨美之心切于中感嘆之詞形
于外以為此萬邦黎民也向嘗拘於氣禀而習
為不善者有之今幸而得聖人為之君師於是
過以改善以遷而舊習脫然以去矣昔嘗溺於
物欲而陷於為惡者有之今幸而有聖德為之
依歸義以徙德以崇而新化昭然以明矣相親
相遜於光天化日之下於是乎雍然而和也以
歡以愛於春風和氣之中於時乎熈然而樂也

乃化天下之本也。聖君推其德以及天下，而天下化之。放勳之盛，固如是哉！昔虞史記帝堯放勳之實，及此，謂夫我帝堯以克明俊德之聖，推而為家國天下之治，而其所以平天下者，果如何哉？彼分土分民，其國以萬數也，堯則合而和之，悉此德以為之甄陶；建師建長，其邦以萬計也，堯則協而和之，一此德以為之沾濡。推欽明文思之餘，為涵養薰融之澤，視天下猶一家也；以允恭克讓之德，為鼓舞作興之具，視萬姓猶一人也。豈但以親九族、平章百姓而已哉！

堯之德化如此，史臣羨美之心切于中，感嘆之詞形于外，以為此萬邦黎民也，向嘗拘於氣禀而習為不善者有之，今幸而得聖人為之君師，於是過以改，善以遷，而舊習脫然以去矣。昔嘗溺於物欲而陷於為惡者有之，今幸而有聖德為之依歸，義以徙，德以崇，而新化昭然以明矣。相親相遜於光天化日之下，於是乎雍然而和也；以歡以愛於春風和氣之中，於時乎熈然而樂也。
translation_en:
…is the foundation for transforming All under Heaven. The sage ruler extends his virtue throughout All under Heaven, and all are transformed by it. Such indeed was the greatness of Yao’s magnificent achievement! When the historian of Yu recorded the substance of Emperor Yao’s magnificent achievement and reached this point, his meaning was this: our Emperor Yao, with the sagely capacity to manifest eminent virtue, extended it to the governance of family, state, and All under Heaven. How, then, did he bring peace to All under Heaven? Lands and peoples were apportioned among states numbering in the tens of thousands; Yao brought them together in harmony, drawing fully upon this virtue to mold and nurture them. Teachers and leaders were established in domains numbering in the tens of thousands; Yao coordinated them in harmony, applying this virtue uniformly to imbue them with its influence. He extended the abundant influence of his reverence, enlightenment, refinement, and thoughtfulness into a beneficence that nourished and gently transformed, regarding All under Heaven as a single family. He used his virtue of true respect and ready deference as the means to inspire and invigorate, regarding the myriad people as a single person. How could this have amounted merely to bringing affection to the nine degrees of kinship and equitably ordering the hundred clans?

Such was the transforming influence of Yao’s virtue. The historian’s admiration was keen within his heart, and words of wonder found outward expression. He considered that among these common people of the myriad states, some had formerly been constrained by their endowments of vital energy and had become accustomed to doing what was not good. Now, fortunately, they had gained a sage to serve as their ruler and teacher. Thus they corrected their faults and advanced toward goodness, casting off their old habits entirely. Some had formerly been submerged in material desires and had fallen into wrongdoing. Now, fortunately, they had sagely virtue upon which to depend and to which to turn. They moved toward righteousness and exalted their virtue, and their new transformation became clearly manifest. Showing affection and deference to one another beneath a radiant heaven and the sun of transforming influence, they were thus united in concord. Rejoicing and loving one another amid spring breezes and gentle air, they were then joyfully at ease.…

有曰大哉堯之為君易有曰大哉乾元盖堯非
大則無以君天下乾非大則無以統四德史臣
紀堯大德而列諸篇首是亦易首乾元之義而
孔子大哉之稱亦本於此然俊德一言既以開
萬世君道之原於變時雍又以為萬世斯民太
平之地此又史臣言外意也愚因表而出之
曰其稽我古人之德矧曰其有能稽謀自

Moreover, I have observed that Confucius said, “Great indeed was Yao as a ruler!” The Book of Changes says, “Great indeed is the originating power of Qian!” Unless Yao were great, he could not have ruled all under Heaven; unless Qian were great, it could not have encompassed the four virtues. title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
表而出之
同考試官編修趙批老臣稽古稽天之
實模寫殆盡且詞語老健文氣舂容當是作手
考試官學士靳批正得老臣告君忠愛之意
考試官大學士劉批說老成所以不可遺處
語有意味
老臣能審於事之已然尤能審於理之自然盖
古德乃事之已然而天乃理之所從出者也老
臣皆能知之為國者豈可以輕遺之哉昔召公
===
陳戒成王盖謂老臣者國家之所倚重臣工之
所視效者也人君豈可不知所重哉何則天下
之事必考之古而後可知彼寡於聞見者孰能
考之惟茲老成閱歷既久諳練亦深一言一行
之出於前哲者爰究爰度而仰見其人於千載
之前若政若令之出於先民者是究是圖而黙
識其志於百世之後孰為敬德而可法考之既
無所遺不徒廣一已之聰明而國家大政將於
是而有證也孰為懋德而可鑒考之亦無不盡

translation_en:
…bring it to prominence.

Associate Examiner Zhao, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: “The substance of how veteran ministers examine antiquity and Heaven is depicted almost exhaustively. Moreover, the language is mature and vigorous, and the flow of the prose is measured and ample. This must be the work of an accomplished writer.”

Examiner Jin, a Hanlin Academician, comments: “This precisely captures the loyal devotion with which a veteran minister counsels his ruler.”

Examiner Liu, a Grand Secretary, comments: “The passage explaining why seasoned elders must not be overlooked is rich in meaning.”

Veteran ministers can discern events that have already occurred, and still more can they discern what is naturally so in principle. For the virtue of the ancients belongs to what has already occurred, while Heaven is the source from which principle proceeds. Veteran ministers can understand both: how could those who govern a state lightly disregard them? In former times, the Duke of Shao presented admonitions to King Cheng. His meaning was that veteran ministers are those upon whom the state relies and whom its officials look to as models. How could a ruler fail to know whom he should value?

Why is this so? The affairs of the world can be understood only after they have been examined against antiquity. Among those of limited learning and experience, who could undertake such an examination? These seasoned elders alone have long experience and deep familiarity with affairs. They investigate and weigh every word and deed of earlier sages, looking back with reverence to behold those men a thousand years before their own time. They investigate and ponder the policies and commands of their predecessors, silently apprehending their intentions a hundred generations later. In examining who revered virtue and can serve as a model, they leave nothing out. This does more than broaden their own understanding: the great policies of the state thereby gain corroboration. In examining who diligently cultivated virtue and can serve as a guide, they likewise leave nothing unexplored…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
不徒資一已之知識而治道訏謨將於是而有
據也老臣之不可遺者如此而況有大於此者
乎何則天下之政必稽諸理而後可行彼淺於
智慮者孰能稽之惟兹老成造詣既深趣識亦
逺凡運籌發慮以定國家之大政者必稽諸天
理而不雜以人偽先天而天弗違也建謀設策
以决天下之大計者必稽之天道而不間以人
欲後天而奉天時也惇典庸禮考之天命而不
悖則天與人無間矣命德討罪考之天道而後
===
行則政與理相通矣老臣之尤不可遺者又如
此夫德稽諸古則於事有所證謀考諸天則於
理無所遺以之輔德則德必修以之圖治則治
必理今王新邑初政豈可不加之意也哉大抵
德盛者如愚質朴者如鈍老成之當重尚矣雖
其計功課最不如新進者之有為然而雍容廟
堂坐鎮雅俗有非躁妄者之所能此固古今當
專重而保全之者也詩曰雖無老成人尚有典
刑蓋言老成之重於典刑也此又君天下者所

不徒資一已之知識，而治道訏謨將於是而有據也。老臣之不可遺者如此，而況有大於此者乎？何則？天下之政，必稽諸理而後可行。彼淺於智慮者，孰能稽之？惟兹老成，造詣既深，趣識亦逺。凡運籌發慮，以定國家之大政者，必稽諸天理，而不雜以人偽，先天而天弗違也；建謀設策，以决天下之大計者，必稽之天道，而不間以人欲，後天而奉天時也。惇典庸禮，考之天命而不悖，則天與人無間矣；命德討罪，考之天道而後行，則政與理相通矣。老臣之尤不可遺者，又如此。夫德稽諸古，則於事有所證；謀考諸天，則於理無所遺。以之輔德，則德必修；以之圖治，則治必理。今王新邑初政，豈可不加之意也哉！

translation_en:
…not merely enriching one’s own knowledge: the grand plans for governing will thereby gain a firm foundation. Such are the reasons why veteran ministers must not be neglected; how much more so when there are still greater reasons! Why is this? Measures for governing the realm must be examined against principle before they can be put into practice. How could those whose wisdom and deliberation are shallow undertake such examination? These seasoned elders alone possess profound attainments and far-reaching understanding. Whenever they devise plans and deliberate to settle the state’s major policies, they invariably examine them against Heaven’s principle, admitting no admixture of human artifice: they act before Heaven, yet Heaven does not run counter to them. Whenever they formulate proposals and strategies to decide the realm’s great affairs, they invariably examine them against Heaven’s Way, allowing no intrusion of human desire: they act after Heaven and observe Heaven’s proper seasons. In upholding the established norms and employing the rites, they examine these against Heaven’s mandate and do not contravene it; thus no gap separates Heaven and humanity. In appointing the virtuous and punishing the guilty, they examine their actions against Heaven’s Way before carrying them out; thus government and principle are in accord. These are further reasons why veteran ministers must above all not be neglected. When virtue is examined against antiquity, affairs have precedents to substantiate them; when plans are tested against Heaven, no principle is overlooked. Employ such men to assist in cultivating virtue, and virtue will surely be cultivated; employ them to plan good government, and government will surely be well ordered. Now that the king is beginning his rule in the new city, how could he fail to give this his attention?

Generally, those of abundant virtue appear foolish, and those of plain sincerity appear dull. The esteem due to seasoned elders has long been recognized. Although, when achievements are reckoned and performance assessed, they may not match the accomplishments of those newly advanced, their dignified composure at court and their steadying influence over both the cultivated and the common accomplish what the rash and reckless cannot. These are indeed men who, in ancient times and today alike, deserve particular esteem and protection. The Book of Odes says: “Though there are no aged and accomplished men, there are still exemplary patterns.” This speaks of the greater importance of seasoned elders than of the exemplary patterns themselves. This, too, is something that the ruler of all under Heaven…

同考試官編修瞿批：「攻之在經營之初，子來非勿亟之後。註中方字、已字、雖字、樂字，血脉自明。作者體貼欠真，卒無定見。此篇獨順傳註口氣，平平演出，而文王得民氣象躍如矣，是用錄之。」

同考試官編修崔批：「華而實，清而婉，盖經義中之最優者。」

同考試官侍講吳批：「篇中叙出文王愛民，而民愛之，藹然溢於言表，真亦善說詩矣。」
translation_en:
…ought to know.

Book of Odes

“He began to plan the Numinous Terrace, laying it out and marking its bounds. The common people worked upon it and completed it in less than a day. He began the work without urging haste; the common people came like children to their parent.”

Chen Cai 陳寀

Comment by Associate Examiner Ma, Left Supervising Secretary: “It brings out the mutual affection between ruler and people, and its language is pure and elegant. I select it for inclusion.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Hanlin Compiler: “It depicts almost fully the harmonious relationship between ruler and people in the established Zhou order. Its author may well be someone with whom one can discuss the Odes.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Qu, Hanlin Compiler: “‘Worked upon it’ belongs to the beginning of the planning and laying out; ‘came like children’ does not occur only after ‘without urging haste.’ In the commentary, the words ‘just then,’ ‘already,’ ‘although,’ and ‘delighted’ make the connected thread of meaning clear in themselves. Writers fail to grasp this precisely and ultimately arrive at no settled understanding. This essay alone follows the tenor of the transmitted commentary, unfolding it in a plain and unforced manner, yet vividly bringing to life the way King Wen won the people’s allegiance. For this reason I select it for inclusion.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Cui, Hanlin Compiler: “Ornate yet substantial, clear yet graceful: surely among the finest essays on the meaning of the Classics.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Hanlin Reader-in-waiting: “The essay describes King Wen’s love for the people and their love for him. Their warm affection overflows beyond the words themselves. This is truly a skillful exposition of the Odes.”

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
考試官學士靳批雅義和平可誦
考試官大學士劉批説君民相愛意甚委曲
聖人之為臺得民之力而感民之心也夫感民
之心則自有以得其力矣文王為臺而功之速
成者其有以哉是詩述民樂之詞盖謂國之有
臺所以望氛祲而察災祥時觀游而節勞佚固
有國者所不能無而用民之力亦固所不免矣
今吾王之為臺也屬謀議之方興適經畫之伊
始度地為基建置之規未定也而岐山之衆已
來荷畚鍤者遠近爭先焉設表正位鳩率之令
未下也而周邦之衆既集操版築者小大恐後
焉先期而會捄度不假于章程是以不終日而
臺告成矣聞風而來築削無煩於教令是以不
竟日而功就緒矣當是時也吾王恐競勸之勞
有乖於生息之道黽勉之力或傷吾休養之仁
是以戒乎下者每語之以勿亟矣而來作之衆
自鼓舞以赴功君固恤之民實樂之如子趨父
事不召而自來也其孰能禦焉令乎衆者恒節

事不召而自來也其孰能禦焉今乎衆者恒節

聖人之為臺，得民之力而感民之心也。夫感民之心，則自有以得其力矣。文王為臺而功之速成者，其有以哉！是詩述民樂之詞，盖謂國之有臺，所以望氛祲而察災祥，時觀游而節勞佚，固有國者所不能無，而用民之力亦固所不免矣。今吾王之為臺也，屬謀議之方興，適經畫之伊始，度地為基，建置之規未定也，而岐山之衆已來，荷畚鍤者遠近爭先焉；設表正位，鳩率之令未下也，而周邦之衆既集，操版築者小大恐後焉。先期而會，捄度不假于章程，是以不終日而臺告成矣；聞風而來，築削無煩於教令，是以不竟日而功就緒矣。當是時也，吾王恐競勸之勞有乖於生息之道，黽勉之力或傷吾休養之仁，是以戒乎下者，每語之以勿亟矣。而來作之衆，自鼓舞以赴功，君固恤之，民實樂之，如子趨父事，不召而自來也，其孰能禦焉？令乎衆者，恒節
translation_en:
Examiner Jin, Academician, comments: “The elegant meaning is expressed with harmony and balance, and merits recitation.”
Examiner Liu, Grand Secretary, comments: “The idea of mutual affection between ruler and people is expounded with great subtlety.”
When the sage built his terrace, he obtained the people’s labor and moved their hearts. Indeed, by moving their hearts, he naturally had the means to obtain their labor. Surely there was a reason why King Wen’s terrace was completed so swiftly! This poem gives voice to the people’s delight. Its meaning is that a state’s terrace serves to observe ominous vapors and discern signs of calamity or good fortune, and to provide occasional sightseeing and recreation, balancing toil and leisure. It is indeed something that the ruler of a state cannot dispense with, and employing the people’s labor is likewise unavoidable.
Now, when our king built his terrace, deliberations had only just begun and planning was still at its outset. The ground was being measured for the foundations, and the plan of construction was not yet settled, yet the people of Qishan had already arrived. Bearing baskets and spades, those from near and far vied to be first. Markers were being set up to establish the positions, and no order had yet been issued to assemble and direct the workers, yet the people of Zhou had already gathered. Carrying boards and earth-rammers, great and small alike feared being left behind. They assembled ahead of the appointed time; their gathering of earth and measuring [?] required no prescribed procedures. Thus, before the day was over, the terrace was declared complete. They came upon hearing the news; ramming and trimming the earth required no troublesome instructions. Thus, before the day had ended, the work was accomplished.
At this time, our king feared that the toil of their eager competition might run counter to the way of nurturing their livelihoods, and that their strenuous exertions might impair his benevolent purpose of allowing them rest and recuperation. Hence, whenever he admonished those below, he told them not to hurry. Yet the multitude who came to work were spontaneously stirred with enthusiasm to hasten to the task. The ruler indeed cared for them, while the people truly delighted in it. Like sons hastening to their father’s business, they came of their own accord without being summoned. Who could restrain them? In giving orders to the multitude, he constantly set limits …

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
之以過勞矣而來攻之民自踴躍以從事君固
憂之民實願之如子幹父蠱不強而自至也其
孰能遏焉上以仁愛下而君人之道以全下以
義奉上而尊君之道以得上下之際藹然情意
之交孚君民之間懽若父子之無間此有周之
治所以為不可及歟抑又論之享天下之樂者
常憂效天下之勞者乃逸稽之於書如文王卑
服以即康功咸和不遑暇食所以憂勞天下者
至矣則民之望靈臺而子來聞鼓鐘而於樂良
===
有以也降及後世如魯有三臺之役而春秋致
譏楚興章華之工而伍舉進諫豈人之心有古
今哉憂樂之情異勞佚之勢殊也有天下者尚
當鑒諸
天命降監下民有嚴不僭不濫不敢怠遑
鄭元

之以過勞矣，而來攻之民自踴躍以從事。君固憂之，民實願之，如子幹父蠱，不強而自至也，其孰能遏焉？上以仁愛下，而君人之道以全；下以義奉上，而尊君之道以得。上下之際，藹然情意之交孚；君民之間，懽若父子之無間。此有周之治所以為不可及歟！抑又論之，享天下之樂者常憂，效天下之勞者乃逸。稽之於《書》，如文王卑服以即康功，咸和，不遑暇食，所以憂勞天下者至矣。則民之望靈臺而子來，聞鼓鐘而於樂，良有以也。降及後世，如魯有三臺之役而《春秋》致譏，楚興章華之工而伍舉進諫，豈人之心有古今哉？憂樂之情異，勞佚之勢殊也。有天下者尚當鑒諸！

天命降監，下民有嚴。不僭不濫，不敢怠遑。
鄭元

同考試官左給事中馬批：題意正大明白，作者自難為工。此篇措辭嚴整，頓挫有法，迥出時作矣。
translation_en:
…restrained them out of concern for excessive toil [?], yet the people who came to build eagerly undertook the work of their own accord. Their ruler certainly worried about them, but the people themselves desired it. Like sons attending to their father’s affairs, they came without being compelled. Who could hold them back? Those above loved those below with benevolence, thereby fulfilling the way of ruling others; those below served those above with righteousness, thereby realizing the way of honoring their ruler. Between high and low, feelings and intentions met in warm mutual trust; ruler and people rejoiced together, as close as father and sons. Was this not what made the governance of Zhou unsurpassable?

Consider it further: one who enjoys the pleasures of All-under-Heaven is constantly concerned, while those who undertake its labors are at ease. Examining the Documents, we find that King Wen wore humble clothing and applied himself to works for the people’s welfare, bringing all into harmony [?], with no leisure even to eat. His concern and toil for All-under-Heaven reached their utmost extent. Thus there was good reason why the people, seeing the Numinous Terrace, came like children to their father, and why, hearing the drums and bells, they rejoiced.

In later ages, however, Lu undertook the construction of three terraces and incurred the criticism of the Spring and Autumn Annals; Chu began work on the Zhanghua Terrace, and Wu Ju remonstrated. Could human hearts differ between antiquity and later times? Rather, their feelings concerning anxiety and pleasure differed, and the distribution of toil and ease was unequal. Those who possess All-under-Heaven should take warning from this!

“Heaven’s mandate descends in scrutiny; the people below are to be held in awe. Neither erring nor acting excessively, he dares not be idle or take his ease.”
Zheng Yuan

Comment by Associate Examiner Ma, Left Supervising Secretary: “The meaning of the topic is upright, grand, and clear, which itself makes it difficult for a writer to achieve excellence. This essay’s wording is dignified and well ordered, and its pauses and turns are skillfully controlled. It far surpasses contemporary compositions.”

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
同考試官編修徐批認理精而措辭整高
宗敬天畏民之意尚于文字間見之
同考試官編修翟批言民而本之天則人
君便當知謹畏言天而歸之民則謹畏工夫有下
手處此正詩人立言之妙是篇發揮明白詞語莊
重而推本數語識高見卓蓋不特用之中式而
已敬羡敬羡
同考試官編修崔批此是守規矩文字詞
致嚴重意思邃密結語推出高宗得師臣之助
尤為卓識非泥於章句者
===
同考試官侍講吳批高宗敬天正在僭濫
怠遑上加謹此篇能道之至結束處尤有警策
是可為經義式矣錄之何疑
考試官學士靳批不類眾作
考試官大學士劉批詞婉旨明
天道不外於民賢君能謹於政善矣天道與民
相關而可畏也賢君能公刑賞之政而謹於一
人得敬天之道乎此祀高宗之樂歌意謂天

translation_en:
Associate Examiner Xu, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: “The principles are understood precisely, and the language is well ordered. Gaozong’s intent to revere Heaven and stand in awe of the people can still be discerned in these words.”

Associate Examiner Zhai, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: “When one speaks of the people and grounds the discussion in Heaven, the ruler should immediately recognize the need for caution and awe. When one speaks of Heaven and brings the discussion back to the people, the work of cultivating caution and awe has a concrete starting point. This is precisely the subtlety of the poet’s expression. This essay develops the meaning clearly, and its language is dignified. The few phrases tracing matters to their foundation display lofty understanding and outstanding insight. Surely its value extends beyond merely qualifying for a passing grade. Admirable! Admirable!”

Associate Examiner Cui, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: “This composition observes the established rules. Its diction and manner are solemn, and its thought is profound and closely reasoned. The conclusion brings out how Gaozong benefited from the assistance of a minister who served as his teacher. This is an especially outstanding insight, showing that the author is not confined to the wording of individual passages.”

Associate Examiner Wu, a Hanlin Expositor, comments: “Gaozong’s reverence for Heaven lay precisely in taking care against wrongful or excessive punishments and rewards, and against negligence and idle ease. This essay succeeds in expressing that. Its conclusion is particularly incisive and admonitory. It can serve as a model for essays on the meaning of the Classics. What doubt can there be about including it in this record?”

Examiner Jin, a Hanlin Academician, comments: “Unlike the common run of compositions.”

Examiner Liu, a Grand Secretary, comments: “The language is graceful, and the meaning clear.”

The Way of Heaven does not lie apart from the people; a worthy ruler can exercise care in government. Excellent indeed! The Way of Heaven is bound up with the people and inspires awe. If a worthy ruler can administer punishments and rewards impartially and exercise care in his own person, has he attained the way to revere Heaven? This hymn for the sacrifices to Gaozong means to say that Heaven…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
之與民觀其勢雖殊究其理則一彼監觀四方
天何嘗有目以視也惟因民之視以為視臨下
有赫天何嘗有耳以聽也惟因民之聽以為聽
民之所予天弗棄也是雖匹庶之微而天之耳
目以在不可畏哉民之所棄天弗予也是雖丘
民之賤而天之聰明攸寄不可畏哉夫天人之
間其理無間如此惟我高宗以為賞罰雖國之
柄而其命則出于天僭濫雖法之弊而其失則
由於君是惟無賞賞必及於有功作福之典與
===
民同之不以私喜或移而使賞有僭焉是惟無
罰罰不及於無辜止辟之令與衆共之不以私
怒或移而使罰有濫焉賞固不僭矣而戒懼之
心常存不僭於終猶其不僭於始也敢有於怠
遑乎刑雖不濫矣而寅畏之心愈切不濫於後
猶其不濫於前也敢有於怠逸乎夫政行於民
者公平正大而得以勸以懲之道民被其政者
懷德畏威而無不勸不懲之心上下交孚天人
合一高宗所以平荆楚服諸侯而致中興之盛
