punctuated: 之與民，觀其勢雖殊，究其理則一。彼監觀四方，天何嘗有目以視也？惟因民之視以為視。臨下有赫，天何嘗有耳以聽也？惟因民之聽以為聽。民之所予，天弗棄也，是雖匹庶之微，而天之耳目以在，不可畏哉？民之所棄，天弗予也，是雖丘民之賤，而天之聰明攸寄，不可畏哉？夫天人之間，其理無間如此。惟我高宗以為賞罰雖國之柄，而其命則出于天；僭濫雖法之弊，而其失則由於君。是惟無賞，賞必及於有功，作福之典與民同之，不以私喜或移而使賞有僭焉。是惟無罰，罰不及於無辜，止辟之令與衆共之，不以私怒或移而使罰有濫焉。賞固不僭矣，而戒懼之心常存，不僭於終，猶其不僭於始也，敢有於怠遑乎？刑雖不濫矣，而寅畏之心愈切，不濫於後，猶其不濫於前也，敢有於怠逸乎？夫政行於民者，公平正大，而得以勸以懲之道；民被其政者，懷德畏威，而無不勸不懲之心。上下交孚，天人合一，高宗所以平荆楚、服諸侯而致中興之盛
translation_en:
…As for Heaven and the people, although their positions appear different, their underlying principle is one. When Heaven “surveys the four quarters,” does it actually have eyes with which to see? It simply takes the people’s sight as its own. When it “looks down in radiant majesty,” does Heaven actually have ears with which to hear? It simply takes the people’s hearing as its own. What the people approve, Heaven does not reject. Thus, even in the humblest commoner, Heaven’s eyes and ears are present. Is this not to be feared? What the people reject, Heaven does not approve. Thus, even among the lowly masses, Heaven’s powers of hearing and sight reside. Is this not to be feared? Such is the seamless unity of principle between Heaven and humanity.

Our Gaozong considered that, although rewards and punishments are instruments of state authority, the mandate for them comes from Heaven; although undeserved rewards and excessive punishments are abuses of the law, responsibility for these failures lies with the ruler. Either he bestowed no reward, or, when he rewarded, it invariably went to those with merit. He shared with the people the standards for bestowing blessings, never allowing personal pleasure to alter them and cause rewards to go to the undeserving. Either he imposed no punishment, or, when he punished, it never fell upon the innocent. He shared with the multitude the ordinances for restraining wrongdoing [?], never allowing personal anger to alter them and cause punishments to become excessive.

Though his rewards were indeed never undeserved, he constantly maintained a vigilant and apprehensive heart: he avoided undeserved rewards at the end just as at the beginning. How could he dare become negligent or idle? Though his punishments were never excessive, his reverence and awe grew still more earnest: he avoided excess later just as he had earlier. How could he dare lapse into indolence and ease?

The government he exercised over the people was impartial, equitable, upright, and open, attaining the proper way to encourage good and deter wrongdoing. The people who received his government cherished his virtue and feared his authority; none failed to feel encouraged toward good and deterred from wrongdoing. Those above and below trusted one another, and Heaven and humanity became one. The means by which Gaozong pacified Jingchu, brought the feudal lords into submission, and achieved the flourishing restoration of his dynasty…

translation_en:
…there was indeed a Way by which Gaozong accomplished this! Yet this Way was something Gaozong had received from another. The Charge to Yue says: “Heaven alone is perceptive and discerning; the sage takes it as his model.” It also says: “Offices must not be given to private favorites, but only to the capable; ranks must not be bestowed upon those of bad character, but only upon the worthy.” He did not rely upon his exalted position, but took a worthy and sagely minister as his teacher; he did not merely delight in that minister’s words, but actually put them into practice. Spring and Autumn Annals

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
覲禮春秋貶之盖朝覲禮也苟因寓因事以舉
之則似禮而非禮矣春秋書所書如以致意也
有以哉昔者周襄之下勞於晉也駐蹕衡雍之
間俯順晉文之請於是乎諸侯各以其職来朝
而我僖亦與至止之列當是時也以上臨下冠
履之大分明矣而君子曰否盖以天子巡狩既
有其時而受朝各有其地今襄之是行以年則
非巡狩之期以地則非方嶽之所宮室辦於倉
卒玉帛委於草野宿衛疎簡不足以聳百辟之
===
觀瞻禮儀荒畧不足以備一王之制度是得為
正乎春秋於是不以就朝者為非而書王所以
正之者以君之於臣天道也父道也不可不正
以臨下而立其大本也其望於周室者何厚哉
至若晉厲之修怨於秦也既欲由王都而行豈
可越天子而往於是乎諸侯稟入覲之職我成
亦有載見之行方是時也以臣尊君天地之大
綱立矣而君子曰慢盖以諸侯朝聘既有其制
而述職亦有其時今諸侯是朝也既非時王之

而述職亦有其時今諸侯是朝也既非時王之
punctuated: 覲禮，《春秋》貶之。盖朝覲，禮也；苟因寓、因事以舉之，則似禮而非禮矣。《春秋》書「所」、書「如」以致意也，有以哉！昔者周襄之下勞於晉也，駐蹕衡雍之間，俯順晉文之請。於是乎諸侯各以其職来朝，而我僖亦與至止之列。當是時也，以上臨下，冠履之大分明矣，而君子曰：「否。」盖以天子巡狩既有其時，而受朝各有其地。今襄之是行，以年則非巡狩之期，以地則非方嶽之所。宮室辦於倉卒，玉帛委於草野，宿衛疎簡，不足以聳百辟之觀瞻；禮儀荒畧，不足以備一王之制度。是得為正乎？《春秋》於是不以就朝者為非，而書「王所」以正之者，以君之於臣，天道也，父道也，不可不正以臨下，而立其大本也。其望於周室者何厚哉！至若晉厲之修怨於秦也，既欲由王都而行，豈可越天子而往？於是乎諸侯稟入覲之職，我成亦有載見之行。方是時也，以臣尊君，天地之大綱立矣，而君子曰：「慢。」盖以諸侯朝聘既有其制，而述職亦有其時。今諸侯是朝也，既非時王之
translation_en:
…the rites of audience, the Spring and Autumn Annals censures them. Court audiences are indeed a matter of ritual; yet if they are held merely because the king happens to be lodging somewhere, or because another undertaking provides the occasion, they resemble ritual without being true ritual. The Annals has good reason for conveying its meaning by writing “the place” (suo) and “went to” (ru)!

Formerly, when King Xiang of Zhou went down to commend Jin, he halted his royal carriage in the vicinity of Hengyong and condescended to grant Duke Wen of Jin’s request. The feudal lords thereupon came to court, each in fulfillment of his duty, and our Duke Xi of Lu was also among those who arrived. At that moment, the superior presided over his inferiors, and the fundamental distinction between crown and shoes—that is, between ruler and subjects—was clear. Yet the gentleman says, “It was not right.” For the Son of Heaven’s inspection tours have their appointed times, and the reception of court audiences has its designated places. On this journey of King Xiang’s, however, the year was not one appointed for an inspection tour, nor was the location one of the sacred mountains of the four quarters. Royal quarters were hastily prepared; jade and silk offerings lay in the open countryside. The palace guards were too few and their arrangements too lax to inspire awe among the assembled lords; the ceremonies were too crude and abbreviated to fulfill the institutions of a royal dynasty. Could this be considered proper?

The Annals therefore does not fault those who came to attend court. Instead, it writes “the king’s place” to correct the king, because the ruler’s relation to his subjects follows the way of Heaven and the way of a father. He must preside over those below with rectitude, thereby establishing the great foundation. How exacting are its expectations of the house of Zhou!

As for Duke Li of Jin’s settling his grievance with Qin, since he intended to travel through the royal capital, how could he pass the Son of Heaven and proceed on his way? The feudal lords accordingly undertook their duty to enter and have audience, and our Duke Cheng of Lu likewise made the journey to appear before the king. At that moment, subjects honored their ruler, and the great ordering principles of Heaven and Earth stood established. Yet the gentleman says, “It was disrespectful.” For the feudal lords’ court audiences and diplomatic visits have their prescribed regulations, and their reports on the discharge of their duties also have appointed times. Now this audience of the feudal lords accorded neither with the reigning king’s…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
制又非述職之時投會伐之戈以陳玉帛借道
途之便以覲闕庭辨色而入有稽首下拜之虚
文鳴玉而趨無天顔咫尺之誠意是得為敬乎
春秋於是不以僅見者為幸而書如以貶之者
以臣之於君地道也子道也不可不敬以事上
而厚乎大倫也其尊乎周室也何至哉吁大本
立推之以盡君道而朝廷無不正大倫厚推之
以盡臣道而藩屏無不固春秋一所一如之書
而治道咸備垂世立教之功有如此哉猶有說
焉周襄實親下勞也則削而不書以全名會伐
本先如京也則書為遂事以存禮或隱或顯或
先或後皆以為王也後之為君臣者其有鑒於
斯

制，又非述職之時，投會伐之戈以陳玉帛，借道途之便以覲闕庭。辨色而入，有稽首下拜之虚文；鳴玉而趨，無天顔咫尺之誠意。是得為敬乎？《春秋》於是不以僅見者為幸，而書「如」以貶之者，以臣之於君，地道也，子道也，不可不敬以事上，而厚乎大倫也。其尊乎周室也何至哉！吁！大本立，推之以盡君道，而朝廷無不正；大倫厚，推之以盡臣道，而藩屏無不固。《春秋》一「所」、一「如」之書，而治道咸備，垂世立教之功有如此哉！猶有說焉：周襄實親下勞也，則削而不書以全名；會伐本先如京也，則書為遂事以存禮。或隱或顯，或先或後，皆以為王也。後之為君臣者，其有鑒於斯！

translation_en:
…prescribed regulations, nor was it the proper time to report on their duties. They set aside the spears of their joint campaign to present jade and silk, taking advantage of their route to seek an audience at the royal court. Entering at first light, they performed the empty formalities of knocking their heads to the ground and bowing low; hastening forward with their jade pendants sounding, they lacked the sincerity appropriate to standing close before the royal countenance. Can this count as reverence? Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals does not regard the mere occurrence of an audience as a fortunate thing, but records “went to” (ru) to censure it. For the minister’s relation to his ruler follows the way of Earth and the way of a son: he must serve his superior reverently and thereby strengthen this cardinal relationship. How far-reaching is its reverence for the house of Zhou! Ah! Once the great foundation is established, extending it to fulfill the ruler’s way leaves nothing in the court unrectified; once the cardinal relationship is strengthened, extending it to fulfill the minister’s way leaves none of the realm’s protective bulwarks insecure. In its recording of a single “place” (suo) and a single “went to” (ru), the Spring and Autumn Annals encompasses the whole way of government. Such is its achievement in establishing teachings for generations to come!
There is still more to say. King Xiang of Zhou actually went down in person to commend his subordinates, but the text omits this to preserve his royal standing. The visit to the capital actually preceded the joint campaign, but the text records it as a subsequent action to preserve ritual propriety. Whether concealing or revealing, placing earlier or later, all is done for the king’s sake. May those who later serve as rulers and ministers take warning from this!
“The Earl of Shan returned from Qi” 〔Fifteenth year of Duke Wen〕; “Shusun She returned from Jin” 〔Twenty-fourth year of Duke Zhao〕.
Wang Ning

text:
詞簡意足而理亦精到可嘉
同考試官編修李批春秋於二臣歸國

時我行人有所謂單伯者使齊而坐商人之忌
見執而勞行父之請齊人釋之於是乎始歸國
焉夫大夫執而致則名單伯胡為而不名盖單
伯以監國為任而簡策出於內史以圻邑為號
而位服掌於宗伯乃王之命大夫也名位既殊
則禮數亦異苟以其被誣見執而名之是以列
國之禮而等天王之尊矣其可乎故春秋書其
至自齊而不名者所以貴之也所以尊王命也
所以謹臣禮也及昭公之世我行人有所謂叔

Its rules are most exacting. This composition alone explains the matter clearly and therefore deserves inclusion.

Examiner Liu, a Grand Secretary, comments: It grasps the fundamental intent of the principles governing the wording of the Annals.

When a royally appointed minister returns to his state, the Spring and Autumn Annals varies its wording to honor him; when a worthy minister returns to his state, it varies its wording to acknowledge his worth. There is indeed good reason why, in recording Shan Bo’s and Shusun’s arrivals from Qi and Jin, the Annals omits their personal names, using instead a courtesy name in one case and a clan designation in the other!

In the time of Duke Wen, an envoy of our state called Shan Bo went on a mission to Qi. He incurred Shangren’s suspicion and was detained, requiring Xingfu to petition for his release. The men of Qi released him, and only then did he return to his state. Now, when a grandee has been detained and his return is recorded, his personal name is given. Why, then, is Shan Bo not named? Shan Bo was charged with overseeing the state, and the tablets of his appointment issued from the Interior Scribe. His designation derived from a fief within the royal domain, while his rank and official robes fell under the authority of the Minister of Rites. He was thus a grandee appointed by the king. Since his status and rank were distinct, the ceremonial treatment accorded him was also different. If his personal name were given merely because he had been falsely accused and detained, this would apply the ritual standards of the various states to the dignity of the Heavenly King, placing them on the same level. Could that be permissible? Thus, when the Spring and Autumn Annals records his arrival from Qi without giving his personal name, it does so to honor him, to respect the royal appointment, and to uphold scrupulously the ritual obligations of a subject. text:
於舍者以邾人之故而被拘於晋沮申豐之請
而久館於箕彌牟逆之於是乎始返魯焉夫大
夫執而致則名叔孫胡為而不名盖叔孫守身
以禮法之嚴而不屈抑於強晋事主以忠誠之
節而不阿附於強臣乃國之良大夫也忠誠顯

辱命之臣而視忠節之士矣其忍乎故春秋書

於舍者，以邾人之故而被拘於晋，沮申豐之請而久館於箕，彌牟逆之，於是乎始返魯焉。夫大夫執而致則名，叔孫胡為而不名？盖叔孫守身以禮法之嚴，而不屈抑於強晋；事主以忠誠之節，而不阿附於強臣，乃國之良大夫也。忠誠顯著，則體貌有加。苟因其奉使被執而名之，是以辱命之臣而視忠節之士矣，其忍乎？故《春秋》書其至自晋而不名者，所以賢之也，所以表其節也，所以勸後世也。吁！貴命臣，則專命者知所警，而君臣之大分以正；賢良臣，則無良者知所愧，而節義之大閑以立。尊卑賢否之際，書法各有攸當，《春秋》之旨，其嚴矣哉！雖然，命臣可重也，而不辱君命者尤可重；良臣可嘉也，而任用忠良者尤可嘉。惜單伯自棄，有孤天子之休命，而昭公棄賢，終為寓公於他國。嗚呼！其可感也夫！

禮記
審樂以知政，而治道備矣。

translation_en:
…[Shusun] She [?] was detained in Jin on account of the people of Zhu. He rebuffed Shen Feng’s request and remained lodged for a long time at Ji. Mi Mou came to meet him, and only then did he return to Lu. Now, when a grand master has been detained and his return is recorded, his personal name is given. Why, then, is Shusun not named? Shusun maintained his conduct with strict observance of ritual and law, refusing to submit to powerful Jin; he served his lord with loyalty and integrity, refusing to curry favor with powerful ministers. He was thus a worthy grand master of his state. When loyalty is manifest, the respect accorded a man should be increased. If he were named merely because he had been detained while carrying out a mission, this would be to treat a man of loyalty and integrity as a minister who had disgraced his commission. How could one bear to do so? Thus, when the Spring and Autumn Annals records his arrival from Jin without giving his personal name, it recognizes his worth, honors his integrity, and encourages later generations.

Ah! When royally commissioned ministers are honored, those who arrogate authority to themselves know to take warning, and the fundamental distinction between ruler and minister is set right. When worthy ministers are esteemed, the unworthy know shame, and the great bounds of integrity and righteousness are established. In distinguishing the exalted from the lowly and the worthy from the unworthy, the conventions of recording each have their proper application. How exacting are the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals! Nevertheless, a royally commissioned minister deserves respect, but one who does not disgrace his ruler’s commission deserves still greater respect. A worthy minister deserves praise, but one who employs loyal and worthy men deserves still greater praise. Alas, Shan Bo abandoned his own standing and failed to live up to the Son of Heaven’s gracious commission, while Duke Zhao rejected the worthy and ended as an exiled lord residing in another state. Ah! How deeply this moves one!

Record of Rites
“Examine music to understand government, and the Way of governing is fully comprehended.”
Wan Chao

道與政通也君子審樂以知政則其觀於樂者

為能知樂而推言之謂夫君子之於樂不獨其
辨析之精而又有會通之妙彼其樂之聲音固
皆通乎倫理而政事之得失若非盡於審樂之

Recent interpretations explain it as “being fully put into effect,” which goes still further astray. This essay seamlessly incorporates the sense of “being fully discerned” and also connects it extensively with practice [?], thus coming close to a complete account of what it means to understand music.

Comment by Examiner Jin, a Hanlin Academician: The explanation of examining music to understand government is clear.

The gentleman’s contemplation of music has profound significance, and through it the principles of governance are grasped. The way of sounds communicates with government. When the gentleman examines music to understand government, his contemplation of music is indeed profound. How could the way of governing be grasped apart from this? The author of the Record discusses how only the gentleman can understand music and develops this point further: in his approach to music, the gentleman possesses not only precision in discriminating and analyzing, but also a marvelous capacity to comprehend its interconnections. The sounds of music certainly all communicate with the ordered patterns of human relationships; yet the successes and failures of government might seem not to fall entirely within what examining music can reveal.

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
臣之政無不宜若宫荒而商陂則知其君臣之
理失矣如審樂之角徵羽而咸得其所歟則知
民事物之政無不當若角憂徵哀而羽危則知
其民事物之理失矣夫政固可於樂而知而治
道之多端若非盡於審樂之所能舉也然而君
子之審樂知政不徒知政之得而已而又有以
識其政之所以得蓋窮深極微而凡其設施措
置之方無不素定也不徒知政之失而已而又
有以究其政之所以失蓋拔本塞源而凡其拯
救改革之宜靡不默識也若何而君臣之道盡
若何而君臣之道虧必將行其所以盡者而去
其所以虧者則立政之具不出於審樂而可以
盡得矣若何而民事物之理得若何而民事物
之理失必將從其所以得者而背其所以失者
則為治之道不假於他求而既已備足矣是則
樂不徒審也而有以知夫政政不徒知也而有
以達夫治非禮樂皆得而明夫制作之原者其
孰能與於此嘗觀季札聘魯觀歷代之樂而論

translation_en:
…the governance of ruler and ministers is entirely fitting. But if the gong tone is disordered and the shang tone uneven, one knows that the proper relationship between ruler and ministers has been lost. Likewise, if, on examining the music, one finds that the jue, zhi, and yu tones each occupy their proper place, one knows that the governance of the people, affairs, and material things is entirely appropriate. But if jue is sorrowful, zhi mournful, and yu precarious, one knows that the proper ordering of the people, affairs, and material things has been lost.

Government can indeed be understood through music, yet the many aspects of the Way of governance would seem to exceed what examining music alone can encompass. Nevertheless, when the gentleman examines music to understand government, he does not merely recognize its successes: he also discerns why it succeeds. By plumbing the depths and pursuing the finest subtleties, he has already settled in his mind every method of putting measures into effect and arranging affairs. Nor does he merely recognize governmental failures: he also investigates why government fails. By rooting out the causes and stopping them at their source, he inwardly apprehends every appropriate means of remedy and reform.

What brings the Way of ruler and ministers to fulfillment, and what impairs it? He will assuredly implement what fulfills it and eliminate what impairs it. Thus all the means of establishing government can be acquired through examining music. What secures the proper ordering of the people, affairs, and material things, and what causes it to be lost? He will assuredly follow what secures it and turn away from what causes its loss. Thus the Way of governance is already fully provided for, without needing to seek elsewhere.

Music, then, is not merely examined: through it government can be understood. Government is not merely understood: through it mastery of good governance can be attained. Who could participate in this unless he comprehended both ritual and music and understood the source from which institutions were created? title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
所謂仁人不過乎物者以其盡理而不違也而
理之大者孰有加於仁孝乎彼事親者不嫌於
無愛而所嫌者無敬也愛而弗敬則父子之間
或幾於褻矣仁人之事親也雖和氣愉色之時
而執玉捧盈之心未嘗不嚴雖怡聲下氣之中
而臨深履薄之戒未始不肅一舉足而不敢傷
一出言而不敢忘何惕厲也愛之則嘉而弗忘
惡之則懼而弗怨何奉順也如是則所以事親
者不異於事天矣何有於褻哉事天者不嫌於
===
無敬而所嫌者無愛也敬而弗愛則天人之情
或幾於疎矣仁人之事天也知乾父坤母之道
而精神志意實與之流通推民胞物與之義而
天下國家若為之一體存心養性而無忝所生
盖不忍失其所受也富貴貧賤而順受其正盖
不忍拂其所施也如是則所以事天者不異於
事親矣而何有於疎哉夫事親如天則孝之道
以全事天如親則仁之道以備仁人不過乎物
有如是夫抑是義也孔子以之告哀公盖欲其

translation_en:
…What is meant by saying that the benevolent person does not overstep the proper bounds of things is that he fulfills principle without departing from it. And among the great expressions of principle, what surpasses benevolence and filial piety? In serving one’s parents, the concern is not a lack of love but a lack of reverence. With love but without reverence, relations between father and son may verge on undue familiarity. When the benevolent person serves his parents, even amid harmonious feelings and a cheerful countenance, his mind remains as solemn as when holding jade or carrying a brimming vessel. Even while speaking pleasantly and humbly, he maintains the vigilance of one standing above a deep abyss or treading on thin ice. At every step he dares not injure himself; with every utterance he dares not forget his parents. How watchful and circumspect he is! When they love him, he rejoices and does not forget it; when they dislike him, he is apprehensive but does not resent them. How obedient and compliant he is! Thus, his manner of serving his parents is no different from serving Heaven. How could there be undue familiarity?

In serving Heaven, the concern is not a lack of reverence but a lack of love. With reverence but without love, the bond between Heaven and humanity may verge on estrangement. When the benevolent person serves Heaven, he understands the Way by which Qian is father and Kun is mother, and his spirit, purpose, and intentions truly communicate with them. He extends the principle that the people are his siblings and all things his companions, so that all under Heaven, the state, and the family seem to form one body with him. He preserves his mind and nourishes his nature, bringing no disgrace upon that which gave him birth, because he cannot bear to lose what he has received. In wealth and honor or poverty and low station, he submissively accepts what is rightly allotted, because he cannot bear to oppose what Heaven bestows. Thus, his manner of serving Heaven is no different from serving his parents. How could there be estrangement?

Serving his parents as he serves Heaven, he fulfills the Way of filial piety; serving Heaven as he serves his parents, he completes the Way of benevolence. Such is the benevolent person’s not overstepping the proper bounds of things! Now, Kongzi explained this principle to Duke Ai because he wished him to…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
同而所感發之者周公獨異此其所以尤有不
容已者乎孟軻氏曰周公思兼三王以施四事
吾於是乎有以知周公之心矣周公之心純亦
不已之心也曷為其感之也時也勢也吾觀自
古聖人處世故之難操心危而慮患深未有如
周公者也武王沒周公相成王以治天下以身
任天下之重而當乎天下之甚難任天下之重
則天下求乎我者不輕也當天下之甚難則天
下之所以責我者亦不小也周公所以有感於
===
此汲汲皇皇仰思而俯得繼夜而待旦有不容
自己者非好勞也宜也吾想周公之心以其身
任天下而以天下為一身思天下之大商人酗
酒之化有未殄于妹邦者乎猶吾之為酒困也
思天下之大有未能胥訓告者乎猶吾訑訑之
聲音也思天下之大有人用側頗僻者乎民用
僭忒者乎猶吾之作好惡而弗中弗極也思天
下之大有非德用乂智藏瘝在者乎猶吾之蔽
賢而不祥之大也思天下之大有不克明保享

同，而所感發之者，周公獨異，此其所以尤有不容已者乎？孟軻氏曰：「周公思兼三王以施四事。」吾於是乎有以知周公之心矣。周公之心，純亦不已之心也。曷為其感之也？時也，勢也。吾觀自古聖人處世故之難，操心危而慮患深，未有如周公者也。武王沒，周公相成王以治天下，以身任天下之重，而當乎天下之甚難。任天下之重，則天下求乎我者不輕也；當天下之甚難，則天下之所以責我者亦不小也。周公所以有感於此，汲汲皇皇，仰思而俯得，繼夜而待旦，有不容自己者，非好勞也，宜也。
吾想周公之心，以其身任天下，而以天下為一身。思天下之大，商人酗酒之化有未殄于妹邦者乎？猶吾之為酒困也。思天下之大，有未能胥訓告者乎？猶吾訑訑之聲音也。思天下之大，有人用側頗僻者乎？民用僭忒者乎？猶吾之作好惡而弗中弗極也。思天下之大，有非德用乂、智藏瘝在者乎？猶吾之蔽賢而不祥之大也。思天下之大，有不克明保享
translation_en:
…was the same; yet what stirred and moved the Duke of Zhou was uniquely different. Was this why he felt an especially irresistible urge to act? Meng Ke said, “The Duke of Zhou sought to combine the achievements of the Three Kings in carrying out four undertakings.” From this I can understand the Duke of Zhou’s heart. His was a heart of unceasing purity. What stirred it? The times and the circumstances. Looking back at the sages of antiquity, I see none who faced the difficulties of worldly affairs with such anxious vigilance and such profound concern for calamity as the Duke of Zhou. After King Wu died, the Duke of Zhou assisted King Cheng in governing the realm. He personally shouldered its weightiest responsibilities while confronting its gravest difficulties. When I shoulder the realm’s weightiest responsibilities, what the realm asks of me cannot be slight; when I confront its gravest difficulties, what the realm holds me accountable for cannot be small. Moved by this, the Duke of Zhou labored anxiously and urgently, looking upward in reflection and downward to find understanding, continuing through the night and awaiting dawn, unable to restrain himself. This was not a fondness for toil: it was what duty required.
I imagine the Duke of Zhou’s heart: he took responsibility for the realm upon himself and regarded the realm as a single body—his own. He thought: “In this vast realm, might the Shang people’s habit of excessive drinking still remain uneradicated in the land of Mei? It would be as though I myself were overcome by drink. In this vast realm, might there be those who still fail to instruct and admonish one another? It would be as though my own voice were arrogantly self-satisfied. In this vast realm, might there be officials whose conduct is biased and perverse, or common people who transgress and err? It would be as though my own likes and dislikes departed from due balance and the proper standard. In this vast realm, might there be those who govern without virtue, leaving the wise in obscurity and the unworthy in office? It would be as though I myself concealed worthy men—the greatest of evils. In this vast realm, might there be those unable to provide enlightened protection and enjoy…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
于民者乎猶吾之恫瘝在身也思天下之大有
非天攸若非民攸訓者乎猶吾之弗克嗣前人
恭明德也有役耳目玩人物者乎猶吾之蔽於
近習也思天下之大海表有不服戎兵有不詰
者乎猶吾之忘遠慮也此周公所以夜思而待
旦汲汲皇皇而不能自已者也是故周公之心
以為吾之家法幸有文武者在不泄邇武王也
不忘遠亦武王也視民如傷文王也望道而未
之見亦文王也吾思之未能焉吾孰若上兼乎
===
文武兼乎文武未能吾不已也文王之上數百
年而有湯者執中湯也立賢無方亦湯也吾思
之未能焉吾又孰若上兼乎湯兼乎湯未能吾
不已也湯之上又數百年而有禹者惡旨酒禹
也好善言亦禹也吾思之未能焉吾又孰若上
兼乎禹兼乎禹弗能吾不已也此其憂勤惕厲
之心純亦不已之誠天理所以常存而人心所
以不泯也自今觀之無逸之戒酗于酒德是惡
旨酒周公優為之矣握髮吐哺以来賢士則好

translation_en:
…among the people? He would feel their suffering as though it afflicted his own body. Considering the vastness of the realm, were there those who failed to accord with Heaven or instruct the people? He would regard this as his own failure to carry on his predecessors’ reverent cultivation of illustrious virtue. Were there those who enslaved their ears and eyes to pleasures and treated people and things as playthings? He would regard this as though he himself were blinded by his intimate attendants. Considering the vastness of the realm, were there lands beyond the seas that had not submitted, or military preparations that had not been put in order? He would regard this as his own neglect of long-term concerns. This is why the Duke of Zhou pondered through the night until dawn, anxious and restless, unable to stop.

Thus the Duke of Zhou thought: “Fortunately, our house has the examples of Kings Wen and Wu. Not treating those nearby with careless familiarity was King Wu’s practice; not forgetting those far away was also King Wu’s practice. Caring for the people as though they were injured was King Wen’s practice; looking toward the Way as though he had yet to see it was also King Wen’s practice. I reflect on these things but have not attained them. What better course could I take than to reach back and embody the virtues of both Wen and Wu? Until I can embody them, I shall not cease. Several hundred years before King Wen there was Tang. Holding fast to the mean was Tang’s practice; appointing the worthy without restriction was also Tang’s practice. I reflect on these things but have not attained them. What better course could I take than to reach further back and embody Tang’s virtues as well? Until I can embody them, I shall not cease. Several hundred years before Tang there was Yu. Disliking fine wine was Yu’s practice; delighting in good counsel was also Yu’s practice. I reflect on these things but have not attained them. What better course could I take than to reach further back and embody Yu’s virtues as well? Until I can embody them, I shall not cease.”

Such was his anxious, diligent, vigilant, and earnest heart, and his sincerity, pure and unceasing. Through these, Heaven’s principle endured constantly and the human moral heart was never extinguished. title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
善言者周公優為之矣其命蔡仲以率自中是
執中者周公優為之矣勿以憸人其惟吉士是
立賢無方者周公優為之矣和恒四方師保萬
民是視民如傷者周公優為之矣公孫碩膚赤
舄几几是望道而未見者周公優為之矣咸秩
無文無逺用戾是不忘逺者周公優為之矣王
宫近習皆隸冢宰則不泄邇者周公優為之矣
優為之而猶思所以兼之其聖不自聖純亦不
已之誠周公所以不可及者以是哉其作禮樂
===
===
立六典以致太平越裳来朝而鳳鳥至盖皆推
三王之意而達之政者周公感發之心於是少
慰而純亦不已者自若也且三王之所為各一
事爾然則周公於是固將事事學之乎曰思曰

通是故思兼乎禹者旨酒善言也則凡有類於

punctuated:
善言者，周公優為之矣。其命蔡仲以率自中，是執中者，周公優為之矣。「勿以憸人，其惟吉士」，是立賢無方者，周公優為之矣。「和恒四方，師保萬民」，是視民如傷者，周公優為之矣。「公孫碩膚，赤舄几几」，是望道而未見者，周公優為之矣。「咸秩無文，無逺用戾」，是不忘逺者，周公優為之矣。王宫近習皆隸冢宰，則不泄邇者，周公優為之矣。優為之而猶思所以兼之，其聖不自聖，純亦不已之誠，周公所以不可及者以是哉！其作禮樂，立六典，以致太平，越裳来朝而鳳鳥至，盖皆推三王之意而達之政者。周公感發之心於是少慰，而純亦不已者自若也。

且三王之所為各一事爾，然則周公於是固將事事學之乎？曰：「思曰睿，睿作聖。」不思則不能通微，不睿則不能無不通。是故思兼乎禹者，旨酒善言也，則凡有類於旨酒善言者，可以通之矣；思兼乎湯者，執中立賢也，則凡有類於執中而立賢者，可以通之矣；思兼乎文王者，視民望道也，則凡有類於視民
translation_en:
…As for loving good counsel, the Duke of Zhou amply accomplished this. In commanding Cai Zhong to follow the mean, he amply accomplished the holding fast to the mean. “Do not employ crafty men; employ only worthy gentlemen”: in this, he amply accomplished the appointment of worthy men without restriction. “Bring harmony and constancy to the four quarters; act as teacher and protector to the myriad people”: in this, he amply accomplished caring for the people as though they were injured. “The duke is modest in his great virtue; his red slippers move with measured dignity”: in this, he amply accomplished seeking the Way as though he had not yet seen it. “Give due order even to what is not prescribed; none from afar fail to come”: in this, he amply accomplished not forgetting those far away. All the palace intimates were subordinate to the Grand Steward: in this, he amply accomplished not neglecting those nearby. Though he amply accomplished these things, he still reflected on how to unite their virtues in himself. A sage who did not regard himself as a sage, possessing a sincerity that was pure and unceasing—was this not what made the Duke of Zhou beyond compare? His establishment of rites and music and institution of the six codes of government brought about great peace; Yueshang came to court, and phoenixes appeared. These were all, surely, instances of extending the intentions of the Three Kings and realizing them in government. The Duke of Zhou’s inspired aspirations thereby found some consolation, yet his pure and unceasing sincerity remained as before.

Moreover, the deeds of the Three Kings were each particular acts. Was the Duke of Zhou therefore necessarily going to imitate them act by act? It is said: “Reflection produces perspicacity; perspicacity makes one a sage.” Without reflection, one cannot penetrate subtleties; without perspicacity, one cannot comprehend everything. Thus, when he reflected on embodying Yu’s virtues, these concerned fine wine and good counsel; he could then extend his understanding to everything analogous to fine wine and good counsel. When he reflected on embodying Tang’s virtues, these concerned holding fast to the mean and appointing the worthy; he could then extend his understanding to everything analogous to holding fast to the mean and appointing the worthy. When he reflected on embodying King Wen’s virtues, these concerned caring for the people and seeking the Way; thus, everything analogous to caring for the people…

translation_en:
…and looking toward the Way: all things of this kind can thus be understood by extension. His thoughts encompassed King Wu’s refusal to slight those nearby or forget those far away; thus, all things resembling such refusal to slight or forget can likewise be understood by extension. Developing these insights through analogous cases, drawing them out and extending them—how could his heart, unceasing in its purity, ever cease? Confucius said: “I no longer dream of seeing the Duke of Zhou.” Confucius, too, was a great sage. He once so admired the Duke of Zhou that he dreamed of him. Confucius’s heart shared with the Duke of Zhou’s heart the same unceasing sincerity. This is what made them great sages.

Comment by Associate Examiner An, Supervising Secretary: When candidates compose discourses, they are generally constrained by the facts, and their phrasing and conception fail to portray the Duke of Zhou’s heart. This composition simply follows the facts and proceeds in an unassuming manner, yet its openings and closings, rises and falls, all observe proper compositional principles. Here is an outstanding and effortless talent.

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Hanlin Compiler: How could Mencius have expressed those four characters, “His thoughts encompassed the Three Kings,” had he not penetrated the Duke of Zhou’s innermost concerns? This reveals precisely what sages and worthies have in common. This essay traces the matter from beginning to end, exploring it repeatedly over several hundred words, and brings out Mencius’s meaning as well. Moreover, its conclusion attributes the credit to King Cheng: this is an especially sound judgment. For this reason, it has been included here as an additional selection.

Comment by Examiner Jin, Academician: Its spirit is vigorous, its language magnificent, and its account of the Duke of Zhou’s heart is also apt.

text:

善於為文者錄之不厭其複也
聖人身任天下之重而思所以自處者亦惟於
前聖已行者而求之焉夫周公聖人也禹湯文
武之儔也其才藝之美豈不足用以治天下哉
而必於其已行者追思而仰求之盖以其時勢
不同而事為政理不能以皆合也苟不以其已

前乎三王有堯舜也自古稱治者必以堯舜為
首周公胡為而弗思哉誠以堯舜之時天下皆
安於無事而堯舜之心亦與天下相安及禹之
時則不然矣觀其言曰堯舜之民皆以堯舜之
心為心予之民各以其心為心則其時可知也
punctuated:
考試官大學士劉批：議論層出，華實兼具，蓋善於為文者，錄之不厭其複也。

聖人身任天下之重，而思所以自處者，亦惟於前聖已行者而求之焉。夫周公，聖人也，禹湯文武之儔也。其才藝之美，豈不足用以治天下哉？而必於其已行者追思而仰求之，盖以其時勢不同，而事為政理不能以皆合也。苟不以其已行者斟酌劑量，會其歸而一之，則天下之道不能本於一，而政不能出於一矣。况夫三聖人之道，行之前代而有效，著之家法而可稽。外是而自異，則必有非道之道、非治之治，而身任天下之責負矣。周公所以自處者，肯如是哉？嗚呼！此周公思兼禹湯文武之道，而所以慮之深也。且前乎三王，有堯舜也。自古稱治者，必以堯舜為首，周公胡為而弗思哉？誠以堯舜之時，天下皆安於無事，而堯舜之心亦與天下相安。及禹之時，則不然矣。觀其言曰：「堯舜之民，皆以堯舜之心為心；予之民，各以其心為心。」則其時可知也。
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Liu, Grand Secretary: Arguments unfold in successive layers, combining literary elegance with substance. This is indeed the work of someone skilled in composition; I do not tire of including it, despite its repetition.

When a sage personally bears the weight of responsibility for all under Heaven and considers how to conduct himself, he seeks guidance only in what earlier sages have already put into practice. The Duke of Zhou was a sage, a peer of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu. Could his outstanding abilities and accomplishments possibly have been insufficient to govern all under Heaven? Yet he insisted on reflecting upon what those sages had practiced and looking up to it for guidance. This was because the circumstances of their times differed, so their undertakings and methods of government could not all coincide. Unless he weighed and assessed their practices, brought together their underlying aims, and unified them, the Way for all under Heaven could not rest upon a single foundation, nor could government proceed from a single source. Moreover, the Way of the three sages had proved effective when practiced in earlier ages and was recorded in dynastic precedents that could be examined. To depart from this and strike out on a different course would inevitably produce a way that was not the true Way and a government that was not true government; he would thereby betray the responsibility for all under Heaven that he personally bore. Would the Duke of Zhou have been willing to conduct himself in this manner? Ah! This explains the depth of his deliberation in seeking to embrace the Ways of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu.

Furthermore, before the Three Kings there were Yao and Shun. Since antiquity, those who speak of good government have invariably placed Yao and Shun first. Why, then, did the Duke of Zhou not reflect upon them? It was truly because, in the time of Yao and Shun, all under Heaven rested peacefully, free from troubles, and the hearts of Yao and Shun were likewise at peace with all under Heaven. By Yu’s time, however, this was no longer so. Consider his words: “The people of Yao and Shun all took the hearts of Yao and Shun as their own hearts; my people each take their own heart as their heart.” From this, the conditions of his time can be understood.

title: 正德六年會試錄

及湯之時則又不然矣觀其言曰有衆率怠弗
協則其時可知也及文武之時則又不然矣觀
其言曰今我民罔弗欲喪則其時又可知也夫
禹湯文武去堯舜之時才數百載而其心已不
能不為之自處於是思所以檢身之道思所以
興邦之助思所以求道之方旨酒是惡也善言

心盖思天下必不能無事而其所以為當世計

punctuated: 及湯之時，則又不然矣。觀其言曰：「有衆率怠弗協。」則其時可知也。及文武之時，則又不然矣。觀其言曰：「今我民罔弗欲喪。」則其時又可知也。夫禹湯文武去堯舜之時才數百載，而其心已不能不為之自處。於是思所以檢身之道，思所以興邦之助，思所以求道之方：旨酒是惡也，善言是拜也，中是執也，立賢無方也，視民如傷也，望道未見也，邇不泄而遠不忘也。夫是數聖人之心，盖思天下必不能無事，而其所以為當世計者固不淺矣。况周公之時，非禹湯也，非文武也，而勢之所在又不能與之皆合，周公所以慮深于中者，又豈特如禹湯文武而已哉！且周公之時何時也？武王既殁，成王嗣政，周公身任天下之重，而匡弼左右。以其位則冢宰也，以其親則叔父也，以其世則殷之頑民尚在、周之德化未洽也。是故有酣飲敗德者焉，是故有侮慢自賢者焉，是故有偏黨反側者焉，是故有朋仇脅權者焉，是故有敷虐肆毒者焉，是故有滅德作威
translation_en:
By the time of Tang, circumstances were different yet again. Consider his words: “The multitude are all indolent and fail to act in harmony.” From this we can understand his age. By the time of Kings Wen and Wu, circumstances were different yet again. Consider the words: “Now there is none among our people who does not desire his destruction.” From this too we can understand the age. Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu lived only a few hundred years after Yao and Shun, yet already they could not but consider how to conduct themselves in response to their circumstances. Thus they pondered ways to discipline themselves, sources of assistance in making the state flourish, and methods of seeking the Way: they abhorred fine wine; bowed upon hearing good counsel; held fast to the mean; appointed worthy men without restriction; regarded the people as though they were wounded; looked toward the Way as though they had not yet seen it; and neither treated those near them with undue familiarity nor forgot those far away. These sages surely reflected that the realm could not remain free of troubles, and their deliberations for their own times were indeed profound. How much more was this true in the Duke of Zhou’s time! His was neither the age of Yu and Tang nor that of Wen and Wu, and the circumstances he faced could not correspond to theirs in every respect. Could the depth of the Duke of Zhou’s inward concern, then, have been merely equal to that of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu?

And what sort of time was the Duke of Zhou’s? King Wu had died, and King Cheng had succeeded to the government. The Duke of Zhou personally bore the weighty responsibility for the realm, standing beside the king to guide and assist him. In office, he was Grand Steward; in kinship, the king’s paternal uncle. As for his age, the recalcitrant people of Yin still remained, and Zhou’s transforming moral influence had not yet spread everywhere. Thus there were those who drank to excess and ruined their virtue; those who were contemptuous and arrogant, deeming themselves worthy; those who formed partisan cliques and were disloyal; those who banded together in enmity and used power to intimidate [?]; those who spread cruelty and freely inflicted harm; and those who extinguished virtue and exercised tyrannical authority…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
者焉是故有忽近遺遠者焉夫舉天下之事與
人皆異於禹湯文武之時而以位以親以責又
皆集于吾身而望之使治則周公於此不能無
慮而亦不可以不慮也固矣夫聖人豈不能自
用其才藝以斡旋轉移而奠天下如禹湯文武
之世哉其心以為己之知識有限而聖人之道
行之自昔傳之後世斟酌於當時者或具於典
謨訓誥或具於禮樂名物吾固可得而知可得
而行可得而兼也况文武之丕顯丕承佑啓罔
===
缺而吾子若孫又在所當世守而行之者也顧
時雖不同而理同勢雖不一而理一事或宜於
前不宜於後則有理以為之裁制或宜於創業
不宜於守成則有理以為之審處或君之所行
有非吾相之所敢專者則有理以為之轉移苟
泥於時格於勢不能以理為之會通則徒負憂
勤而無以慰天下之望副身任之責周公所以
自處者固不如是也是故仰而思焉俯而求焉
使理之在禹湯文武者猶在我焉而我之所惡

translation_en: …there were such men; thus there were also those who neglected those nearby and disregarded those far away. All the affairs and people of the realm differed from those of the times of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu. Yet obligations arising from office, kinship, and responsibility all converged upon his own person, and he was expected to bring about good government. It was therefore certain that the Duke of Zhou could not be free of concern, nor could he permit himself to be unconcerned. Could a sage not employ his own talents and abilities to redirect affairs and bring stability to the realm, as in the ages of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu? In his heart, however, he thought: “My own knowledge is limited. Yet the Way of the sages, practiced since antiquity and transmitted to later generations, with adaptations to the circumstances of each age, is embodied either in the canons, counsels, instructions, and announcements, or in rites, music, and the names and forms of institutions and objects. These I can certainly come to know, put into practice, and bring together. Moreover, the great achievements of Wen and the great continuation of them by Wu, their assistance and guidance, left nothing lacking; these are also what our sons and grandsons ought to preserve and practice from generation to generation.” Although the times differ, the principle remains the same; although circumstances vary, the principle is one. If something is appropriate to an earlier time but not to a later one, principle provides the means to determine and regulate it. If something is appropriate to founding a dynasty but not to maintaining its accomplishments, principle provides the means to consider and handle it. If a ruler performs acts over which I, as his minister, would not dare claim independent authority, principle provides the means to adapt them. If one clings to the times and is constrained by circumstances, unable to use principle to reconcile and integrate them, one merely bears the burden of anxious toil, without satisfying the expectations of the realm or fulfilling the responsibilities one has undertaken. This was certainly not how the Duke of Zhou conducted himself. Thus he looked upward in reflection and bent downward in inquiry, so that the principle embodied in Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu might likewise reside in himself, and what he abhorred…

text:
所拜所執所立所視所望所不泄而忘者猶禹
湯文武也盖必如是而後吾之相天下之責可
以無媿矣故自今觀之鄉飲之禮終日百拜以
去酒禍而康叔之誥戒諄諄懇至禹之惡旨酒
也瞽矇諷誦士傳民語以及徽言之受民謠之
采禹之拜善言也克自抑畏天命自度以至所
其無逸之言反復曉告其君湯執中文王之望
道也同姓異姓之封一視功能而吐哺握髮若
不自逸者則又湯之立賢無方也井田學校教

所拜、所執、所立、所視、所望、所不泄而忘者，猶禹、湯、文、武也。盖必如是，而後吾之相天下之責可以無媿矣。故自今觀之，鄉飲之禮，終日百拜，以去酒禍，而康叔之誥戒諄諄懇至，禹之惡旨酒也；瞽矇諷誦，士傳民語，以及徽言之受、民謠之采，禹之拜善言也；克自抑畏，天命自度，以至所其無逸之言，反復曉告其君，湯執中、文王之望道也；同姓異姓之封，一視功能，而吐哺握髮，若不自逸者，則又湯之立賢無方也；井田學校，教養斯民者，纖悉備具，而多士、多方之書，所以訓殷民者，惟恐逆其意，則又文王之視民如傷也；綴衣虎賁之賤，亦必擇人，以詔王之出入，而無文咸秩，無遠用戾，則又武之不泄邇忘遠也。故一時禮樂大備，刑措不用，《行葦》歌其忠厚，《既醉》嘉其太平。成周之治，直追三王之盛，而衍八百年之久者，要皆周公之功也。嗚呼！至是而後，周公慮天下之心可少釋矣。

雖然，輔君者，大臣之責；任大臣者，人君之責。向使羣叔獲行其言，王
translation_en:
…those before whom I bow, what I hold fast to, those whom I establish in office, how I regard the people, what I aspire to, and those whom I neither neglect nor forget would be as they were for Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu. Only then could I discharge my responsibility for assisting in the government of the realm without shame.

Viewed from our own time, the ceremony of communal drinking, with its hundred bows throughout the day to avert the evils of wine, and the earnest, heartfelt admonitions addressed to Kang Shu exemplified Yu’s aversion to fine wine. The blind musicians’ recitations, the officers’ transmission of the people’s words, the acceptance of excellent sayings, and the collection of popular songs exemplified Yu’s bowing before good counsel. The repeated explanations and admonitions to his ruler about exercising restraint and reverence, measuring oneself against Heaven’s mandate, and making freedom from ease one’s abiding concern exemplified Tang’s holding fast to the Mean and King Wen’s yearning for the Way. In granting fiefs to those of the royal surname and those of other surnames, he considered their achievements and abilities equally; he spat out his food and grasped his unbound hair to receive visitors, as though allowing himself no ease. This also exemplified Tang’s appointment of worthy men without restriction. The well-field system and schools, through which the people were nurtured and instructed, were provided in every detail. The documents “The Many Officers” and “The Many Regions,” which admonished the people of Yin, showed constant concern lest their sentiments be offended. This also exemplified King Wen’s care for the people as though they were wounded. Even for such humble duties as attending to the royal robes or serving as guards, men had to be carefully selected to guide the king as he went out and returned. “All without cultured refinement were duly ordered” [?], and none were too distant to be brought into accord. This also exemplified King Wu’s refusal to neglect those nearby or forget those far away.

Thus, in that age, rites and music were fully established, and punishments were set aside unused. “The Spreading Reeds” celebrated its generosity and kindness; “Already Drunk” praised its great peace. That the government of the established Zhou matched the flourishing rule of the Three Kings and endured for eight hundred years was, in essence, entirely the achievement of the Duke of Zhou. Ah! Only at this point could the Duke of Zhou’s concern for the realm be somewhat relieved.

Nevertheless, assisting the ruler is the responsibility of the great ministers; entrusting responsibilities to great ministers is the responsibility of the ruler. Had the royal uncles succeeded in having their words acted upon, the king…

translation_en:
Your servants, so-and-so and others, state: On the specified day and month of the Zhengde reign, we humbly received through Your Majesty’s sagely grace a bestowed copy of the Compendium of Essentials from the Comprehensive Mirror of Successive Dynasties (Lidai tongjian zuanyao). We respectfully reflect that, with the bamboo slips now compiled, the rise and decline of successive dynasties are fully set forth; with the command to bestow it issued from the vermilion court, the work initiated and carried forward across two reigns shines still more brightly. Our joy overflows in cries of delight; our honor surpasses that of receiving repeated royal gifts.

We venture to reflect that the government of emperors and kings is rooted in the Way: without examining antiquity, how could they govern the present? The learning of an enlightened ruler differs from that of other men: only by knowing the essentials can he hold fast to the fundamental principles. We reverently recall that the late emperor deeply cherished the teachings of the past. He considered Master Zhu’s Outline and Details of the Comprehensive Mirror (Tongjian gangmu) to have captured the purport of Confucius’s Spring and Autumn Annals. Yet the period preceding King Weilie of Zhou had not been brought together into a complete compilation, while the period from the founding emperor of the Song onward formed a separate work. Taking up these volumes, one sighed at their vast bulk; reading their text, one lacked ready material for enlightening and nourishing the imperial mind.

He therefore commanded his Confucian officials to compile a compendium of essentials. He personally settled its principles and conventions and selected its auspicious title in advance. He assigned the compilation work among offices of historiography and permitted the work to be presented and expounded at the Classics Colloquium. While we were still laboring diligently over the writing, we were suddenly stricken with grief at his death. The beginning of Your Majesty’s sagely and inspired rule coincided with the completion of this historical work. It was as though the undertaking had awaited this moment; the Way was not put into practice in vain.

The cultural undertakings of our illustrious court have been renewed, and the examples from the past that encourage good and warn against evil have at last been made manifest. Where the words bear directly upon the art of government, their judgments are indeed well grounded; where actions concern the ruler’s virtue, truly their inclusion…

以無遺。于刪繁就簡之中，有原始要終之妙，大彰數千年之殷監，聿洗十九史之彌文。事雖因舊以為新，體則似疎而實密。宸章煥爛，首垂龍鳳之文；玉板精明，中鮮豕魚之誤。載惟監觀意切，足徵父子之一心；至於將順情勞，尤見明良之合德。蓋自韋布之賤，罔不欲觀；謂有書契以來，未嘗見此。功非小補，裒會大成。爰煥發于殊恩，遂匪頒于近弼。無功是懼，厚德難酬。

translation_en:
…so that nothing is omitted. In pruning the profuse and making it concise, it wonderfully traces matters to their beginnings and brings their outcomes into view. It makes manifest the cautionary lessons of several thousand years and clears away the excessive verbiage of the Nineteen Histories. Though its material draws upon the old to produce something new, its structure, seemingly loose, is in fact closely knit. The imperial composition shines brilliantly, its dragon-and-phoenix writing gracing the opening; the exquisite printing blocks are clear and accurate, with few errors confusing similar characters, such as shi 豕 and yu 魚. Reflecting upon the earnest concern with which it was inspected, we find ample proof that father and son are of one mind. As for the devoted efforts to carry out the sovereign’s wishes, these especially reveal the concordant virtue of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers. Even humble scholars in plain clothing all wish to see it. They declare that since writing first existed, nothing like it has ever been seen. Its achievement is no small contribution: it gathers together a great synthesis. Thus exceptional imperial favor has been splendidly manifested, and gifts have been distributed to the sovereign’s close assistants [?]. We fear that we have rendered no service; such generous kindness is difficult to repay.
This is because we have humbly had the good fortune to serve Your Majesty the Emperor, endowed with sagely intelligence and commanding resolution, whose consummate nature communicates with the spirits. Embodying Heaven’s primal power, you carry forward the successive brilliance of the imperial line, capable of ruling and discerning the worthy. Establishing the sovereign standard, you rectify the people’s virtue, without faction or partiality. All your efforts to follow in your predecessor’s footsteps take as their model …

translation_en:
…the resolve to honor learning. This gracious bestowal further manifests Your Majesty’s filial devotion. In conferring blessings, you extend them throughout the common people; in bringing benefits to all, you naturally begin with the assembled officials. The community of scholars gains distinction, like a dazzling display of precious jade; humble dwellings shine, as though illuminated from afar by the sun and stars. In former times, Xun Yue’s Imperial Annals was presented to a Tang emperor, and Ban Gu’s Book of Han was distributed in the Song era. Their historical accounts concerned only a single dynasty, and their instructive judgments did not originate within the imperial palace. Even so, these acts were celebrated and lent glory to trustworthy history. How much more is this so of the present Mirror of Governance, which truly embodies Your Majesty’s sagacious counsels! Compared with what Han Xuanzi was able to view, our good fortune is already far greater; yet when we consider the learning that enabled Yi Xiang of Chu to read the ancient records, we privately feel ashamed.

How could we, your servants, fail to appreciate your solicitous care and diligently attend to our duties? We shall make this compilation a treasure handed down in our families and draw upon its principles to sustain our personal resolve to serve the state. The tracks of overturned carriages ahead will forever warn those following behind; the lofty mountain invites us to look upward, and we shall not shrink from the labor of adding even a single basketful of earth. We shall take goodness as our guide and teacher, hoping to follow the same path as good government. We humbly wish that Your Majesty will cultivate Gaozong’s learning that brought attainment and preserve King Cheng’s determination to avoid ease. Renewing yourself day after day, may you leave enduring provision for your descendants through ten thousand generations; sagacious without claiming sagacity, may your great renown stand foremost among the hundred kings. We, your servants, cannot contain our utmost feelings of reverence and ardor [?]. We respectfully present this memorial to express □ and thereby □…

translation_en:
…yet many could not carry their achievement through to the end, simply because arrogance and indolence overtook them. Our Taizu established the dynasty through righteousness and preserved its achievements through vigilance and diligence. His divine accomplishments and sagely virtue were equally suited to founding and preserving the dynasty; here precisely lies the method by which his sagely descendants should preserve their inheritance. This composition probes the roots and traces matters to their source, depicting them thoroughly and in detail. Presented to the sovereign, it may perhaps contribute, even in the smallest measure, to the way of taking him as a model.
Associate Examiner Cui, Compiler, comments: Our sagely founder’s achievement in expelling the barbarians was unprecedented in antiquity. As for his diligence and exertion amid hardship and danger, through which he accomplished his great undertaking, these are precisely what should command attention today, with thought given to preserving that undertaking. This essay is lucid and fluent in expression, and earnest and sincere in intent. Loyalty and devotion such as these allow us to anticipate the author’s future conduct. Moreover, his compositions in all three sessions are accomplished and precise. He should rank first in this examining section.
Associate Examiner Wu, Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: Our imperial ancestor’s divine accomplishments and sagely virtue surpass all past and present examples. All arose from his vigilance and diligence: these are what emperors and kings for ten thousand generations should emulate. Few candidates writing in the policy-essay session have addressed this; those who occasionally do fall far short in developing it. This policy essay alone expounds it with grandeur and beauty, inspiring reverence. At its close, it further offers the counsel that the present emperor should emulate his ancestor through vigilance and diligence. It is tactful yet pointed, earnest and true; its feelings of loyalty and devotion are vividly apparent. To obtain a scholar such as this is cause for rejoicing at the prospects of the age.
Examiner Jin, Academician, comments: Reading this policy essay with solemn respect, I find our ancestor’s virtue in overcoming hardship as clearly displayed as something pointed out in one’s own palm. Only someone of outstanding discernment could accomplish this; hence I have selected it.
Examiner Liu, Grand Secretary, comments: This composition succeeds in singling out the two words ‘vigilance’ and ‘diligence’…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
於問目外作一大議論豈亦通達國體者邪
帝王以仁義而基鴻庬之業以憂勤而厲
仁義之志盖仁義得天下之本也然不有
憂勤以厲其志則怠荒得以乘之而仁義
之德因以隳矣其何以協羣情膺景命而
基鴻庬之業於無窮哉知此則我
聖祖及漢二帝所以創業於前而貽訓於後者
其本固有在矣請因執事之問而申之漢
高初以試吏而為亭長再以送徒而蹈等
===
死其跡固甚微也然其寬仁愛人彷彿乎
惠鮮鰥寡之德納善從諫彷彿乎改過不
吝之美視西漢二百年之曆固已具其掌
握矣然其心何敢侈然以自肆哉草創倥
傯日不暇給修禮樂而君臣上下之分罔
有瀆亂善新語而古今成敗之迹恒加警
省憂勤一念固等死之初心也故以之誅
秦而秦亡以之蹙項而項滅前日斷蛇一
劍盖已兆天戈一揮之功矣何賴於土地

死其跡固甚微也然其寬仁愛人彷彿乎
惠解縲寡之德納善從諫彷彿乎改過不
吝之美視西漢二百年之曆固已具其掌
握矣然其心何敢侈然以自肆哉草創倥

有瀆亂善新語而古今成敗之迹恒加警
省憂勤一念固等死之初心也故以之誅
秦而秦亡以之蹙項而項滅前日斷蛇一
劒盖已兆天戈一揮之功矣何頼於上地
punctuated:
於問目外作一大議論，豈亦通達國體者邪？

帝王以仁義而基鴻庬之業，以憂勤而厲仁義之志。盖仁義，得天下之本也。然不有憂勤以厲其志，則怠荒得以乘之，而仁義之德因以隳矣。其何以協羣情、膺景命，而基鴻庬之業於無窮哉？知此，則我聖祖及漢二帝所以創業於前而貽訓於後者，其本固有在矣。請因執事之問而申之。

漢高初以試吏而為亭長，再以送徒而蹈等死，其跡固甚微也。然其寬仁愛人，彷彿乎惠鮮鰥寡之德；納善從諫，彷彿乎改過不吝之美。視西漢二百年之曆，固已具其掌握矣。然其心何敢侈然以自肆哉？草創倥傯，日不暇給，修禮樂而君臣上下之分罔有瀆亂，善新語而古今成敗之迹恒加警省。憂勤一念，固等死之初心也。故以之誅秦而秦亡，以之蹙項而項滅。前日斷蛇一劍，盖已兆天戈一揮之功矣。何賴於土地
translation_en:
…to develop a substantial argument beyond the scope of the question. Might he also be someone who thoroughly understands the principles of governing the state?

Emperors and kings lay the foundations of vast achievements through benevolence and righteousness, and through anxious diligence strengthen their resolve to practise these virtues. Benevolence and righteousness are indeed the foundation for winning All under Heaven. Yet without anxious diligence to strengthen that resolve, indolence and neglect can intrude, and the virtue of benevolence and righteousness will consequently crumble. How, then, could they win the people's united allegiance, receive Heaven's great mandate, and lay the foundations of an enduring imperial enterprise? Understanding this, we see that there was indeed a firm foundation for what our Sagely Founder and the two Han emperors accomplished in establishing their rule and leaving instruction to posterity. Allow me to elaborate in response to your question.

Gaozu of Han began as a probationary official serving as a station chief; later, while escorting convicts, he found himself facing death whichever course he took [?]. His beginnings were certainly very humble. Yet his generosity, benevolence, and love for others resembled the virtue of bestowing kindness upon the widowed and bereft; his acceptance of good counsel and willingness to follow remonstrance resembled the excellence of correcting faults without hesitation. Viewed in this light, the Western Han's two hundred years of rule were already within his grasp. Yet how could he dare let his heart grow extravagant and indulge himself? Amid the haste and turmoil of founding his dynasty, each day afforded insufficient time for his tasks. He established rites and music so that the distinctions between ruler and minister, superior and subordinate, were neither violated nor confused. He esteemed the New Discourses (Xin yu), constantly taking warning from and reflecting upon the record of success and failure, ancient and modern. His single-minded anxious diligence was indeed the resolve he had held from the outset, when he faced death either way. Thus, through it he punished Qin, and Qin fell; through it he pressed Xiang Yu hard, and Xiang Yu perished. That earlier sword stroke which severed the serpent had already foreshadowed the achievement of sweeping Heaven's halberd in a single stroke. What need had he to rely upon land…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
人民之資哉世祖以帝室之胄而立於搖
手觸禁之日其為力誠甚難也然其明明
廟謨庶幾乎丕顯之聖糾糾雄斷庶幾乎
寵綏之仁東漢二百年中興之祚已入其
籌筭矣然其心何敢倨然以自放哉總攬
權綱明謹政體退功臣而進文吏戢弓矢
而散馬牛不敢怠荒一心猶搖手觸禁之
故念也故漢運中否而復興炎燼已滅而
復續前日資身一牛蓋已兆六龍御天之
===
時矣豈假於百里七十里為之助哉恭惟
我
太祖高皇帝方潛龍之期逢逐鹿之運嘗以避
亂而遊於光黃汝潁之間以布衣而立於
羣雄角逐之地其值時甚艱而為力甚難
也然
神武之德出於天縱
聖敬之懿躋於日新于是而復帝王所立之中
國紹帝王相傳之大統蓋有出於必然而

translation_en:
…and the resources of the people! Shizu, a descendant of the imperial house, rose at a time when merely moving a hand could violate a prohibition; his task was indeed exceedingly difficult. Yet his brilliantly conceived plans at court approached the wisdom of the gloriously manifest sage, and his vigorous, heroic decisiveness approached the benevolence that favored and pacified the people. The two-hundred-year destiny of the restored Eastern Han already lay within his calculations. Yet how could he dare indulge himself in arrogance? He held firm control of authority, conducted government with clarity and care, retired meritorious commanders and advanced civil officials, put away bows and arrows, and released horses and oxen. Never daring to lapse into indolence, he retained the same resolve he had possessed when every movement risked violating a prohibition. Thus the fortunes of Han, obstructed midway, flourished again; its fiery embers, already extinguished, were rekindled. The single ox that had once sustained him already foreshadowed the time when he would ride six dragons through Heaven as sovereign. How could he have needed the assistance of a territory of a hundred or seventy li?
We reverently consider our Emperor Taizu Gao. While still a hidden dragon, he encountered an age of contention for the empire. Fleeing disorder, he once traveled among Guang, Huang, Ru, and Ying; as a commoner, he stood amid contending warlords. The times he encountered were exceedingly troubled, and his task exceedingly difficult. Yet his divinely martial virtue was Heaven-given, and his excellent sagely reverence advanced anew each day. Thus he restored the Central Realm established by the ancient emperors and kings and continued the great imperial succession they had handed down. This surely arose from an inescapable necessity and…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
不可釋者然其兢兢戒謹恒若上帝之在
臨業業恐懼恒若神明之在監觀其嘗諭
輔臣有云心為身之主帥若一事不合理
則百事皆廢所以常自點檢必求至當其
形於正心修身者如此
天地廟社必皆親祀每遇齋戒必整心志對越
神明其形於敬天孝祖者如此至於嚴
宫闈之法正禮樂之失厲忠節之訓其形於
齊家治國平天下者又如此其心如是故
===
不十年間北定中原而掃除九十餘年之
腥羶削平僭亂而收復四百餘年之疆土
以布衣而
登九五以無家而化有國天命有所歸依人
心有所仰賴矣一牛一劔人民土地何足
以置諸贊論哉雖然同是憂勤也在前日
為創業之本在後日即守成之訓而使為
漢之子孫者能謹聿修之戒而以祖宗之
心為心篤繩武之志而以祖宗之憂為憂

punctuated:
不可釋者。然其兢兢戒謹，恒若上帝之在臨；業業恐懼，恒若神明之在監。觀其嘗諭輔臣有云：「心為身之主帥，若一事不合理，則百事皆廢，所以常自點檢，必求至當。」其形於正心修身者如此。天地廟社，必皆親祀；每遇齋戒，必整心志，對越神明。其形於敬天孝祖者如此。至於嚴宫闈之法，正禮樂之失，厲忠節之訓，其形於齊家治國平天下者又如此。其心如是，故不十年間，北定中原，而掃除九十餘年之腥羶；削平僭亂，而收復四百餘年之疆土。以布衣而登九五，以無家而化有國，天命有所歸依，人心有所仰賴矣。一牛一劔，人民土地，何足以置諸贊論哉！

雖然，同是憂勤也，在前日為創業之本，在後日即守成之訓。而使為漢之子孫者，能謹聿修之戒，而以祖宗之心為心；篤繩武之志，而以祖宗之憂為憂，
translation_en:
…and could not be relinquished. Yet he remained ever vigilant and cautious, as though the Lord on High stood over him; ever apprehensive and fearful, as though the spirits were watching him. Consider what he once told his assisting ministers: “The heart is the commander of the body. If a single matter fails to accord with principle, then all affairs fall into ruin. Thus I constantly examine myself, always seeking what is most fitting.” Such was the expression of his concern for rectifying the heart and cultivating the person. He invariably performed in person the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, at the ancestral temple, and at the altars of soil and grain. Whenever he observed ritual purification and fasting, he invariably composed his heart and intentions to stand reverently before the spirits. Such was the expression of his reverence for Heaven and filial devotion to his ancestors. As for enforcing the regulations of the palace’s inner quarters, correcting errors in rites and music, and strengthening instruction in loyalty and integrity, these likewise expressed his concern for regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to all under Heaven. Because his heart was thus disposed, in fewer than ten years he pacified the Central Plain in the north and swept away more than ninety years of rank and fetid rule; he crushed usurpation and disorder and recovered territories lost for more than four hundred years. From a commoner he rose to the imperial throne; from having no home he came to possess a state. Heaven’s Mandate found its resting place, and the people’s hearts found someone to look up to and rely upon. What standing could a single ox, a single sword, people, or territory have in an appraisal of his greatness?

Nevertheless, this same anxious diligence, which in earlier days formed the foundation for establishing the dynasty, became in later days an admonition for preserving its achievements. If the descendants of the Han could have earnestly heeded the injunction to continue cultivating their ancestral virtue, taking their ancestors’ hearts as their own; if they could have firmly resolved to follow in their ancestors’ footsteps, taking their ancestors’ cares as their own…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
則由四百餘年可傳於萬年由二十四世
可保於萬世雖有莽卓百輩徒為机上肉
耳安能為哉惜乎其不足以語此而使二
帝在天之靈不能不為之扼腕也洪惟我
朝
列聖以及
今上仰思
聖祖之鴻圖保守靈長之大業盖餘百四十年
于茲一念憂勤形諸
===
宵旰萬幾警戒永為家法頃者討叛誅奸之
典既正于

成之道為久安長治之圖
皇祖貽訓於是有徵億萬載靈長之慶於是有
在矣詩曰不愆不忘率由舊章愚敢上以
為
聖天子獻而下為天下頌之

大庭釐訛糾繆之令再頒於庶府謹持盈守
成之道爲久安長治之圖
皇祖貽訓於是有徵億萬載靈長之慶於是有
在矣詩曰不愆不忘率由舊章愚敢上以
爲
聖天子獻而下爲天下頌之
第二問
punctuated:
則由四百餘年可傳於萬年，由二十四世可保於萬世。雖有莽卓百輩，徒為机上肉耳，安能為哉？惜乎其不足以語此，而使二帝在天之靈不能不為之扼腕也！
洪惟我朝列聖以及今上，仰思聖祖之鴻圖，保守靈長之大業，盖餘百四十年于茲。一念憂勤，形諸宵旰；萬幾警戒，永為家法。頃者，討叛誅奸之典既正于大庭，釐訛糾繆之令再頒於庶府。謹持盈守成之道，為久安長治之圖。皇祖貽訓於是有徵，億萬載靈長之慶於是有在矣。《詩》曰：「不愆不忘，率由舊章。」愚敢上以為聖天子獻，而下為天下頌之。
第二問
translation_en:
…then a reign of more than four hundred years could have been extended to ten thousand years, and a succession of twenty-four generations preserved for ten thousand generations. Even a hundred men like Wang Mang and Dong Zhuo would have been mere meat on the chopping block: what could they have accomplished? Alas, they were unworthy to be addressed on such matters, leaving the spirits of the two emperors in Heaven unable to refrain from wringing their hands in distress!
Considering with reverence our dynasty’s successive sage rulers down to His Majesty, they have looked up to the grand design of the Sagely Progenitor and preserved the great enterprise of enduring imperial rule for more than one hundred and forty years now. Their constant concern and diligence find expression in rising before dawn and eating late; vigilance amid the myriad affairs of state remains forever the rule of the imperial house. Recently, the prescribed punishments for rebels and traitors have been duly enforced at the great court, and orders to rectify errors and correct abuses have again been promulgated to the various offices. By carefully following the way of maintaining prosperity and preserving established achievements, plans are laid for lasting peace and enduring good government. The instructions bequeathed by the Imperial Ancestor are thereby vindicated, and therein rests the blessing of imperial rule enduring for countless ages. The Book of Odes says: “Neither erring nor forgetting, follow the old statutes.” I, in my ignorance, venture to offer this to the sagely Son of Heaven above, and to celebrate it before all under Heaven below.
Second Policy Question

Yang Shen

Associate Examiner Li, Acting Vice Director, comments: “Diligence in learning, rectifying the mind, employing the worthy, and accepting remonstrance: upon these depend order and disorder in the realm. To conclude a discussion of upholding established laws with these matters shows an understanding of the foundations. In selecting this essay to head our examination section, could we have valued only the excellence of its language?”

Associate Examiner Mu, Examining Editor, comments: “Since the fully established Zhou dynasty, none has matched our dynasty in the refinement and completeness of its legislation. The establishment of the Six Ministries derives indeed from the Rites of Zhou; beyond this there is no other model. Candidates in the examination hall have offered a profusion of itemized answers, without grasping the essentials. You alone have answered by citing the Six Ministries and have further laid responsibility upon those charged with upholding the laws. You see deeply into the substance of government, neither impractical nor superficial. This deserves to be recorded and presented to the throne.”

Associate Examiner Dong, Compiler, comments: “This policy essay enumerates the failings of earlier dynasties in changing their laws, providing ample warning from past precedents. It also states that our sagely founder established detailed and comprehensive laws, unlike those of the Han and Song, which required further enhancement and expansion. This makes clear the intent that these laws should be reverently upheld. At the end, it again identifies sustained devotion to learning as the foundation for upholding the laws. The argument returns repeatedly to its themes, subtly and tactfully, without pressing unduly, while loyalty and earnestness overflow its words. I certainly know that what he wishes to lay before the vermilion steps of the throne does not stop here.”

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
詳實本房之冠舍子
考試官學士靳批今日臣下所以將順
德意者恐當出此天下士吾於子有望焉勗哉
考試官大學士劉批此策不為竒論而愛
君之誠經世之學亦自具見非特該博雅健可錄也佳士佳士
法垂於後而無弊者善立法者也法承於
前而無改者善守法者也何則法立而有
弊則非可久可大之規法守而或移則非
善繼善述之道故非天下之至聖不足以
===
言立非天下之至明又烏足以言守哉此
非愚之言也書曰有典有則貽厥子孫立
法者然也詩曰不愆不忘率由舊章守法
者然也古之聖帝明王盖莫不然然豈有
如我
國家之盛者哉請條陳之漢高承嬴秦之暴
以寬仁為治三章約法而御民無苛政十
五稅一而賦民無橫征此誠繼體者所宜
敬承而弗失也若孝文加以恭儉孝景恪

translation_en:
…detailed and sound. First among the candidates in this examining section—who but you [?]?
Examiner Jin, Academician, comments: The means by which ministers today support and carry out His Majesty’s virtuous intentions should, I think, follow this approach. Among the scholars of the realm, I place my hopes in you. Strive on!
Examiner Liu, Grand Secretary, comments: This policy essay advances no extraordinary argument, yet its sincerity in loving the sovereign and its learning in the governance of the world are fully apparent. It merits selection for more than its comprehensive knowledge and elegant, vigorous prose. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!
One whose laws are handed down to later generations without harmful consequences is skilled at establishing laws; one who receives laws from earlier generations and preserves them unchanged is skilled at maintaining laws. Why is this? If laws are established but produce harmful consequences, they are no framework capable of enduring and extending far. If laws are maintained but sometimes altered, this is not the way to carry forward and fulfill one’s predecessors’ work well. Thus, none but the greatest sage in the world is qualified to speak of establishing laws; and how could anyone but one of the world’s most discerning rulers be qualified to speak of maintaining them? These are not merely my own humble words. The Book of Documents says: “There are statutes and rules to be handed down to their descendants.” This is how those who establish laws act. The Book of Odes says: “Neither erring nor forgetting, they follow the old regulations.” This is how those who maintain laws act. The sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity surely all acted thus. Yet was there ever anything to match the flourishing achievement of our own dynasty? Allow me to set this out point by point.
Gaozu of Han succeeded the violent rule of the Ying house of Qin and governed with generosity and benevolence. He reduced the laws to three articles, ruling the people without oppressive policies; he taxed them at one part in fifteen, levying no arbitrary exactions. This was indeed what succeeding rulers ought reverently to have inherited and preserved without loss. Emperor Xiaowen added reverence and frugality, while Emperor Xiaojing scrupulously…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
遵洪業而幾致海内刑措之效殆善于敬
承者乎使承之者皆若人焉則漢至今存
可也夫何孝武好大喜功任用新進刑獄
之濫罪及腹誹賦斂之重筭及舟車而漢
初之元氣索然矣幸承其後者有昭宣焉
任霍光則罷榷酤而减租賦用魏相則戒
煩擾而寢屯田于是乎史稱民安而四百
年之基賴以存焉則昭宣之再變非變也
變武帝之弊政以復高皇之舊也宋祖承
===
五代之亂以仁厚立國重農桑而頒勸課
之詔恤刑獄而定覆奏之法此誠繼體者
所宜率循而無改也若真宗之寬仁慈愛
仁宗之恭儉仁恕而共培社稷遠長之澤
殆善于率循者乎使循之者皆若人焉則
宋至今存可也夫何神宗銳於圖治任相
非人均輸之政同乎商賈手實之禍及于
雞豚而宋初之惠政蕩然矣幸繼其後者
有元祐焉相司馬光而盡除新法任吕公

遵洪業，而幾致海内刑措之效，殆善于敬承者乎？使承之者皆若人焉，則漢至今存可也。夫何孝武好大喜功，任用新進，刑獄之濫，罪及腹誹；賦斂之重，筭及舟車，而漢初之元氣索然矣！幸承其後者有昭宣焉，任霍光則罷榷酤而减租賦，用魏相則戒煩擾而寢屯田。于是乎史稱民安，而四百年之基賴以存焉。則昭宣之再變，非變也，變武帝之弊政以復高皇之舊也。

宋祖承五代之亂，以仁厚立國，重農桑而頒勸課之詔，恤刑獄而定覆奏之法，此誠繼體者所宜率循而無改也。若真宗之寬仁慈愛，仁宗之恭儉仁恕，而共培社稷遠長之澤，殆善于率循者乎？使循之者皆若人焉，則宋至今存可也。夫何神宗銳於圖治，任相非人，均輸之政同乎商賈，手實之禍及于雞豚，而宋初之惠政蕩然矣！幸繼其後者有元祐焉，相司馬光而盡除新法，任吕公
translation_en:
…followed the great undertaking of his predecessors and nearly brought about a condition throughout the realm in which punishments could be laid aside. Was he not adept at reverently carrying on their legacy? Had all who inherited it been like these men, the Han could have survived to this day. Yet how was it that Emperor Xiaowu, craving grandeur and delighting in achievements, employed newcomers, imposed punishments so indiscriminately that even unspoken criticism became a crime, and levied taxes so heavily that boats and carts were assessed, leaving the vital strength of the early Han utterly depleted? Fortunately, among his successors were Emperors Zhao and Xuan. With Huo Guang entrusted with office, the liquor monopoly was abolished and land taxes and other levies reduced; with Wei Xiang employed, vexatious interference was guarded against and military agricultural colonies suspended. Thus the histories record that the people lived in peace, and on this depended the preservation of the dynasty’s four-hundred-year foundation. The further changes made under Zhao and Xuan were therefore no true departure: they changed Emperor Wu’s harmful policies to restore the old institutions of Emperor Gao.

The founding emperor of the Song inherited the disorder of the Five Dynasties and established his state upon benevolence and generosity. He valued agriculture and sericulture, issuing edicts to encourage and oversee them; he took compassionate care in penal matters, establishing procedures for resubmitting cases to the throne for review. These were indeed practices that his successors ought to have followed without alteration. Consider Zhenzong’s magnanimity, benevolence, and loving kindness, and Renzong’s reverence, frugality, humanity, and forbearance: together they nurtured benefits that would sustain the dynasty far into the future. Were they not adept at following their predecessors? Had all who followed been like these men, the Song could have survived to this day. Yet how was it that Shenzong, eager to achieve good government, appointed the wrong man as chief councilor? His equitable-transport policy resembled the dealings of merchants, while the harm caused by mandatory personal declarations of property extended even to chickens and pigs, utterly sweeping away the benevolent policies of the early Song. Fortunately, the Yuanyou era followed: Sima Guang was made chief councilor and all the New Policies were abolished; Lü Gong… was appointed…

punctuated: 著而復用老成，於是乎乾旋坤轉，而三百年之基賴以定焉。則元祐之再變，非變也，變神宗之弊政以復藝祖之舊也。由是言之，祖宗之法之當守，較然矣。而賈誼、仲舒乃有定制更化之請者，盖漢初寬大之規模，其不可變固也。若夫收拾三代之遺文，以為增光之地，固其善繼者之責。不然，則禮樂不興，而德色誶語之俗何以革？經制不定，而正朔學校之制何以興？二子之請，正因其不可變者而潤色之耳，豈如張湯、桑弘羊輩之紛更邪？余靖、宋綬復有總攬乾綱之議者，盖宋初仁厚之法度，其不可易固也。若乃全復帝王之中國，以光一統之盛，固其善述者之事。不然，則北無燕雲，而洛陽豈有息肩之日？西無寧夏，而關中豈有安枕之期？二臣之議，正欲因其不可易者而充拓之耳，豈如安石、惠卿之徒之改作邪？至于唐，則又有可言者，盖其閨門
translation_en: …Lü Gongzhu and once again employed seasoned men. Thus Heaven and Earth turned about, and the foundations of a three-hundred-year dynasty were secured thereby. The further changes of the Yuanyou era were therefore no true departure: they changed Shenzong’s defective policies to restore the old institutions of the founding emperor, Taizu. From this it is plain that the laws of the ancestors ought to be preserved. Yet Jia Yi and Dong Zhongshu requested that institutions be established and governance reformed. Certainly, the broad and generous framework of the early Han could not be changed. But gathering the surviving cultural institutions of the Three Dynasties to lend it greater splendor was precisely the responsibility of those who would carry on that inheritance well. Otherwise, if rites and music were not promoted, how could the habits of arrogant looks and abusive speech be reformed? If enduring institutions were not established, how could the systems of the calendar and schools be brought into being? These two men’s requests merely sought to embellish what could not be changed. How could they be compared with the disruptive alterations of Zhang Tang, Sang Hongyang, and their like? Yu Jing and Song Shou likewise proposed that the sovereign take full command of imperial authority. Certainly, the humane and generous laws and institutions of the early Song could not be altered. But fully recovering the central lands of the emperors and kings, to enhance the grandeur of unified rule, was precisely the task of those who would faithfully carry on their predecessors’ work. Otherwise, without Yan and Yun in the north, how could Luoyang ever have a day of respite? Without Ningxia in the west, when could Guanzhong ever rest securely? The proposals of these two ministers sought only to build upon and extend what could not be altered. How could they be compared with the innovations of Wang Anshi, Lü Huiqing, and their followers? As for the Tang, there is still more to say, for within its palace households…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
之化有虧華夷之辨未正誠有以啟程氏
之嘆然以租庸調定田賦以府衞寓兵法
以六典定官制庶幾乎三代之遺意又豈
特一世二世之可守哉惜也一變於玄宗
而肇天寶之亂再變於德宗而啟奉天之
難而唐亦浸以不國矣夫然則祖宗之法
之善其當守邪否邪然陸贄之於玄宗有
變稅法之請者蓋以楊炎創兩稅之法征
斂過重故欲更之以復租庸之舊耳李泌
===
之於德宗有變兵制之請者蓋以張說建
彍騎之法兵民始分故欲議之以復府兵
之舊耳使當時能用其策則唐雖至今存
亦可也大抵創業之君憂深慮遠莫不有
仁心以凝天命亦莫不有仁政以結人心
一法立必參之眾論一令出必酌之時宜
不能無害也而利常多於害不能無失也
而得每倍於失嗣其後者顧可以肆意改
作為哉洪惟我

作為哉洪惟我
punctuated:
之化有虧，華夷之辨未正，誠有以啟程氏之嘆。然以租庸調定田賦，以府衞寓兵法，以六典定官制，庶幾乎三代之遺意，又豈特一世二世之可守哉？惜也！一變於玄宗，而肇天寶之亂；再變於德宗，而啟奉天之難，而唐亦浸以不國矣。夫然則祖宗之法之善，其當守邪否邪？然陸贄之於玄宗有變稅法之請者，蓋以楊炎創兩稅之法，征斂過重，故欲更之以復租庸之舊耳。李泌之於德宗有變兵制之請者，蓋以張說建彍騎之法，兵民始分，故欲議之以復府兵之舊耳。使當時能用其策，則唐雖至今存亦可也。大抵創業之君，憂深慮遠，莫不有仁心以凝天命，亦莫不有仁政以結人心。一法立，必參之眾論；一令出，必酌之時宜。不能無害也，而利常多於害；不能無失也，而得每倍於失。嗣其後者，顧可以肆意改作為哉？

洪惟我
translation_en:
…its moral influence within the household was deficient, and the distinction between Chinese and barbarians was not properly maintained: these indeed gave Master Cheng cause to lament. Yet it fixed agricultural taxation through the grain tax, labor-service commutation, and cloth levy; embodied military organization in the militia commands and guards; and established the official system through the Six Statutes. These came close to preserving the intentions of the Three Dynasties. Surely they deserved to be maintained for more than just one or two reigns? Alas! A first alteration under Xuanzong initiated the disorder of the Tianbao era; a second under Dezong brought on the crisis at Fengtian. Thus the Tang gradually ceased to function as a state. Should the good laws of the imperial ancestors, then, be preserved or not?

As for Lu Zhi’s request to Xuanzong [?] to change the tax laws, this was because Yang Yan had instituted the twice-yearly tax system and its exactions were excessively heavy. He therefore wished to change it simply to restore the old grain-tax and labor-service system. As for Li Mi’s request to Dezong to change the military system, this was because Zhang Yue had established the Expanded Cavalry system, under which soldiers and civilians first became separate. He therefore wished to deliberate on it simply to restore the old militia system. Had their proposals been adopted at the time, the Tang might even have survived to the present day.

In general, founding rulers worry deeply and consider the distant future. All possess a benevolent heart with which to secure Heaven’s Mandate, and all practice benevolent government with which to bind the people’s hearts to them. Whenever they establish a law, they consult a range of opinions; whenever they issue a command, they weigh what is appropriate to the times. Harm cannot be entirely avoided, but the benefits usually exceed the harm; shortcomings cannot be entirely avoided, but the gains regularly double the losses. How, then, could their successors presume to alter these arrangements at will?

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
太祖高皇帝大德受命稽古立法規模宏大節
目周詳如銓選有定員考課有定法則所
以正百官者善矣墾田有定數賦稅有定
額則所以厚百姓者善矣禮儀有定式軍
政有條例則所以辨上下詰戎兵者善矣
律令有定條工匠有定役則所以詰姦慝
時地利者善矣其他善政有不可以縷舉
者此豈前代所能及哉是故禮樂交脩法
制具舉則視彼有望於後人之增光者不
===
侔也車書一統玉帛萬國則視彼有待於
後人之充拓者不侔也華夷之辨明彝倫
之理正則視彼雜夷而不悟者又不可同
年語也借使賈董復生于今亦將何以獻
其謀哉
列聖相承克守鴻業外寧內安固其所也然治
久而弊生則作聰明以亂舊章者固容有
焉亦不能不上厪
宵旰之憂也邇者

punctuated:
太祖高皇帝大德受命，稽古立法，規模宏大，節目周詳。如銓選有定員，考課有定法，則所以正百官者善矣；墾田有定數，賦稅有定額，則所以厚百姓者善矣；禮儀有定式，軍政有條例，則所以辨上下、詰戎兵者善矣；律令有定條，工匠有定役，則所以詰姦慝、時地利者善矣。其他善政，有不可以縷舉者。此豈前代所能及哉？是故禮樂交脩，法制具舉，則視彼有望於後人之增光者不侔也；車書一統，玉帛萬國，則視彼有待於後人之充拓者不侔也；華夷之辨明，彝倫之理正，則視彼雜夷而不悟者，又不可同年語也。借使賈董復生于今，亦將何以獻其謀哉？
列聖相承，克守鴻業，外寧內安，固其所也。然治久而弊生，則作聰明以亂舊章者，固容有焉，亦不能不上厪宵旰之憂也。邇者，
translation_en:
…Taizu, the Exalted Emperor, received the Mandate through his great virtue. He examined antiquity and established laws, grand in scope and comprehensive in detail. In personnel selection, posts had fixed quotas, and evaluations of officials followed established rules: thus the means of setting the officials in order were sound. Cultivated land had prescribed quantities, and taxes had fixed quotas: thus the means of enriching the common people were sound. Ritual observances had established forms, and military administration had regulations: thus the means of distinguishing superior from inferior and putting the armed forces in order were sound. Statutes and ordinances had established provisions, and artisans had prescribed service obligations: thus the means of suppressing wickedness and exploiting the land’s resources in their proper seasons were sound. His other good measures are too numerous to enumerate. How could previous dynasties have matched this?
Thus, with rites and music cultivated together and laws and institutions fully established, his achievement was unlike that of those who looked to their successors to add further glory. With carriage gauges and writing unified, and the myriad states presenting jade and silk in tribute, his achievement was unlike that of those who depended on their successors for further expansion. With the distinction between Chinese and barbarians made clear and the principles of the enduring human relationships set right, he cannot even be spoken of in the same breath as those who mingled with barbarians without recognizing their error. Even if Jia Yi and Dong Zhongshu were brought back to life today, what counsel could they offer?
The successive sage emperors have inherited the throne and faithfully preserved this great undertaking. Tranquillity abroad and peace within are naturally the fitting result. Yet when orderly government has endured long, abuses arise; there may indeed be those who parade their cleverness and disrupt the established institutions. These matters cannot but trouble the sovereign, causing him to rise before dawn and eat only late in the day. Recently, …

text:

祖宗之舊非天下之至明其孰能與於此一時
士慶于朝農歌于野商賈咏于市行旅舞
于途頌聲四作泰道一新億萬年無疆之
休端在是矣有
君如此奚忍負之故將順
德意者必惟實政之是修奉行
