…His Majesty issued a special edict to all offices within the capital and beyond, commanding that their policies and orders conform entirely to the precedents of the imperial ancestors. Who but one possessed of the greatest discernment under Heaven could accomplish this? At once, scholars rejoiced at court, farmers sang in the fields, merchants chanted in the markets, and travelers danced along the roads. Voices of praise arose on every side, and the course of peace and prosperity was renewed. Here indeed lies the beginning of boundless blessings for countless ages. With such a ruler, how could anyone bear to fail him? Thus, those who carry forward his virtuous intentions must devote themselves to substantive administration; those who implement his enlightened edict must steadfastly preserve the established statutes.

If those responsible for governing the realm emulate Mao Jie in promoting the incorruptible and upright, and Du Yan in curbing those who seek advancement through unmerited favor, there need be no fear that appointments will fall short of former standards. If those responsible for the realm’s revenues emulate Li Jiang in refusing to present fiscal surpluses to the throne, and Chen Shu in declining to submit fiscal accounts, there need be no fear that financial administration will fall short of former standards. If those responsible for the realm’s rites emulate Wang Ning in upholding what is right without currying favor, and Wei Chun in restraining superficial display and valuing substance, there need be no fear that ritual forms will fall short of former standards. If those responsible for the realm’s military administration emulate Shan Tao in never neglecting military preparedness, and Song Jing in withholding rewards for frontier exploits, there need be no fear that military administration will fall short of former standards. 祖宗之盛不復見於今日哉抑愚又聞商書之

攸居政事惟醇終之曰念終始典于學誠

translation_en:
…there will be no fear that public works fall short of former standards. In this way, the sage Son of Heaven can take the mind of his sagely ancestor as his own, and worthy dukes and ministers can likewise take the mind of the sage Son of Heaven as their own. Why, then, should the flourishing age of the ancestors not appear again today? Moreover, I have heard that the Documents of Shang, in discussing government, begins by saying, “When the ruler follows remonstrance, he becomes a sage”; continues, “In the position he occupies, let his administration be wholly pure”; and concludes, “Mindful of the end and the beginning, abide in learning.” Truly, abiding in learning is essential to rectifying the mind, and the ruler’s mind is the source from which good government issues. Entrusting worthy assistants to serve as one’s closest confidants, and opening avenues of speech to extend one’s hearing and sight, are also things that one who would preserve good government must understand. If you, honored officials, should favor me with advancement, I ought then to set these matters before the sage Son of Heaven at the foot of the vermilion steps.

Third Question
Ma Xinglu

translation_en:
…Their achievements in suppressing heterodoxy and upholding orthodoxy certainly cannot be effaced. Yet they fall far short when compared with the benevolence and righteousness of the seven books of our Mengzi, which truly convey the tradition of Confucius. This policy essay carefully weighs its praise and criticism, and its language is pure and correct. Even habitual admirers of Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu cannot help being inwardly convinced.

Associate Examiner Zhan, Junior Compiler, comments: The seven books of the Mengzi, devoted to benevolence and righteousness, are writing that bears the Way. Later men of letters frequently rank Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu alongside him, but they do not belong in the same class. This essay’s insights stand far apart from those of the other compositions. Its language and tone convey praise and criticism, and it also offers decisive judgments. It should therefore be recorded to instruct those who study writing but do not understand the Way.

Associate Examiner Zhao, Junior Compiler, comments: Earlier Confucian scholars have already reached a settled judgment on the claim that Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu apprehended the Way through writing. This composition further singles out points in their writings and in the book of Mengzi, examining and testing them repeatedly, thus making the relationship between writing and the Way still clearer. Moreover, its prose flows smoothly and freely, with abundant vigor and robust diction. Its author is evidently also one who devotes himself deeply to this Way; hence it has been selected for inclusion.

Examiner Jin, Academician, comments: This policy essay identifies benevolence and righteousness as the Way transmitted by Mengzi, and this account is fitting. Its further assertion that Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu’s achievements in saving the world did not rest solely upon writing is likewise a sound judgment.

Examiner Liu, Grand Secretary, comments: Where this policy essay discusses the transmission from sage to sage, it seems to show insight. At its close, it further takes the learning of Mengzi as its guide, revealing the author’s aspirations especially clearly.

translation_en:
To win preeminence in literary reputation for an age is easy; to carry forward the thread of the Way across a thousand years is difficult. It is not that literary achievement is easy in itself: viewed in comparison with the Way, it is easy. Nor is the Way difficult in itself: viewed in comparison with literary achievement, it is difficult. Once this is understood, the distinctions between the weighty and the slight, the root and the branches, and the proper ordering of what comes first or later, what may wait and what is urgent, become clearly discernible. Alas! This is why, in judging Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu, the gentleman cannot but esteem their achievement in saving the world through literature, yet ultimately dares not acknowledge them as rightful transmitters of the Way.

What, then, did Mengzi transmit? Benevolence and righteousness, and nothing more. What did Mengzi mean by benevolence and righteousness? He said: “Benevolence is the human heart; righteousness is the human path.” He also said: “The heart of compassion is the beginning of benevolence; the heart of shame and aversion is the beginning of righteousness.” That is all. How, then, could what we call benevolence and righteousness lie outside this heart? Such was Mengzi’s own grasp of the essential meaning of what was taught and received in the school of Kongzi. When Master Han spoke of transmitting ‘this’ from one to another, this was indeed what was transmitted. Yet although Master Han could speak of it, his understanding was not entirely true. When Master Ouyang spoke of government proceeding from a single source, he too meant this. Yet although Master Ouyang could speak of it, his insight was not exhaustive. Under these circumstances, could I, in my ignorance, dare to approve of elevating them to the ranks of Mengzi, so that they might continue the orthodox transmission of the Way?

Thus, before Mengzi there were Yao and Shun. Yao and Shun were those through whom the Way was transmitted. Their words were: “Only…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
精惟一允執厥中若與孟子異矣然惟精
者即其明善之極惟一者即其誠身之事
其理果有二乎後乎孟子而有程子程子
道之所賴以復傳者也其曰涵養須用敬
進學則在致知若與孟子殊矣然用敬者
即其集義之本致知者即其知言之要其
理果有二乎故嘗究而論之堯舜之所以
為堯舜以其盡此心之體而已禹湯文武
周公孔子傳之以至於孟子其間相望有
===
或數百年者非特口傳耳授密相付屬也
特此心之體隱乎百姓日用之間賢者識
其大不賢者識其小而體其全且盡則為
得其傳耳雖窮天地亘萬世而其心所同
然若合符節由是而出宰制萬物酬酢萬
變莫非此心之妙用而其時措之宜不必
同也故堯舜與賢禹則與子文王事殷湯
武則順天應人孔子作春秋以翼衰周孟
子則說諸侯以行王道皆不害其相傳之

translation_en:
…“Be discerning and single-minded; faithfully hold fast to the Mean.” This may seem different from Mengzi’s teaching. Yet being discerning is precisely the utmost development of his understanding of goodness; being single-minded is precisely the work of making oneself sincere. Can their underlying principle really be two different things? After Mengzi came Master Cheng, upon whom the renewed transmission of the Way depended. His saying, “In nurturing oneself, one must employ reverent attentiveness; advancement in learning lies in extending knowledge,” may seem different from Mengzi’s teaching. Yet employing reverent attentiveness is precisely the foundation of Mengzi’s accumulation of righteousness, and extending knowledge is precisely the essential point of his understanding of words. Can their underlying principle really be two different things?

I have therefore investigated this and offer the following account. What made Yao and Shun who they were was simply their complete realization of the essential constitution of this heart-mind. Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius transmitted it down to Mengzi. Sometimes several hundred years separated them; this was no mere transmission from mouth to ear, secretly entrusted from one to another. Rather, the essential constitution of this heart-mind lies hidden within the everyday activities of the common people. The worthy recognize its greater aspects, and the unworthy its lesser aspects; those who embody it wholly and completely are deemed to have received its transmission. Even across the full extent of Heaven and Earth and throughout ten thousand generations, what their heart-minds alike affirm fits together like the matching halves of a tally. Proceeding from this to govern all things and respond to myriad changes, everything is a wondrous functioning of this heart-mind. Yet what is appropriate in putting it into practice at a particular time need not be the same.

Thus Yao and Shun bestowed the realm upon worthy men, whereas Yu bestowed it upon his son. King Wen served Yin, whereas Tang and Wu followed Heaven and responded to the people. Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals to uphold the declining Zhou, whereas Mengzi persuaded the regional lords to put the Kingly Way into practice. None of these differences compromised what they transmitted to one another…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
一道而孟子所謂仁義者又不過使天下
之人各得其本心之所同然者耳此其放
淫辭距詖行救世之功所以大也嗚呼是
豈世儒之以詞章記誦為賢者所能與哉
故自孟子既沒之後程子未出之前斷斷
乎無其人也唐之大儒莫如韓子其所以
起八代之衰者力去陳言以追詩書六藝
之作正以文耳宋景文謂其奥衍宏深佐
佑六經固以其文言之而愚則以為亦有
===
不徒以其文者如原道諸篇深達聖道之
用佛骨一表酷排釋氏之非比之孟子之
闢楊墨功同而力倍之若所謂軻死而不
得其傳者則又秦漢以来人鮮能知而程
子嘗稱其必有所見當矣但以博愛為仁
則不知仁之所以為仁而况望其能盡此
心之體也哉故雖汲汲以道為已任而光
範三書未免雜於貪位慕祿之私其視孟
子之富貴不能淫貧賤不能移者不侔矣

一道，而孟子所謂仁義者，又不過使天下之人各得其本心之所同然者耳。此其放淫辭、距詖行、救世之功所以大也。嗚呼！是豈世儒之以詞章記誦為賢者所能與哉？故自孟子既沒之後，程子未出之前，斷斷乎無其人也。
唐之大儒莫如韓子，其所以起八代之衰者，力去陳言，以追詩書六藝之作，正以文耳。宋景文謂其奥衍宏深，佐佑六經，固以其文言之。而愚則以為亦有不徒以其文者，如原道諸篇，深達聖道之用；佛骨一表，酷排釋氏之非。比之孟子之闢楊墨，功同而力倍之。若所謂軻死而不得其傳者，則又秦漢以来人鮮能知，而程子嘗稱其必有所見，當矣。但以博愛為仁，則不知仁之所以為仁，而况望其能盡此心之體也哉？故雖汲汲以道為已任，而光範三書未免雜於貪位慕祿之私。其視孟子之富貴不能淫、貧賤不能移者，不侔矣。
translation_en:
…the single Way they transmitted to one another. What Mengzi called benevolence and righteousness likewise amounted to nothing more than enabling everyone under Heaven to recover what their original hearts alike affirm. This is why his achievement in banishing licentious speech, resisting biased conduct, and saving the world was so great. Alas! Could those worldly scholars who esteem literary composition and memorization possibly equal him? Thus, after Mengzi died and before Master Cheng appeared, there was decidedly no such person.
Among the great Confucian scholars of the Tang, none equaled Master Han (Han Yu). What enabled him to revive learning after eight dynasties of decline was his strenuous rejection of stale expressions in pursuit of writings like the Poetry, the Documents, and the works of the Six Arts: it was precisely through his literary writing. Song Jingwen said that his writings were profound, expansive, broad, and deep, supporting the Six Classics; he was certainly speaking of Han’s literary work. Yet I, in my humble judgment, believe that some of his achievements were not merely literary. Essays such as Inquiry into the Way deeply apprehended the practical operation of the sages’ Way, while his memorial on the Buddha’s bone vehemently attacked the errors of Buddhism. Compared with Mengzi’s rejection of Yang Zhu and Mo Di, his achievement was the same, but his exertion twice as great. As for his statement that after Ke—that is, Mengzi—died, no one received the transmission, this was something few people since the Qin and Han had understood. Master Cheng once said that Han must have had some insight, and rightly so. Yet by defining benevolence as universal love, Han failed to understand what makes benevolence benevolence. How much less could one expect him fully to realize the essential substance of this heart? Thus, although he earnestly took responsibility for the Way upon himself, his three letters submitted at the Guangfan Gate were still mingled with selfish desires for office and emolument. He did not measure up to Mengzi’s ideal of one whom wealth and rank cannot corrupt, and whom poverty and low station cannot turn from his purpose.

translation_en: Su Dongpo nevertheless said that five hundred years after Mengzi there appeared Master Han, and wished to rank him alongside Mengzi. In terms of achievements, this is permissible; but to say that he could continue the transmission of this Way—this is what I, in my humble judgment, dare not accept. Among the great Confucian scholars of the Song, none surpassed Master Ouyang. He transformed the habits of an entire age by vigorously suppressing strained and eccentric writing and striving to restore a style of richness, solidity, classical refinement, and elegance. This was, to be sure, accomplished through writing. Zeng Zigu described him as pure and profound, brilliant and richly accomplished, with an entirely natural quality; he too was praising his writing. Yet I believe there was more to him than writing alone. For example, the Way and virtue he advocated in his Discourse on Fundamentals were sufficient to assist the work of government; and in his Discourse on Factions, his forthright words were sufficient to settle the proper course of state policy. Compared with Master Han’s rejection of Buddhism and Daoism, his intention was the same, and his achievements were similar. As for his statement that under the Three Dynasties and earlier, governance issued from a single source, even Master Han had not attained this insight. Master Zhu was right to regard it as a definitive judgment that would remain unaltered for ten thousand generations. Yet in saying that human nature was not the first concern in the sages’ teaching, he failed to understand what makes human nature what it is. How, then, could one expect him to illuminate the essential substance of this mind? Thus, although he earnestly set his heart on putting the Way into practice, his Biography of the Retired Scholar of the Six Ones still betrayed an indulgent partiality for the zither, wine vessels, calligraphy, and the arts. He did not measure up to Mengzi, who would undertake nothing contrary to benevolence and perform no act contrary to ritual propriety. Su Dongpo nevertheless said that three hundred years after Master Han there appeared Master Ouyang, and wished to rank him alongside Han as a successor to Mengzi. This, too, is why I, in my humble judgment, dare not agree…

translation_en:
…that this is so. The reason is that these two masters originally perceived the Way through literary composition, rather than making the Way the basis of their writing. They exhausted their spirits and squandered their years, yet their lifelong pursuits amounted merely to such peripheral accomplishments as writing radiant as sunlight and pure as jade, expressing the sentiments of the Duke of Zhou and the thoughts of Confucius, discussing affairs like Lu Zhi, recording events like Sima Qian, and composing poetry and rhapsodies like Li Bai. Since they did not devote themselves exclusively to the learning of Mengzi, what wonder is it that they could not carry forward his transmission?
On this point I have a particularly strong feeling. Those in our age who pursue literary composition write of wind and clouds, moonlight and dew. Their compositions are certainly skillful, but what connection have they with the work of aiding their age and putting the Way into practice? Their intricate embellishments and parallel phrases are certainly beautiful, but what part do they play in defending orthodoxy and refuting heterodoxy? Here the Way scarcely bears mentioning [?]; but even as literature, is this what those two masters pursued?
At this spring Metropolitan Examination, when you, sir, are testing scholars through their writing, you have chosen to ask about the learning of the Way taught by the sages and worthies. Presumably you hope that the candidates will pursue substantial learning that strengthens the foundations, and thereby seek to obtain men of genuine ability to govern the world. In my ignorance, I am not such a man. Nevertheless, to make reverence central and thereby bring principle together within the single mind; to extend knowledge and thereby investigate principle exhaustively in the myriad affairs; and, through the learning of Mengzi, gradually to accord with the purport of the teachings of Shun’s court—these are indeed my aspirations, though I have not yet been able to fulfill them.

Zou Shouyi

…exuberant in spirit and magnificent in diction, they had already struck me as exceptional. Upon reading the five policy essays, I found them surging like a cascading river. The essay on government, in particular, discusses affairs on the basis of laws, displaying exceptional order and coherence. At its close it again draws an analogy with Heaven and Earth, the two vital forces, and the Five Phases, bringing the argument back to those who uphold the laws and would raise this sagely age above the Three Dynasties. This is an incontrovertible argument. Your outstanding understanding and distinctive insights far surpass those of others. Can you, then, fail to be called an outstanding scholar of the realm?
Associate Examiner Li, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: All five policy essays reveal profound learning and magnificent talent. The essay on benevolence and righteousness also penetrates the workings of affairs and weighs the principles of government. Precise, appropriate, and exhaustive, neither intemperate nor sycophantic, it may be called a work that surpasses all others in the examination. When the realm selects its men, I am certain you cannot be passed over. Yet what I expect of you certainly does not stop here. You should continue to cherish these gifts for the sake of the realm.
Examiner Jin, a Hanlin Academician, comments: The five policy essays display brilliant literary accomplishment, and their arguments consistently accord with what is right. Could anyone without accumulated learning and sustained cultivation achieve this? We have specially selected the essay on the Way of government to manifest his aspiration to serve the world. Its merits certainly do not stop here.
Examiner Liu, a Grand Secretary, comments: In discussing government, most candidates can say that it ultimately depends on obtaining the right men. translation_en:
…the constant norms of Heaven and Earth and the great principles for governing the world certainly contain things fixed and unalterable. Yet with laws derived from benevolence and righteousness, as times change and circumstances differ, abuses may inevitably arise. Unless remedies are applied as the times require, how can one restore the constant norms, put the great principles into practice, and bring the world to order and peace? Allow me to explain.

Showing affection for one’s kin is benevolence. Benevolence produces a generous, unhurried, profound, and substantial disposition, without haste to secure achievements or advantages. Thus the Duke of Zhou reported on his administration after a full year; yet in later generations there arose the danger of indolence, slackness, and gradual decline. Promoting the worthy and honoring achievement is righteousness. Righteousness produces stern resolve, clarity, and integrity, consistently emphasizing decisiveness. Thus, when the Grand Duke governed Qi, he reported on his administration after five months; yet in later generations the calamities of undue haste and contentious rivalry could not be avoided. Benevolence without righteousness errs through excessive leniency; righteousness without benevolence errs through excessive severity. Had the descendants in Qi and Lu always governed as the Duke of Zhou and the Grand Duke did, applying benevolence and righteousness, leniency and severity, appropriately to the times, then the Qi and Lu of today would be like the Three Dynasties of old. What abuses could there be?

Emperor Wen of Han, moved by the words of a girl, abolished mutilating punishments; unwilling to expend the equivalent of an ordinary household’s property, he abandoned the construction of the Dew Terrace. His government thus seemed lenient and benevolent. Yet he bestowed an armrest and staff upon one who failed to attend court, and granted money to one who accepted bribes. Was this not verging on leniency that indulged wrongdoing? That he nevertheless avoided the abuses of neglect and failure to act was probably because he could accept remonstrances offered with deep sighs and flowing tears. He wished to use law to restrain the feudatory princes, clarify rites and music, and rectify customs, putting into practice some of the remonstrant’s…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
該博時出不窮而又曲中程度五策詞氣充溢
光燄逼人而時務一道尤為議論根據識見練
達刻此亦足以見其餘矣然吾求子之言而得
其所存當自有重於此者則又豈必盡錄其文
為哉
同考試官編修溫批此卷初塲精瑩明
暢細讀之已知為竒士後兩塲又皆渾備無一
可指議處一論五策氣之昌才之偉事之核若
探囊倒物曾不經意者此對斟酌時務卓有定
===
見安民敷教之本尤復歸重於
上非勦古人之說而敷演於文字者其殆先憂後樂而有志於用世者歟
大廷之對端有望於子矣
考試官學士靳批此策直寫所懷豈亦
知所儆者乎

保太平之治於無疆必君臣交儆而後可

儆則必思副明君之託上下交修吾見先

The five policy essays overflow with verbal energy, their brilliance dazzling the reader. In particular, it places primary responsibility for the foundations of bringing peace to the people and spreading moral instruction upon His Majesty. title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
事而慮有備無患危可使安亂可使治而
況當太平全盛之時有不能保之於無疆
者乎昔者有虞之世四方風動黎民於變
萬世一時也然舜方以股肱之良望其臣
皐陶方以元首之明望其君至於無怠無
荒之規慢遊敖虐之戒面相儆告而不為
異凛乎若有危亂之萌者豈聖人過為憂
慮哉危平易傾理所必至而兢業萬幾固
其所以聖也唐虞之治所以為萬世君臣
===
之龜鑑者其以是哉我
國家承平日久天下事之可憂者盖亦多矣
姑以其急者籌之今天下之民東南厄於
水旱而溝壑是虞西北迫於饑寒而桴鼓
未息民生之不安執事以為守令之罪是
也然
朝廷四方之楨榦惟行之上者有恭儉節用
之實斯承於下者無侵漁厲民之政如其
不然徒責之守令抑末矣觀夫不虐無

…deliberating before events arise: with preparation, calamity can be avoided; danger can be made secure, and disorder brought under control. How much more, then, in an age of flourishing peace: could there be any inability to preserve it forever? In the age of Youyu, the four quarters responded as grass bends before the wind, and the common people were transformed—a time such as comes but once in ten thousand ages. Yet Shun still expected his ministers to be worthy limbs supporting him, while Gao Yao expected his sovereign to be an enlightened head. Admonitions against indolence and neglect, and warnings against idle pleasure, arrogance, and cruelty, were delivered face to face without anyone finding this strange. They stood in solemn apprehension, as though danger and disorder were already beginning to emerge. Were the sages excessively anxious? Peace is easily overturned [?], as the course of things inevitably shows; their vigilance over the myriad affairs of government was precisely what made them sages. Surely this is why the government of Tang and Yu serves as a guide and mirror for rulers and ministers throughout the ages!
Our dynasty has long enjoyed peace, yet there are probably many matters in the realm that warrant concern. Let us consider just the most urgent. title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
皆實本於克艱政在養民先戒乎從欲則
所以安民者不有本乎誠率是道以先天
下又擇賢守令而久任之夫然後如龔遂
如張詠者始得以行其志而民有恒產可
期矣何憂潢池有弄兵之警樂歲無擊壤
之歌哉天下之士急於溫飽者以奔競為
得計溺於詞章者以經濟為迂談人才之
未盛執事以為師儒之罪是也然
朝廷教化之本原惟位乎上者有振作之方
===
斯化於下者有丕變之應如其不然而徒
責之師儒抑末矣觀夫明揚側陋而後野
無遺賢敬敷五教而後帝臣時舉則所以
育才者不有道乎誠率是道以先天下又
擇賢師儒而尊用之夫然後如胡安定如
孫明復者始得以安其官而學有成效可
必矣何患德不立而有奔競之風才不充
而無經濟之實哉此皆執事之所慮而事
之最急者然愚猶有說焉蓋聞守太平之

…all are truly rooted in being mindful of the difficulty of rule. Government consists in nourishing the people, and its first warning is against indulging desires. Does securing the people's welfare not therefore have a foundation? If those above sincerely follow this way in leading all under Heaven, and also select worthy prefects and magistrates and retain them long in office, only then can men such as Gong Sui and Zhang Yong carry out their aspirations, and the people may be expected to have secure livelihoods. Why then fear reports of people taking up arms beside the stagnant pools, or the absence, in years of plenty, of songs sung while striking the earth in contentment?

Among the scholars of the realm, those anxious for food and clothing consider scrambling for advancement a sound strategy, while those absorbed in literary composition regard the ordering of the realm and relief of its people as impractical talk. You attribute the failure of talent to flourish to the fault of the Confucian teachers, and rightly so. Yet the court is the source of moral instruction: only when those occupying the highest positions have a means of invigorating it will those below respond with a profound transformation. If this is not done, merely blaming the Confucian teachers is to concern oneself with the branches rather than the root. Consider how only after worthy men in humble obscurity were openly recommended and promoted were no worthy men left undiscovered in the countryside; only after the five teachings were reverently disseminated were the emperor's ministers duly raised to office. Does nurturing talent not therefore have its proper way? If those above sincerely follow this way in leading all under Heaven, and also select worthy Confucian teachers and honor and employ them, only then can men such as Hu Anding and Sun Mingfu serve securely in their posts, and successful learning can be assured. Why then worry that virtue will fail to take root and a fashion for scrambling for advancement will prevail, or that abilities will remain undeveloped and there will be no practical achievement in ordering the realm and relieving its people? These are all matters that concern you, and they are the most urgent affairs. Yet I, in my ignorance, still have something to say. I have heard that preserving an age of peace…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
業如守巨室然必固其堂基壯其柱石強
其棟梁高其垣墉嚴其扃鑰欹者扶之敝
者補之日省月視常以頹壞為虞則亘千
載猶一日也民生安人才育所以為固堂
基計者則誠當矣然柱石可弗壯乎棟梁
可弗強乎垣墉可弗高乎扃鑰可弗嚴乎
此亦今之當慮者獨不可一致其儆而豫
為之處邪雖然臣知所儆而進言者固不
易君知所儆而用言者尤不易盖自古然
===
矣是故眾建諸侯之策賈誼所以儆漢文
也使漢文能聽之則何至有七國之變徙
戎邊塞之議郭欽所以儆晉武也使晉武
能用之則何至有五胡之擾十漸之疏魏
徵所以儆太宗之克終者至矣太宗顧知
納之而不能從其有征遼之悔何恠哉十
事之要姚崇所以儆玄宗之謹始者至矣
玄宗顧能用之而不能終其有西蜀之行
何過哉仁宗開天章閣以訪治道固亦知

矣是故衆建諸侯之策賈誼所以儆漢文
也使漢文能聽之則何至有七國之變從
戎邊塞之議郭欽所以儆晉武也使晉武
能用之則何至有五胡之擾十漸之疏魏
徵所以儆大宗之克終者至矣太宗顧知
納之而不能從其有征遼之悔何怪哉十
事之要姚崇所以儆玄宗之謹始者至矣
玄宗顧能用之而不能終其有西蜀之行
何過哉仁宗開天章閣以訪治道固亦知
punctuated:
業，如守巨室然，必固其堂基，壯其柱石，強其棟梁，高其垣墉，嚴其扃鑰；欹者扶之，敝者補之，日省月視，常以頹壞為虞，則亘千載猶一日也。民生安，人才育，所以為固堂基計者，則誠當矣。然柱石可弗壯乎？棟梁可弗強乎？垣墉可弗高乎？扃鑰可弗嚴乎？此亦今之當慮者，獨不可一致其儆，而豫為之處邪？雖然，臣知所儆而進言者固不易，君知所儆而用言者尤不易，盖自古然矣。
是故眾建諸侯之策，賈誼所以儆漢文也。使漢文能聽之，則何至有七國之變？徙戎邊塞之議，郭欽所以儆晉武也。使晉武能用之，則何至有五胡之擾？十漸之疏，魏徵所以儆太宗之克終者至矣。太宗顧知納之而不能從，其有征遼之悔，何恠哉？十事之要，姚崇所以儆玄宗之謹始者至矣。玄宗顧能用之而不能終，其有西蜀之行，何過哉？仁宗開天章閣以訪治道，固亦知
translation_en:
…the work of preserving an age of peace is like maintaining a great house. One must secure its foundations, strengthen its pillars and stone supports, reinforce its beams, raise its enclosing walls, and make its locks and bolts secure. Whatever leans must be propped up; whatever is worn must be repaired. Inspecting it daily and examining it monthly, always taking precautions against collapse and decay, one can keep it unchanged for a thousand years. Securing the people's livelihood and nurturing talented men are indeed proper measures for making the foundations firm. Yet may the pillars and stone supports go unstrengthened? May the beams go unreinforced? May the walls go unraised? May the locks and bolts go unsecured? These too are matters that demand concern today. Should we not likewise take warning and make provision for them beforehand? Nevertheless, it is certainly difficult for a minister to recognize what calls for vigilance and offer advice; it is still more difficult for a ruler to recognize it and act upon that advice. This has been so since antiquity.
Thus Jia Yi's proposal to establish numerous feudal princes was his means of warning Emperor Wen of Han. Had Emperor Wen heeded it, how could the Rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms have occurred? Guo Qin's proposal to relocate the Rong peoples to the frontier was his means of warning Emperor Wu of Jin. Had Emperor Wu adopted it, how could the disturbances of the Five Hu peoples have occurred? In his memorial on the ten gradual changes, Wei Zheng went to the utmost in admonishing Emperor Taizong to carry his good rule through to the end. Yet Taizong knew to accept the memorial but could not follow its advice. What wonder, then, that he came to regret his expedition against Liaodong? In his ten essential measures, Yao Chong went to the utmost in admonishing Emperor Xuanzong to exercise care at the outset. Yet Xuanzong could adopt them but could not sustain them to the end. What fault was there, then, in his journey to western Shu [?]? Emperor Renzong opened the Tianzhang Pavilion to seek counsel on the way to govern; he too certainly knew…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
所儆者矣范文十事之條陳胡既行而復
罷此慶曆之所以止於慶曆也神宗銳意
圖治不知所儆者能之乎呂誨新參之彈
文胡雖知而不用此熙寧之所以為熙寧
也夫以諸臣之賢其所事者又皆一時之
英主乃或知之而不能用或用之而不能
終此愚所以謂保治之要必在君臣之交
儆如有虞斷斷乎不可易也仰惟
聖天子在上運持盈之道賢公卿在下盡輔佐
===
之力釐正弊端圖惟治理太平無疆之盛
天下方拭目焉愚言雖贅然亦杞人之誠
之不能已也
alt_text:
所儆者矣余 文于事之條陳胡既行而復
罷此慶曆之 所以止於慶曆也神宗銳意
圖治不知所儆者能之乎呂誨新衆之彈
文胡雖知而不用此熙寧之所以為熙寧
也夫以諸臣之賢其所事者又皆一時之
英主乃或知之而不能用或用之而不能
終此愚所以謂保治之要必在君臣之交
儆如有虞斷斷乎不可易也仰惟
聖天子在上運持盈之道賢公卿在下盡輔佐
之功釐正弊端圖惟治理本乎無疆之盛
天下方拭目焉愚言雖贅然亦杞人之誠
之不能已也
punctuated:
所儆者矣。范文十事之條陳，胡既行而復罷？此慶曆之所以止於慶曆也。神宗銳意圖治，不知所儆者能之乎？呂誨新參之彈文，胡雖知而不用？此熙寧之所以為熙寧也。夫以諸臣之賢，其所事者又皆一時之英主，乃或知之而不能用，或用之而不能終，此愚所以謂保治之要必在君臣之交儆，如有虞，斷斷乎不可易也。
仰惟聖天子在上，運持盈之道；賢公卿在下，盡輔佐之力，釐正弊端，圖惟治理。太平無疆之盛，天下方拭目焉。愚言雖贅，然亦杞人之誠之不能已也。
translation_en:
…what to guard against. Why were Fan Wen’s [?] ten proposals implemented only to be abandoned? This is why the achievements of the Qingli era went no further than Qingli itself. Emperor Shenzong resolutely sought good government; could he have done so without knowing what to guard against [?]? Why, although aware of Lü Hui’s impeachment of the newly appointed participant in determining governmental matters, did he fail to act upon it? This is what made the Xining era what it was. Those ministers were worthy men, and the rulers they served were all outstanding sovereigns of their times. Yet some rulers understood their advice but could not put it into practice; others put it into practice but could not carry it through. This is why I say that the essential means of preserving good government must lie in ruler and ministers admonishing one another, as under the sovereign of Yu, Shun. This principle most assuredly cannot be changed.
Looking reverently upward, I reflect that our sage Son of Heaven above practices the way of sustaining prosperity, while the worthy dukes and ministers below devote their utmost efforts to assisting him, correcting abuses and planning good government. All under Heaven now eagerly await the flourishing of boundless peace. Though my words may be superfluous, they spring from a sincerity that cannot be suppressed, like that of the man of Qi who feared the sky would fall.

title: 正德六年會試錄

會試錄後序
正德六年春二月禮部會試
天下士
上特命大學士臣忠主試事而臣
貴亦濫與焉事竣僉以兹所
得士行對
大廷第進士則服有官政公卿
===

會試錄後序

正德六年春二月，禮部會試天下士。上特命大學士臣忠主試事，而臣貴亦濫與焉。事竣，僉以兹所得士行對大廷，第進士，則服有官政，公卿輔相寔自兹始。乃刻其姓氏，并其文之尤粹者為錄，以獻，且以傳示天下。臣貴宜序其後。

竊惟自古帝王代天理物，以圖天下之治，未有不以得天下之才為急者。顧其取之之制，代各不同，然莫有重于
translation_en:
Postface to the Metropolitan Examination Record

In the second month of spring in the sixth year of Zhengde [1511], the Ministry of Rites conducted the Metropolitan Examination for scholars from throughout the realm. His Majesty specially commanded Grand Secretary Zhong, his servant, to preside over the examination, and I, his servant Gui, unworthily participated as well. When the work was completed, all considered that the scholars selected on this occasion would soon answer questions at the imperial court and be ranked as metropolitan graduates (jinshi), thereafter undertaking the duties of government office. Indeed, it is from this point that the careers of high ministers and chief councillors begin. Their names, together with the finest of their writings, were therefore engraved for printing as a record, to be presented to His Majesty and also circulated throughout the realm. It falls to me, your servant Gui, to supply its postface.

I humbly reflect that, since antiquity, emperors and kings have governed all things on Heaven’s behalf to bring order to the realm. None has failed to regard securing the talents of the realm as an urgent task. Yet the institutions by which they recruited such men have differed from age to age. Nevertheless, none has been more important than…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
進士一途焉蓋天下之選也
夫天下之選固將以天下之
士望之而天下士豈易言哉
然士不以是自期則亦不足
以為士矣我
太祖高皇帝之有天下首表章六
經使聖賢脩齊治平之道一
===
===
旦大明于世學校非此不以
教科目非此不以取凡詞賦
一切不根之說悉屏不用
太宗文皇帝又修性理大全諸書
以嘉惠四方則夫以天下士
望于天下之學者固我
聖祖

進士一途焉盖天下之選也
夫天下之選固將以天下之
士望之而天下士豈易言哉
然士不以是自期則亦不足
以為士矣我
太祖高皇帝之有天下首表章六
經使聖賢脩齊治平之道一
===
旦大明于世學校非此不以
教科目非此不以取凡詞賦
一切不根之説悉屏不用
太宗文皇帝又修性理大全諸書
以嘉惠四方則夫以天下士
望于天下之學者固我
聖祖
punctuated: 進士一途焉，蓋天下之選也。夫天下之選，固將以天下之士望之，而天下士豈易言哉？然士不以是自期，則亦不足以為士矣。我太祖高皇帝之有天下，首表章六經，使聖賢脩齊治平之道一旦大明于世。學校非此不以教，科目非此不以取。凡詞賦、一切不根之說，悉屏不用。太宗文皇帝又修性理大全諸書，以嘉惠四方，則夫以天下士望于天下之學者，固我聖祖
translation_en:
…the path of the metropolitan graduate (jinshi), for it selects the finest men of the realm. Those selected from throughout the realm are surely expected to be scholars worthy of the whole realm; yet how could such a designation be lightly bestowed? Nevertheless, scholars who do not set this standard for themselves are unworthy even of being called scholars.

When our Emperor Gao, Taizu, came to rule All under Heaven, he first gave prominence to the Six Classics, causing the way of the sages and worthies—cultivating oneself, ordering the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to All under Heaven—to shine forth throughout the world. Schools taught only on this basis, and the examinations selected men only on this basis. Verse and rhapsodies, together with all unfounded doctrines, were entirely excluded from use. Emperor Wen, Taizong, further commissioned the compilation of the Great Compendium of Human Nature and Principle (Xingli daquan) and other works, bestowing his beneficence upon the four quarters. Thus, to expect the realm’s students to become scholars worthy of the whole realm was indeed what our sagely progenitor…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
祖宗之意也天生斯民其左右輔
翼之責寔惟賢智是託故凡
天下民物有一不得其所君
子必怵惕惻隱思有以濟之
盖非特其道當然而其責亦
有不容辭者則學而至於稱
天下士以慰斯民之望者亦
===
上天之意也嗚呼士之自挾
者其重如此而顧於科目焉
求之今日之事其關於天下
之治不亦大哉臣以是懼校
閱之際惟慎惟勤務求其人
以仰副我
皇上側席之心以為恢弘治道之

天下士以慰斯民之望者亦
===
上天之意也嗚呼士之自挾
者其重如此而顧於科目焉
求之今日之事其關於天下
之治不亦大哉〔臣〕以是懼校
閱之際惟慎惟勤務求其人
以仰副我
皇上側席之心以為恢弘治道之
punctuated:
祖宗之意也。天生斯民，其左右輔翼之責，寔惟賢智是託。故凡天下民物有一不得其所，君子必怵惕惻隱，思有以濟之。盖非特其道當然，而其責亦有不容辭者。則學而至於稱天下士，以慰斯民之望者，亦上天之意也。
嗚呼！士之自挾者，其重如此，而顧於科目焉求之。今日之事，其關於天下之治，不亦大哉？臣以是懼，校閱之際，惟慎惟勤，務求其人，以仰副我皇上側席之心，以為恢弘治道之
translation_en:
…the intention of the imperial ancestors. Heaven gives birth to these people and entrusts responsibility for supporting and assisting them to the worthy and wise alone. Thus, whenever any person or thing under Heaven fails to find its proper place, the gentleman must feel alarm and compassion and consider how to bring relief. This is not merely what his Way requires: it is also a responsibility he cannot decline. That one should learn until one merits being called a scholar of the realm, thereby fulfilling these people's hopes, is likewise Heaven's intention.
Alas! So weighty is what scholars bear within themselves, yet it is through the examinations that we seek such men. Is not the business before us today of great consequence for the governance of the realm? Your servant is therefore apprehensive. In assessing the papers, I have been cautious and diligent, striving to find the right men, so as to fulfill Your Majesty's eager desire for worthy talent and to contribute to the broadening and advancement of the Way of governance…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
助雖其一日之文若不足以
盡其所蘊而其終身志嚮之
所在固亦可以預卜而前知
也根茂者其實遂膏沃者其
光曄乃若言不本於道而能
自顯於人人者世寧有是哉
或謂以文取士類多大言無
===
當竊以為未然夫伊尹堯舜
君民之志見於應聘數語傅
說四海仰德之功見于對揚
三篇而謂言不足以得士而
可乎諸士子既登名是錄天
下之人望之誠有若景星鳳
凰之為瑞者不以天下士自

勛雖其一日之文若不足以
盡其所蘊而其終身志嚮之
所在固亦可以預卜而前知
也根茂者其實遂膏沃者其
光曄乃若言不本於道而能
自顯於人人者世寧有是哉

===

punctuated: 助。雖其一日之文若不足以盡其所蘊，而其終身志嚮之所在，固亦可以預卜而前知也。根茂者其實遂，膏沃者其光曄。乃若言不本於道而能自顯於人人者，世寧有是哉？或謂以文取士，類多大言無當，竊以為未然。夫伊尹堯舜君民之志，見於應聘數語；傅說四海仰德之功，見于對揚三篇。而謂言不足以得士，而可乎？諸士子既登名是錄，天下之人望之，誠有若景星鳳凰之為瑞者。不以天下士自
translation_en: …as an aid. Although a composition written in a single day may seem insufficient to reveal all that a man holds within, it nevertheless allows us to foresee the direction of his lifelong aspirations. Where roots flourish, fruit reaches maturity; where oil is abundant, the light shines brightly. But could there truly be anyone in this world whose words are not grounded in the Way, yet who can distinguish himself among men [?]? Some say that selecting scholars through their writing generally yields many whose grand words lack substance. I venture to disagree. Yi Yin’s aspiration to make his ruler a Yao or Shun and his people like theirs appears in the few words with which he responded to the invitation to serve. Fu Yue’s achievement in causing all within the Four Seas to look up to his ruler’s virtue appears in the three chapters of his replies to the king. Can it then be right to say that words are insufficient for identifying worthy scholars? Now that the names of these candidates have been entered in this record, the people of the realm look to them much as they regard an auspicious star or a phoenix as a favorable portent. If they do not regard themselves as scholars bearing responsibility for the realm…

title: 正德六年會試錄
text:
期待而奚以哉所謂天下士
者非他伊傅之徒是也尚以
其著於言者允蹈而實踐之
不徒以膺天下之選為榮而
必以慰天下之望為慊不徒
以得天下之名為幸而必以
成天下之治為難務期格天
===
之宏勳綏民之偉績上與伊
傅並而不得讓焉則人人曉
然知天下士果不出于賢科
之外也顧不偉哉愚不佞謹
以是為諸士子勸

alt_text:
斯待而奚以哉所謂天下士
者非他伊傅之徒是也尚以
其著於言者允蹈而實踐之
不徒以選為榮而
必以慰天下之望為慊不徒
以得天下之名為幸而必以
成天下之治為難務期格天
===
之宏勲綏民之偉績上與伊
傅並而不得讓焉則人人曉
然知天下士果不出于賢科
之外也顧不偉哉愚不佞謹
以是為諸士子勸
掌詹事府事通議大夫吏部
右侍郎兼翰林院學士靳貴
punctuated:
期待，而奚以哉？所謂天下士者，非他，伊傅之徒是也。尚以其著於言者允蹈而實踐之，不徒以膺天下之選為榮，而必以慰天下之望為慊；不徒以得天下之名為幸，而必以成天下之治為難。務期格天之宏勳、綏民之偉績，上與伊傅並，而不得讓焉，則人人曉然知天下士果不出于賢科之外也。顧不偉哉？愚不佞，謹以是為諸士子勸。
掌詹事府事、通議大夫、吏部右侍郎兼翰林院學士靳貴。
translation_en:
…set such expectations for themselves, what else should they aspire to? Those called scholars of the realm are none other than men of the same kind as Yi Yin and Fu Yue. May they faithfully carry out and put into practice what they have expressed in words. Let them not merely take pride in being selected from throughout the realm, but find satisfaction only in fulfilling the realm’s hopes; not merely count themselves fortunate to win renown throughout the realm, but regard bringing good government to the realm as their demanding task. They must strive for great achievements that move Heaven and mighty accomplishments that bring peace to the people, rising to stand alongside Yi Yin and Fu Yue without falling short of them. Then everyone will clearly understand that scholars of the realm indeed come from the examinations for selecting the worthy. Would this not be magnificent? Unworthy and untalented as I am, I respectfully offer these words as encouragement to the candidates.
Jin Gui, in charge of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, Right Vice Minister of Personnel, and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy.
